Unit 1 · Introduction to business management
1.1

What is a business?

Real company case
Innocent Drinks (UK, founded 1999)

Innocent was started by three Cambridge graduates, Richard Reed, Adam Balon and Jon Wright. In 1998 they spent about £500 on fruit, made smoothies and sold them from a stall at a small London music festival. Customers dropped their empty bottles into a bin marked "YES" or "NO" to answer one question: should the three quit their jobs to make smoothies? The YES bin filled up, so they quit and launched in 1999.

Banks and investors were reluctant to back three people with no food-industry experience. A business angel, Maurice Pinto, eventually invested about £250,000. Innocent bought fruit from farms around the world, paid existing bottling firms to make the drinks instead of building its own factory, and sold first through a few London shops, then supermarkets. From the start it promised to give 10% of its profits to charity.

Read more: Innocent Drinks (Wikipedia)

But 1.1 ideas feed AO3 questions elsewhere, e.g. "Recommend whether a start-up like Innocent should accept a large supermarket contract" uses start-up challenges plus finance (3.2) and growth (1.5).

Key terms AO1

Business
An organisation that uses resources to produce goods or services that meet people's needs and wants.
Goods vs services
Goods are physical, tangible products. Services are intangible activities performed for a customer.
Factors of production
The inputs a business uses: land (natural resources), labour (human effort), capital (man-made tools and equipment) and enterprise (the risk-taking and organising).
Added value
The difference between the selling price of a product and the cost of the bought-in materials used to make it.
Needs and wants
Needs are essentials for survival, such as food, water and shelter. Wants are desires beyond those needs, and they are unlimited.
Entrepreneur
A person who identifies an opportunity, organises resources and takes the financial risk of starting a business in return for profit.
Intrapreneur
An employee who acts entrepreneurially inside an existing organisation, developing new products or processes with the firm's resources and risk.
Start-up
A newly established business, usually small and in its first few years of trading.
Sectoral change
A shift in the share of output or employment between the primary, secondary, tertiary and quaternary sectors over time.
Business plan
A document that sets out a firm's objectives, market, marketing, operations, people and financial forecasts. It is used to plan the business and to raise finance (toolkit).
Consumer
The person who uses or consumes a good or service, who may or may not be the person who buys it.
Customer
A person or organisation that buys a good or service from a business.
Producer
A person or business that makes goods or provides services to sell.

The nature of business AO1

Every business converts inputs into outputs that customers value more than the inputs cost. The difference is added value, which pays for wages, overheads and profit.

Inputs: land, labour, capital, enterprise→Process: production, adding value→Outputs: goods and services→Customers pay; revenue

Exam tipThe functions are interdependent. A good answer on any topic shows the knock-on effect: a marketing campaign raises demand, so operations needs more capacity, HR more staff and finance more working capital.
Added value worked example

Say a bottle of Innocent smoothie sells for £2.50 and the bought-in fruit, bottle and label cost £1.00 (illustrative figures). Added value = 2.50 − 1.00 = £1.50 per bottle. Added value is not profit: wages, marketing, rent and other overheads still have to be paid from the £1.50.

Sectoral change and why it matters to businesses (AO2)

Causes

  • As incomes rise, people spend more on services such as tourism, leisure and health, so the tertiary sector grows.
  • Automation and new technology replace many jobs in farming, mining and manufacturing.
  • Globalisation moves manufacturing to countries with lower costs, which is called offshoring.
  • As education levels rise, there are more knowledge workers, which supports growth in the quaternary sector.

Effects on businesses

  • Businesses find new markets and opportunities in services and knowledge-based activities.
  • Firms need staff with different skills, so they must retrain workers or recruit new ones (link to HR planning in 2.1).
  • Industries in decline face falling demand and closures, which can leave structural unemployment in their regions.
  • As factories close (deindustrialisation), the manufacturers that remain have fewer local suppliers to buy from.
Common mistakes with sectors
  • Don't place a whole firm in one sector. Classify each activity instead: growing fruit on Innocent's supplier farms is primary, blending and bottling the drinks is secondary, selling them to shops is tertiary, and developing new recipes is quaternary.
  • Don't describe the quaternary sector as just IT. It covers any knowledge-based activity, such as research, consulting, education and financial analysis.

Entrepreneurship AO2

FeatureEntrepreneurIntrapreneur
SettingStarts a new, independent businessWorks inside an existing organisation
Financial riskPersonal: own savings, loans, possibly unlimited liabilityBorne by the employer
RewardProfit and the value of the businessSalary, bonus, promotion, recognition
ResourcesMust find own finance, staff and premisesUses the firm's brand, money, staff and data

Examples
  • The Innocent founders
  • Founders of Wolt or Airbnb
  • 3M's Post-it Note
  • Gmail from Google's "20% time"
FeatureEntrepreneurIntrapreneur
SettingAn entrepreneur starts a new, independent business.An intrapreneur works inside an existing organisation.
Financial riskThe entrepreneur bears the risk personally, through savings, loans and possibly unlimited liability.The employer bears the financial risk.
RewardThe reward is the profit and the value of the business.The reward is a salary, bonus, promotion or recognition.
ResourcesThe entrepreneur must find their own finance, staff and premises.The intrapreneur uses the firm's brand, money, staff and data.
FreedomThe entrepreneur has full control of decisions.The intrapreneur must work within the company's objectives and approvals.
Examples
  • The Innocent founders are entrepreneurs.
  • So are the founders of Wolt and Airbnb.
  • 3M's Post-it Note came from intrapreneurship.
  • So did Gmail, from Google's "20% time".

Why people become entrepreneurs

  • Financial reasons: running a business can earn more than a job, and the owner builds an asset that can later be sold.
  • Independence: entrepreneurs are their own boss and can choose their own hours.
  • Self-actualisation: they can turn a passion or an idea into reality, which links to the top of Maslow's hierarchy.
  • Necessity: some people start a business because they were made redundant or cannot find a job.
  • Social purpose: some want to solve a social or environmental problem.
  • Spotting a gap: they see an unmet need, a new technology or a trend that others have not yet served.

Characteristics often seen

  • They are willing to take calculated risks.
  • They show initiative and creativity.
  • They are resilient and determined when things go wrong.
  • They have a clear vision and the self-confidence to pursue it.
  • They can lead people and build networks of contacts.
  • They can plan ahead and manage money carefully.
Why entrepreneurship matters (AO2 analysis)Entrepreneurs create jobs, bring innovation and competition (lower prices, better quality), raise tax revenue and can regenerate local areas. For established firms, intrapreneurship keeps innovation alive and helps keep talented staff who might otherwise leave to start their own firms.

Opportunities for start-ups

  • New businesses can serve unmet needs and new trends, such as healthy drinks or sustainable products.
  • Technology lowers the cost of starting up, because online shops, social media and cloud tools are cheap to use.
  • Start-ups can serve niche markets that large firms ignore.
  • Small firms are flexible and fast: they can decide quickly and build close relationships with customers.
  • Governments often help with grants, start-up programmes and tax relief.
  • A partnership with a larger firm, such as getting listed by a supermarket, can bring sales quickly.

Why so many start-ups fail

  • Poor cash-flow management is the most common reason start-ups fail.
  • Overtrading means growing faster than the firm's finance allows, so it runs out of cash.
  • Weak market research means the founders discover too late that there is no real demand.
  • Some start-ups set prices too low because they do not know their full costs.
  • The founder may lack key skills, or burn out from working too hard.
Common mistakes in start-up questions
  • A weak answer says, "Start-ups lack money." A strong answer explains the cause and the effect: "Because Innocent had no trading record, banks saw it as high-risk, so the founders depended on one business angel's £250,000, which limited how fast they could grow."
  • Don't confuse a cash-flow problem with being unprofitable. Innocent could make a profit on paper but still run short of cash if supermarkets pay weeks after delivery (see 3.7).
The case in brief: Innocent
  • Test demand cheaply: they spent about £500 on fruit before deciding whether to quit their jobs.
  • Start-up finance gap: banks and investors were reluctant, so a £250,000 business angel filled it for a share of the firm.
  • Low fixed costs: they paid existing bottlers instead of building a factory.

Exam corner: 1.1

Exam tips

  • Define the term first, then apply it with numbers from the case, such as Innocent's £500 of fruit, the angel investor's £250,000 and the 10% of profits given to charity.
  • When a question asks you to explain a challenge, give its cause, its effect on the firm and the consequence that follows.
  • Link start-up problems to finance (3.2 and 3.7) and to marketing (4.2) for richer analysis.

Common pitfalls

  • Don't treat added value as profit. Added value is the selling price minus the cost of bought-in materials, and the firm's other costs still have to be paid out of it.
  • Don't write an AO3 judgement in an AO2 "explain" question, because it earns no extra marks and wastes time.
  • Don't list many challenges without developing any of them. Two well-explained points score more than five listed ones.
  • Don't mix up an entrepreneur and an intrapreneur. An entrepreneur risks their own money, while an intrapreneur develops new ideas inside a firm, using the employer's money.

Model answers

AO1 Define the term entrepreneur. [2]

An entrepreneur is a person who identifies a business opportunity and organises the factors of production to exploit it, taking the financial risk in return for possible profit, such as the three Innocent founders quitting their jobs to start the business.

Mark scheme: 1 for organising resources / spotting opportunity; 1 for risk-taking for profit or a clear example.

AO2 Explain two challenges Innocent faced as a start-up. [4]

K Start-ups often struggle with cash flow because costs are paid before revenue arrives. App Innocent had to buy fruit and pay its bottlers before shops paid for the drinks, E so without the angel investment the founders could not have bought enough stock to supply new shops, even though demand was strong.

K New firms also face strong competition from established businesses with brand loyalty. App Big drinks firms already sold juices and smoothies, E and their economies of scale let them charge lower prices and pay for wide distribution, so Innocent had to differentiate with 100% fruit recipes and a friendly, chatty brand to justify a higher price.

Mark scheme: 1 for each relevant challenge explained; 1 for each applied to Innocent.

AO2 Analyse how sectoral change created opportunities for Innocent. [6]

K Sectoral change is the shift of output and jobs from primary and secondary activities towards tertiary and quaternary ones as incomes rise. App E The UK, like most high-income economies, has a very large tertiary sector, which gives Innocent many outlets: supermarkets, cafés, offices and online grocers. As incomes rise, demand for convenient, healthy drinks grows, so Innocent could widen distribution from a few London shops to supermarkets and then to other countries.

E Growth of the quaternary sector also helps. Sales data from supermarkets and online grocers lets a firm like Innocent track which recipes sell where, cutting the cost of market research. E However, Innocent still relies on primary producers such as fruit farms around the world, so poor harvests or rising commodity prices raise its costs, showing that its supply chain spans all four sectors.

Mark scheme: up to 2 for understanding sectoral change; up to 4 for two developed, applied points.

Practice questions (tap to reveal the marking points)

AO1 State the four factors of production. [2]
Land, labour, capital, enterprise (2 marks for all four; 1 for two or three).
AO1 Describe the term added value. [2]
Selling price minus the cost of bought-in materials (1); it pays for other costs and profit / example (1).
AO2 Distinguish between an entrepreneur and an intrapreneur. [4]
Entrepreneur: starts own business, bears personal risk (2). Intrapreneur: innovates within an existing firm, employer bears risk (2). Explicit contrast required.
AO2 Explain two opportunities for starting a business in the quaternary sector. [4]
Low start-up capital (laptop, cloud); growing demand for data and digital services; can sell globally online; high margins on intellectual property. 2 marks each, applied.
AO2 Analyse the role of each business function in helping Innocent grow from a festival stall to supermarket shelves. [6]
Operations: enough bottling capacity, consistent quality. Finance: working capital to buy fruit before retailers pay. Marketing: price, packaging, brand voice. HR: hiring staff as sales grow. Credit links between functions.
1.2

Types of business entities

Real company case
Innocent Drinks: changing legal form as it grew

Innocent (from 1.1) shows how one business can move through several types of ownership. The founders set up a private limited company (Fresh Trading Ltd), so limited liability protected their personal savings. To fund growth they sold part of the company to a business angel, Maurice Pinto.

As Innocent spread across Europe it needed far more money and distribution power. In 2009 it sold a minority stake to Coca-Cola, a publicly held company listed on the New York Stock Exchange, for about £30 million. Coca-Cola became the majority owner in 2010 and owned over 90% by 2013. Innocent still gives 10% of its profits to charity, mostly through the Innocent Foundation, and in 2018 it became a certified B Corporation, a label for companies that meet standards on social and environmental performance.

Read more: Innocent Drinks (Wikipedia) · B Corporation (Wikipedia)

What the AO ceiling means for youLegal forms are AO3, so expect "Discuss whether Innocent's founders were right to sell a majority stake to Coca-Cola" for 10 marks. Use the criteria below (liability, finance, control, continuity, privacy, cost) and judge against the owner's objectives.

Key terms AO1

Private sector
Organisations owned and controlled by private individuals or shareholders, usually aiming for profit.
Public sector
Organisations owned and controlled by the government, providing goods and services for the public.
Unlimited liability
The owners are personally responsible for all the business's debts, so their personal assets can be taken to pay them.
Limited liability
The owners can lose only the money they invested, so their personal assets are protected.
Legal personality (incorporation)
A company is a separate legal entity from its owners: it can own assets, sue and be sued, and continues if owners change.
Shareholder
A person or organisation that owns part of a company by holding its shares. Shareholders receive dividends and can vote at the annual general meeting.
Privately held company
A limited company whose shares are not traded on a stock exchange. Shares can only be sold with the agreement of the existing shareholders (for example, a company ending in "Ltd").
Publicly held company
A limited company whose shares can be bought and sold by the public on a stock exchange (e.g. PLC).
Initial public offering (IPO)
When a company first sells its shares to the public on a stock exchange.
Social enterprise
An organisation whose main aim is a social or environmental purpose. It earns revenue by trading and reinvests its surpluses in that purpose.
Cooperative
A business owned and run by its members (workers, customers or producers), each usually with one vote, sharing the profits.
NGO
A non-governmental organisation: non-profit, independent of government, pursuing social or environmental aims, funded by donations, grants and some trading.
Partner
A co-owner of a partnership who shares the capital, decisions, profits and, usually, the liabilities of the business.
Share
A unit of ownership in a company; shareholders own part of the company in proportion to the shares they hold.
Stock exchange
A regulated market where shares in publicly held companies are bought and sold.
Board of directors
The group of people elected by shareholders to set the strategy of a company and oversee its senior managers.
Annual general meeting (AGM)
A yearly meeting at which a company's shareholders can question the directors, vote on resolutions and elect the board.
For-profit social enterprise
A business that earns revenue to meet a social or environmental need and reinvests most of its surplus in that purpose, which may be privately owned, publicly owned or a cooperative.
Non-profit social enterprise
An organisation that meets a social or environmental need and does not distribute any surplus to owners, such as a charity or non-governmental organisation (NGO).
B Corporation (B Corp)
A business that has been certified by the non-profit B Lab as meeting standards of social and environmental performance, transparency and accountability.
Memorandum of association
A document needed to register a company, stating its name, registered address and the people forming it.
Articles of association
A document setting out the internal rules of a company, such as the rights of shareholders and how directors are appointed.

Private vs public sector AO2

Private sectorPublic sector
Owned byIndividuals, partners, shareholders, membersCentral or local government, on behalf of citizens
Main aimsProfit, growth, shareholder value (some also social aims)Public service, access for all, social welfare, strategic control
FinanceOwners' capital, loans, retained profit, share issuesTaxation, government borrowing, user charges
Accountable toOwners and shareholdersGovernment, parliament, voters
ExamplesInnocent Drinks, HSBC, AppleState hospitals, public schools, national electricity or water utilities
Private sectorPublic sector
Owned byIndividuals, partners, shareholders or members own it.Central or local government owns it on behalf of citizens.
Main aimsIt aims for profit, growth and shareholder value, and some firms also have social aims.It aims to serve the public, give access to all, support welfare and keep strategic control.
FinanceIt uses owners' capital, loans, retained profit and share issues.It uses taxation, government borrowing and charges to users.
Accountable toIt answers to its owners and shareholders.It answers to the government, parliament and voters.
ExamplesInnocent Drinks, HSBC and Apple are private sector firms.State hospitals, public schools and national electricity or water utilities are public sector.

Arguments for public ownership

  • The public sector provides essential services, such as healthcare and education, that private firms would under-supply because they are not profitable enough.
  • Public ownership can control natural monopolies, such as a water network, where competition makes little sense.
  • It can protect strategic industries and the jobs that depend on them.

Arguments for private ownership

  • The profit motive pushes private firms to be efficient and to innovate.
  • Competition between private firms gives consumers more choice and lower prices.
  • Private ownership reduces the burden on taxpayers.

Privatisation moves organisations from public to private ownership; nationalisation does the reverse. Public-private partnerships share projects (e.g. a privately built hospital run under government contract).

Moving from sole trader to company: gains

  • Limited liability protects the founders' homes and savings if the business fails.
  • A company can sell shares to investors more easily: Innocent sold a stake to a business angel.
  • Being a company gives the business more status and credibility with large customers such as supermarkets.
  • A company has continuity, so it carries on when its founders leave, as Innocent did.

Moving from sole trader to company: costs

  • Setting up a company costs money for registration and accounting, and its accounts must be filed publicly.
  • The founders must share profits, and possibly control, with the new investors.
  • Decisions can become slower if shareholders disagree.
  • The owners have less privacy, because some financial information becomes public.
Divorce of ownership and controlIn large publicly held companies, shareholders own the firm but directors and managers run it. Managers may chase growth or salaries while shareholders want dividends (link to stakeholder conflict, 1.4).
Key points
  • An IPO (initial public offering) is when a company first sells shares to the public on a stock exchange.
  • A publicly held company must publish its accounts and hold an annual general meeting.
  • Separation of ownership and control: in large companies, shareholders own the firm but directors run it, and their goals can differ.

  • One member one vote

Democratic, motivated members, fair distribution, strong loyaltySlow decisions, limited capital (members only), may lack professional managementMondragon (Spain), producer co-operatives in fair-trade supply chains
NGO (non-profit social enterprise)
  • Independent of government, no owners taking profit
  • Funded by donations, grants and trading
Public trust, tax benefits, volunteers, focus on missionUnstable funding, donor dependence, may lack business skills, accountability concernsMédecins Sans Frontières, Oxfam, WWF
TypeHow it worksStrengthsWeaknessesExample
Private sector company (for-profit social enterprise)
  • A company pursues a social mission alongside profit.
  • Most profit is reinvested in the mission.
  • It has business discipline.
  • It can raise investment.
  • It can sustain itself without donations.
  • Profit and purpose can pull against each other.
  • The mission may drift.
Patagonia's founder transferred its ownership to a trust and a non-profit in 2022.
Public sector company (for-profit social enterprise)A government-owned company trades commercially and returns surpluses for public benefit.
  • It serves all citizens.
  • It takes a long-term view.
  • It can charge fair prices.
  • Politicians may interfere.
  • There is less pressure to be efficient.
Some state-owned utilities and postal services work this way.
Cooperative (for-profit social enterprise)
  • Members own it: workers, consumers or producers.
  • Each member has one vote.
  • Profits are shared or reinvested.
  • Decisions are democratic.
  • Members are motivated and loyal.
  • Profit is shared fairly.
  • Decisions are slow.
  • Capital is limited to what members provide.
  • It may lack professional managers.
Mondragon in Spain and fair-trade producer cooperatives are examples.
NGO (non-profit social enterprise)
  • It is independent of government, and no owners take profit.
  • Donations, grants and trading fund it.
  • The public trusts it.
  • It gets tax benefits and volunteers.
  • It stays focused on its mission.
  • Funding is unstable.
  • It depends on donors.
  • It may lack business skills.
  • Its accountability can be questioned.
Médecins Sans Frontières, Oxfam and WWF are examples.

Evaluating social enterprises (AO3)

  • Does the social enterprise achieve its mission? Its success should be measured by its social impact, not just its profit.
  • Is it financially sustainable without relying on grants?
  • Can it compete on price with rivals that only aim for profit?
  • Does its purpose attract motivated staff (link to motivation in 2.4)?
  • Many social enterprises judge themselves on a triple bottom line: people, planet and profit.

Link to Paper 3 (HL)

Paper 3 is a case study on a social enterprise. You will analyse its human resource needs and recommend a decision, so knowing how cooperatives and NGOs raise money and make decisions directly earns marks there.

Choosing the right form: decision framework AO3

Question to askPoints towards
How much finance is needed?
  • Small: sole trader/partnership. Large: company
  • Very large: publicly held
How much risk is involved?High risk: limited liability (company)
How important is control and privacy?High: sole trader or privately held company
Are extra skills needed?Partnership or bringing in shareholders
Is the main aim social?Cooperative, social enterprise company or NGO
Will the business need to outlive the founder?Company (continuity)
Question to askPoints towards
How much finance is needed?
  • A small sum suits a sole trader or partnership.
  • A large sum needs a company.
  • A very large sum needs a publicly held company.
How much risk is involved?High risk calls for limited liability, so a company.
How important is control and privacy?If control and privacy matter most, a sole trader or privately held company fits.
Are extra skills needed?Extra skills point to a partnership or to bringing in shareholders.
Is the main aim social?A social aim points to a cooperative, a social enterprise company or an NGO.
Will the business need to outlive the founder?A company continues after the founder leaves, so it suits a business that must outlive them.
The case in brief: Innocent
  • Limited liability and control: it began as a private limited company.
  • Growth needs finance: it needed more money and distribution, so it sold a stake to Coca-Cola for about £30 million.
  • Trade-off: the founders lost control, as Coca-Cola owned over 90% by 2013.

Exam corner: 1.2

Exam tips

  • Always compare the current legal form with the proposed one, rather than describing only one form.
  • Use the owner's objectives, such as keeping control, growing or acting ethically, to decide which form suits them.
  • Quantify your points from the case, for example about £250,000 from an angel investor in 1999 compared with about £30 million for Coca-Cola's first stake in 2009.
  • Mention the short-term costs, such as fees and administration, as well as the long-term benefits, such as growth and protection.

Common pitfalls

  • Don't say that a private limited company is in the public sector. The public and private sectors are about whether the government owns the organisation, not about shares.
  • Don't say that a public limited company is owned by the government. It is owned by private shareholders, and its shares can be bought by the public.
  • Don't claim that NGOs cannot make a surplus. They can make a surplus, but they reinvest it in their cause instead of paying it to owners.
  • Remember that limited liability makes banks more cautious about lending to small companies, so they often ask the owners for personal guarantees.

Model answers

AO2 Distinguish between the private sector and the public sector. [4]

The private sector consists of organisations owned by individuals or shareholders, mainly aiming to make a profit, such as Innocent Drinks. The public sector consists of organisations owned and controlled by the government, which mainly aim to provide services to citizens, such as state hospitals. The key difference is ownership and purpose: private firms are accountable to owners and funded by capital and profit, while public organisations are accountable to government and funded mainly by taxation.

Mark scheme: 1+1 for each sector defined with example; 2 for an explicit contrast.

AO3 Discuss whether operating as a private limited company, and later selling a majority to Coca-Cola, was right for Innocent. [10]

K A sole trader is owned by one person with unlimited liability, while a privately held company is a separate legal entity owned by shareholders with limited liability, whose shares are not sold to the public.

App E Innocent needed money for stock, marketing and expansion into new countries, far more than three founders could provide. As a private limited company it could sell shares to a business angel and later to Coca-Cola, and lenders are more willing to deal with an incorporated business that files accounts. Limited liability also protected the founders' personal assets if expansion failed.

E Incorporation also brings continuity and credibility: supermarket buyers prefer a registered company as a long-term supplier, and the business could carry on after the founders left.

E However, the founders gave up control. Each share sale gave the new owners votes, and once Coca-Cola held a majority it could, in principle, overrule decisions on prices, recipes or the 10%-of-profits pledge. A company must also file accounts publicly, so it loses some privacy.

Ev Overall, becoming a private limited company was essential once Innocent grew beyond a market stall, because the scale of finance and risk made limited liability and share capital necessary. Selling a majority to Coca-Cola is a harder judgement: it brought money and global distribution, but some customers felt an ethical brand had sold out to a multinational. Whether it was right depends on the founders' objectives: if the aim was to reach as many people as possible, the sale fits; if independence was central to the brand, it did not.

Why this reaches 9–10: clear definitions, case numbers integrated, balanced points for and against, judgement conditional on the growth decision, practical safeguard (majority shareholding).

Practice questions (tap to reveal the marking points)

AO1 Define limited liability. [2]
Owners' responsibility for debts is limited to their investment (1); personal assets protected (1).
AO2 Explain two disadvantages for the three Innocent founders of running the business as a partnership rather than a company. [4]
Unlimited (joint) liability; disagreements over decisions; profit sharing; continuity if a partner leaves. 2 each, applied.
AO3 Evaluate whether a cooperative structure suits dairy farmers, using Arla Foods, a dairy company owned by thousands of farmers in northern Europe. [10]
For: bulk buying and selling power, shared costs, democratic, fair share of profits, member loyalty. Against: slow decisions, limited capital, free-riders, lack of professional management. Judgement with conditions.
AO3 To what extent should a large private hospital group become a publicly held company? [10]
Capital for expansion, status, liquidity for owners vs loss of control, takeover risk, short-term shareholder pressure possibly conflicting with patient care, cost of IPO and disclosure.
AO3 Discuss the advantages and disadvantages for an NGO of relying on donations. [10]
Free income, public trust, tax benefits vs unpredictability, donor influence on priorities, competition for donations; compare with trading income or grants.
1.3

Business objectives

Real company case
H&M Group (Sweden)

H&M Group is a Swedish clothing retailer with thousands of stores in more than 70 markets and brands including H&M, COS and Weekday. Its stated business idea is "fashion and quality at the best price in a sustainable way". It faces fierce competition from Inditex (Zara) and from ultra-cheap online sellers such as Shein and Temu.

Much of its clothing is made by supplier factories in countries such as Bangladesh, where low wages keep costs down but safety and working conditions are closely watched, especially since the Rana Plaza factory collapse in 2013 killed more than 1,100 garment workers. H&M was one of the first brands to sign the Bangladesh Accord on fire and building safety. It has set a goal for all its materials to be recycled or more sustainably sourced by 2030, collects used clothes in its stores, and owns a majority of the resale platform Sellpy. Critics argue that selling huge volumes of cheap clothing sits uneasily with sustainability claims.

Read more: H&M (Wikipedia) · Rana Plaza collapse (Wikipedia)

Syllabus map

Syllabus pointHighest AOYou must be able toTypical command terms

Key terms AO1

Vision statement
A long-term, aspirational description of what the organisation wants to become or achieve.
Mission statement
A statement of the organisation's purpose now: what it does, for whom and how, guided by its values.
Aim
A broad, general intention. Objectives are specific, measurable targets that help achieve aims.
Strategic objective
A long-term (usually 3+ years), organisation-wide target set by senior management.
Tactical objective
A short- to medium-term target, often for a department, that helps achieve a strategic objective.
Operational objective
A day-to-day target for individuals or teams. This is a useful extra term that the guide does not name.
Shareholder value
The return to shareholders from dividends and rises in share price.
Ethical objective
A target based on moral principles, beyond what the law requires (fair pay, sustainability, honest marketing).
Corporate social responsibility (CSR)
A business voluntarily taking responsibility for the impact of its activities on stakeholders, society and the environment.
SMART
Objectives that are Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant and Time-bound.

Vision and mission statements AO2

Vision statementMission statement
Question answered"Where do we want to be?""Why do we exist and what do we do?"
Time frameLong term, futurePresent, ongoing
StyleInspirational, broadPractical, describes purpose, customers and values
AudienceMainly internal: inspires staff and leadersInternal and external: customers, investors, staff
ExampleIKEA: "To create a better everyday life for the many people"IKEA: offer well-designed, functional home furnishings "at prices so low that as many people as possible will be able to afford them"
Vision statementMission statement
Question answeredIt answers "Where do we want to be?"It answers "Why do we exist and what do we do?"
Time frameIt looks to the long-term future.It describes the present and ongoing work.
StyleIt is inspirational and broad.It is practical and describes purpose, customers and values.
AudienceIt mainly inspires staff and leaders inside the firm.It speaks to customers, investors and staff, inside and outside.
ExampleIKEA's vision is "to create a better everyday life for the many people".IKEA's mission is to offer well-designed, functional home furnishings at prices so low that as many people as possible can afford them.

Benefits

  • A clear vision and mission give everyone in the business a shared sense of direction and purpose.
  • They guide strategic decisions, because managers can ask whether an option fits the mission.
  • They can motivate staff and attract employees who share the same values.
  • They communicate the firm's values to customers and investors.

Limitations

  • Statements are often vague or generic: they are easy to write but hard to live by.
  • They can become public-relations slogans that do not change how the firm behaves.
  • They can conflict with objectives, for example when a sustainability promise clashes with pressure to cut costs.
  • They need updating as the business changes.

Common business objectives AO2

Growth

Increasing size: sales, market share, stores, employees or countries.

Why firms pursue it
  • Growth brings economies of scale, which lower unit costs (see 1.5).
  • A larger firm has more market power and is safer from takeover.
  • Managers of larger firms gain more status and higher pay.
Risks
  • Growing too fast can lead to overtrading.
  • The firm may suffer diseconomies of scale.
  • It may lose its brand identity.

Profit

Revenue minus costs; the reward for risk and the main source of internal finance.

Variants
  • Profit maximisation means earning the highest possible profit.
  • Profit satisficing means making enough profit to keep the owners content while pursuing other goals.

Note: start-ups often aim to survive or break even first.

Protecting shareholder value

Maintaining dividends and the share price so owners are rewarded.

How
  • The firm aims for steady profit growth and pays dividends or buys back shares, which supports the share price.
  • It avoids risky decisions that could damage its reputation and its share price.
Risk
  • Managers may become short-termist, cutting investment or R&D to boost this year's figures.

Ethical objectives

Acting in a morally right way beyond legal requirements.

Examples
  • The firm makes sure that workers in its supply chain are paid fairly.
  • It uses sustainable materials and cuts its emissions.
  • It markets its products honestly and protects customers' data.

Trade-off: higher costs vs brand loyalty, motivation and lower risk of scandal.

Why objectives change (AO2)Objectives shift with the internal and external environment: a new CEO, a recession (survival over growth), a scandal (ethics), stronger competition, new technology, or a move from private to publicly held status (shareholder value). In 2022, as costs rose and rivals competed hard, H&M Group launched a cost-cutting programme, shifting weight from growth to cost control.

Evaluating objectives (AO3)Ask: are they SMART? Consistent with the mission and with each other (growth vs ethics)? Realistic given finance and the external environment? Owned by the people who must deliver them? Flexible enough to change if conditions change?

Corporate social responsibility AO3

Benefits of CSR

  • CSR can strengthen the brand image and customer loyalty, which may let the firm charge a premium price.
  • It attracts and motivates staff who want meaningful work (link to motivation in 2.4).
  • It attracts ethical investors and lowers the risk of scandals, fines and boycotts.
  • It improves relations with the government and the local community.
  • It can save money, for example by using less energy and producing less waste.

Costs and problems

  • CSR raises costs, for example through fair wages, certified materials and audits.
  • Profit may fall in the short term, which can cause conflict with shareholders.
  • The social and environmental impact is hard to measure.
  • If the firm exaggerates its claims, it may be accused of greenwashing.
  • Competitors that do not spend on CSR may be able to undercut its prices.
Approach to CSR (useful extra)Attitude
Self-interest
  • Only what the law requires
  • Profit is the only responsibility
AltruisticGives back to society through donations and sponsorship
StrategicCSR used because it also benefits the business (brand, staff, efficiency)
Ethical / responsibleBuilt into the core of the business model regardless of profit
Approach to CSR (useful extra)Attitude
Self-interest
  • The firm does only what the law requires.
  • It sees profit as its only responsibility.
AltruisticThe firm gives back to society through donations and sponsorship.
StrategicThe firm uses CSR because it also benefits the business, through its brand, staff or efficiency.
Ethical / responsibleThe firm builds responsibility into its core business model, whatever the effect on profit.
Why CSR expectations change
  • Social media spreads scandals quickly.
  • Younger consumers and employees care more about sustainability.
  • Regulations are tightening, for example the EU's sustainability reporting rules.
  • Investors now judge firms on ESG (environmental, social and governance) criteria.
Two views of CSR
  • Shareholder view (Friedman): a firm's duty is to make profit within the law.
  • Stakeholder view: a firm has duties to everyone it affects, and acting responsibly protects profit in the long run.
  • Expectations keep rising because of social media, younger consumers, new regulations and ESG investors.
The case in brief: H&M
  • Conflicting aims: low prices and sustainability pull against each other under fierce competition.
  • Supply-chain risk: Rana Plaza killed over 1,100 workers, which damaged every brand involved.
  • Judge the evidence: a measurable 2030 materials target is real progress, but critics argue fast fashion cannot be sustainable.

Exam corner: 1.3

Exam tips

  • Distinguish vision from mission with a time word: the vision is about the future, while the mission is about what the firm does now.
  • Test any stated objective against the SMART criteria and against the firm's mission.
  • In CSR questions, separate the short-term cost from the long-term benefit.
  • Name the stakeholders who gain and those who lose (link to 1.4).

Common pitfalls

  • Don't treat the vision and the mission as the same thing.
  • Don't say that profit is the objective of every organisation. NGOs, cooperatives and public-sector bodies have other main aims.
  • Don't call a legal requirement CSR. CSR is voluntary and goes beyond what the law requires.
  • Don't write a one-sided CSR answer that ignores the cost.

Model answers

AO2 Distinguish between a strategic and a tactical objective. [4]

A strategic objective is a long-term, organisation-wide target set by senior management, such as H&M Group's goal for all its materials to be recycled or more sustainably sourced by 2030. A tactical objective is a shorter-term, often departmental target that helps achieve the strategy, such as placing clothes-collecting bins in its stores to gather used garments for recycling. Tactical objectives are the steps; strategic objectives are the destination.

AO3 Evaluate H&M Group's switch to recycled materials and in-store clothes collection as part of its CSR. [10]

K CSR means a business voluntarily accepts responsibility for its impact on society and the environment, beyond legal requirements.

App E H&M Group's 2030 goal for recycled or more sustainably sourced materials fits its business idea of fashion "in a sustainable way". This strengthens its brand against ultra-cheap online rivals that compete on price alone. Customers and investors who value sustainability may stay loyal, and it prepares the firm for tougher EU rules on textile waste.

E It can also motivate staff who identify with the brand's purpose and attract investors who screen companies on environmental and social performance.

E However, recycled fibres usually cost more and supply is limited, which squeezes margins while Shein and Temu push prices down. Critics also point to a contradiction: a model built on selling huge volumes of cheap clothes creates waste, so the goal may be called greenwashing if total production keeps rising.

Ev Overall, the switch is a sound long-term decision because sustainability is one of the few areas where H&M can stand apart from ultra-cheap rivals, and regulation is moving the same way. It is only credible if progress is measured and reported every year and if H&M also tackles volume, for example through resale (Sellpy), repair and collection. Its success depends on whether customers will pay slightly more, which H&M must keep testing.

Practice questions (tap to reveal the marking points)

AO1 Define mission statement. [2]
A statement of the organisation's current purpose (1), including what it does, for whom and its values (1).
AO2 Explain why a business's objectives might change over time. [4]
Two developed reasons: economic change, competition, change of ownership or leadership, growth stage, scandal or stakeholder pressure. Apply to a firm.
AO2 Explain why protecting shareholder value may conflict with ethical objectives. [4]
Ethical choices raise costs and cut short-term profit/dividends (2); shareholders may push for cheaper suppliers, leading to conflict (2).
AO3 Discuss whether H&M Group's aim of fashion "in a sustainable way" is consistent with selling large volumes of cheap clothing. [10]
SMART analysis; fit with business idea; cost and supply of recycled fibre; competition from ultra-cheap rivals; risk of greenwashing claims vs brand benefits. Conditional judgement.
AO3 To what extent is CSR just a marketing tool? [10]
Strategic CSR and greenwashing examples vs genuine ethical business models; benefits to stakeholders; depends on transparency, measurement and leadership.
1.4

Stakeholders

Real company case
Tesla Gigafactory Berlin-Brandenburg (Germany)

Tesla opened its first European car factory in Grünheide, near Berlin, in 2022. It employs more than 10,000 people. Tesla then planned to expand the site, which meant clearing around 100 hectares of pine forest for a freight yard and warehouses.

In a non-binding local vote in February 2024, a majority of Grünheide's residents voted against the expansion. Environmental activists set up a protest camp in the forest, and residents worried about the factory's water use, because part of the site lies in a drinking-water protection area. In March 2024 an arson attack on a nearby electricity pylon, claimed by a far-left group, cut the factory's power and stopped production for about a week. The local council later approved a smaller expansion that kept more of the forest.

Read more: Gigafactory Berlin-Brandenburg (Wikipedia)

Syllabus pointHighest AOYou must be able toTypical command terms

What the AO ceiling means for you1.4 is AO2: explain and analyse. But stakeholders appear in almost every AO3 answer in the course, because judging "who wins and who loses" is how you evaluate any decision.

Key terms AO1

Stakeholder
An individual or group with an interest in, or affected by, the activities of a business.
Shareholder
An owner of shares in a company. All shareholders are stakeholders, but not all stakeholders are shareholders.
Internal stakeholder
A stakeholder inside the organisation: owners/shareholders, managers, employees.
External stakeholder
A stakeholder outside the organisation: customers, suppliers, lenders, government, local community, pressure groups, competitors.
Pressure group
An organised group that tries to influence business or government decisions (e.g. environmental campaigners).
Stakeholder conflict
When the objectives of different stakeholder groups cannot all be met by the same decision.
Employees
People who work for a business under a contract of employment in return for wages or a salary.
Suppliers
Businesses that provide goods, materials or services to another business.
Lenders
Banks and other organisations that lend money to a business and expect it to be repaid with interest.
Government (as a stakeholder)
National and local authorities that collect taxes from businesses, regulate them and want them to create jobs and economic growth.
Local community
The people and organisations living or working near a business, who are affected by its jobs, traffic, noise and pollution.
Competitors
Other businesses selling the same or similar products in the same market.

  • Growth creates jobs for employees and the community, profit for shareholders and tax revenue for the government.
  • Higher productivity can pay for both pay rises and higher dividends.
  • CSR can satisfy the community while also protecting long-term shareholder value.
  • Paying suppliers reliably helps them and also wins the firm better terms.

How businesses manage conflict

  • The firm communicates and consults early, for example through town-hall meetings.
  • It compromises: in this case, the council approved a smaller expansion that kept more forest and set strict limits on water use.
  • It offers compensation, such as a community fund or a promise to hire locally.
  • It prioritises stakeholders according to their power and interest.
  • It aligns objectives, for example through CSR targets or profit-sharing schemes.
Using stakeholders for evaluation in any topic(1) Name two stakeholders who are affected. (2) Explain how each gains or loses. (3) Decide whose interest is more important here (power, legal duty, long-term reputation). (4) Suggest a compromise that reduces the conflict.
Stakeholder mapping
  • Plot each group by its power to influence the firm and its interest in the decision.
  • High power, high interest: key players, so manage them closely.
  • High power, low interest: keep them satisfied.
  • Low power, high interest: keep them informed and consult them.
  • Low power, low interest: monitor them.
The case in brief: Tesla Grünheide
  • Conflict: shareholders backed clearing 100 hectares of forest, while most residents voted against.
  • Interest is not power: the vote was not binding, although the water-protection risk was real.
  • Cost and resolution: production stopped for a week, and a smaller expansion was the compromise.

Exam corner: 1.4

Exam tips

  • Always name specific groups from the case instead of writing "stakeholders" in general.
  • A conflict question needs two named groups and one specific decision that affects them differently.
  • Show the chain of effects: the decision affects group A in one way, and this harms group B for a stated reason.
  • Mention that stakeholders' interests and power change over time.

Common pitfalls

  • Don't confuse stakeholders with shareholders. Shareholders own the company, and they are only one group of stakeholders.
  • Don't list every stakeholder in a 4-mark question. Choose the two most relevant and develop them.
  • Don't assume that all employees want the same thing.
  • Don't call competitors irrelevant. They are external stakeholders.

Model answers

AO1 Distinguish between a stakeholder and a shareholder. [2]

A shareholder owns shares in a company, whereas a stakeholder is anyone with an interest in or affected by the business. All shareholders are stakeholders, but the residents of Grünheide are stakeholders in Tesla without being Tesla shareholders.

AO2 Explain one area of conflict between two stakeholder groups at Tesla's Grünheide factory. [4]

K Shareholders want higher profit from expansion, while the local community wants a safe, quiet environment and secure water supplies. App Expanding Grünheide means clearing forest and using more water in a protected area. E Extra capacity raises output and future profit for shareholders, but residents fear water shortages, more traffic and the loss of woodland, lowering their quality of life. Measures that reduce the impact, such as recycling more water or a smaller site, add cost or limit output, so both interests cannot be fully met.

AO2 Analyse how stakeholders could benefit mutually from the expansion. [6]

E Thousands of jobs benefit employees and the region, and the government gains income-tax and corporation-tax revenue. Local suppliers and services receive more orders, and shareholders gain profit. E By accepting a smaller expansion and investing in water recycling, Tesla could turn some opponents into partners, protecting its reputation and making planning approval more likely.

Practice questions (tap to reveal the marking points)

AO1 Identify two internal and two external stakeholders of a school. [2]
Internal: teachers, management, owners. External: parents, students (debatable: often treated as customers), government, suppliers, community. 1 mark per correct pair.
AO2 Explain why the local council is an important stakeholder in the Grünheide expansion. [4]
Grants or refuses planning permission; can attach conditions on water and forest; gains jobs and tax but answers to voters who opposed the plan. Applied.
AO2 Explain how a pressure group might influence Tesla's plan to expand its Grünheide factory. [4]
Protest camps and media coverage that damage reputation; lobbying the council to refuse planning permission; legal challenges on water and forest rules; pressure on customers and investors with green targets.
AO2 Analyse why managers and shareholders might disagree over the expansion. [6]
Divorce of ownership and control; managers' growth targets vs shareholders' worries about cost, risk and reputation; time horizons; how disruption such as the March 2024 shutdown affects returns.
1.5

Growth and evolution

Real company case
Starbucks (USA): four ways to grow

Starbucks grew from one Seattle store into one of the world's largest restaurant chains using several growth methods at once:

How Starbucks has grown
  • Organic growth: it opens its own company-operated stores.
  • Acquisition: it bought the tea retailer Teavana in 2012 for about $620 million. The shops struggled, and Starbucks closed all 379 of them by 2018, keeping the brand for tea sold in its cafés and supermarkets.
  • Joint venture: it entered India in 2012 through Tata Starbucks, a 50:50 joint venture with the Tata group.
  • Licensing and alliances: partners run Starbucks stores in places such as airports and bookshops, and in 2018 Nestlé paid about $7.15 billion for the right to sell Starbucks coffee in supermarkets worldwide.

Read more: Starbucks (Wikipedia) · Teavana (Wikipedia)

Syllabus map

Syllabus pointHighest AOYou must be able toTypical command terms
Internal and external economies and diseconomies of scaleAO2Explain specific types and their effect on unit costs for a named firmExplain, distinguish
Internal vs external growthAO2Distinguish the two and explain implicationsDistinguish, explain

  • Reasons to stay small
AO3Judge whether a named firm should growDiscuss, evaluate, to what extent
External growth methodsAO3Compare methods and recommend one with conditionsEvaluate, recommend, compare

Key terms AO1

Economies of scale
Falls in average (unit) cost as a business increases its scale of operation.
Internal economies of scale
Cost advantages that a firm gains from inside itself as it grows, which lower its average costs.
External economies of scale
Cost advantages that come from the growth of the whole industry or area. They are available to every firm in it.
Diseconomies of scale
Rises in average cost when a firm or industry grows beyond its most efficient size.
Internal (organic) growth
Growth from within, using the firm's own resources: more products, outlets, capacity or markets.
External (inorganic) growth
Growth by joining with or working with other firms: M&As, takeovers, joint ventures, alliances, franchising.
Merger
Two firms agree to combine into one new organisation.
Acquisition / takeover
When one firm buys a controlling interest (over 50% of the shares) in another. A takeover may be hostile.
Joint venture
Two or more firms create a new, separate business they jointly own and control, sharing costs, risks and profits.
Strategic alliance
An agreement in which firms cooperate on a shared goal while remaining independent. No new company is created.
Franchising
A franchisor sells the right to trade under its name and system to a franchisee, for a fee and royalties.
Integration
Horizontal (same industry, same stage), vertical backward (supplier), vertical forward (customer/distributor), conglomerate (unrelated).
Minimum efficient scale
The lowest level of output at which a business achieves the lowest possible average cost.

External diseconomies: when an area or industry grows too much, firms face higher land and rent prices, congestion, competition for skilled workers (higher wages) and stricter regulation.

Common mistake
  • Don't write that economies of scale make total costs fall. They make average (unit) costs fall, while total costs usually rise as output rises.
Key points
  • Internal diseconomies come from the firm's own size: slow communication, poor coordination and low motivation.
  • External diseconomies hit every firm in a crowded area: higher wages and rents, congestion and skill shortages.
  • The optimum size is the scale at which average cost is lowest. Beyond it, growth adds more problems than savings.
  • Firms reduce diseconomies by decentralising, using profit centres and keeping teams small.

Reasons to grow and to stay small AO3

Reasons to grow

  • Economies of scale lower unit costs and raise profit margins.
  • A larger market share gives the firm more market power over prices and more bargaining power with retailers.
  • Selling more products in more markets spreads risk.
  • Growth helps the firm survive, because it is harder to take over and can keep up with rivals.
  • Owners earn higher profits, and managers gain status and higher pay.
  • A larger firm attracts investors and talented staff more easily.

Reasons to stay small

  • A small firm can give personal service, stay flexible and keep close relationships with customers.
  • The owners keep control and avoid bringing in outside investors.
  • The firm may serve a niche or local market that is too small to grow in.
  • Staying small avoids diseconomies of scale and the risk of losing quality or culture.
  • Financial risk is lower, because the firm needs to borrow less.
  • Some owners choose a small business for their lifestyle, and governments often support small firms.
Judging growth (AO3)Ask: does growth fit the owners' objectives? Is there enough demand? Can the firm finance it without overtrading? Will quality and culture survive? Which method of growth carries least risk for the benefit gained?

Merger
  • It combines the strengths of both firms.

  • It brings economies of scale.
  • The deal is agreed and friendly.
  • Cultures may clash.
  • Roles are duplicated, so jobs are cut.
  • Each side loses some control.

It suits two firms of similar size with complementary strengths.
Acquisition / takeover
  • Growth and market share come fast.
  • The buyer gains brands, customers, patents and capacity.
  • It removes a competitor.
  • The buyer usually pays a premium.
  • Hidden problems may appear later.
  • Staff may resist.
  • Borrowing for the deal raises gearing.
  • Hostile bids damage morale.
  • It suits a buyer with the finance and a clear plan to integrate the target.
  • It works best when the target is undervalued.
Joint venture
  • Costs and risks are shared.
  • It combines expertise, such as local market knowledge.
  • It allows entry to countries that limit foreign ownership.
  • Profits and control are shared.
  • Disputes can arise.
  • The partner may become a competitor.
  • Ending it can be messy.
It suits entering a new market or a large project where a partner has missing skills.

  • It costs little.
  • It is flexible.
  • The firms stay independent.
  • It is quick to set up.
  • Commitment is weaker.
  • The alliance may collapse.
  • Know-how may leak to the partner.
It suits specific shared goals, such as joint distribution, airline code-sharing or research.
Franchising (as franchisor)
  • The franchisor grows fast using franchisees' capital.
  • It earns fees and royalties.
  • Owner-managers are motivated.
  • Franchisees bring local knowledge.
  • The franchisor has less control over quality.
  • Poor franchisees damage the brand.
  • It receives only a share of the profit.
It suits a proven, easily copied format with a strong brand.

Franchising from the franchisee's side

  • For the franchisee, the advantages are a proven brand and system, training, bulk-buying discounts, a lower failure rate and easier access to bank loans.
  • The disadvantages are the initial fee and ongoing royalties, little freedom, sharing the profit and the restrictions in the contract.

Types of integration

  • Horizontal integration joins firms at the same stage of production, as when Starbucks bought the tea retailer Teavana, which gave it more market share and economies of scale.
  • Backward vertical integration moves towards the suppliers: Starbucks owns a coffee farm in Costa Rica, which gives it research and supply knowledge.
  • Forward vertical integration moves towards the customer, for example by owning restaurants or shops, so the firm controls the customer experience and keeps the retailer's margin.
  • Conglomerate integration joins firms in unrelated businesses, which spreads risk.

The case in brief: Starbucks
  • Organic growth: its own stores give control but are slow.
  • Acquisition risk: it bought Teavana for $620 million and closed all 379 shops.
  • Joint venture: the Tata JV shares risk and brings local knowledge.
  • Licensing: the $7.15 billion Nestlé deal earns income without running stores.

Exam tipAnsoff tells you where to grow; 1.5 methods tell you how. A strong answer combines them: "market development (India) through a joint venture (Tata Starbucks) to share risk and gain local knowledge".

Exam corner: 1.5

Exam tips

  • Name the specific type of economy of scale. "Bulk-buying economies" earns more credit than "economies of scale".
  • For external growth, discuss what happens after the deal: joining the two firms, their cultures and the finance.
  • Use numbers from the case, such as the $620 million Starbucks paid for Teavana and the 379 Teavana shops closed by 2018.
  • Make your recommendation conditional, for example on careful checks before the deal (due diligence) and on keeping key staff.

Common pitfalls

  • Don't confuse a joint venture with a strategic alliance. A joint venture creates a new firm, while a strategic alliance does not.
  • Don't assume that growth always lowers costs, because diseconomies of scale exist.
  • Don't mix up a merger and a takeover. A merger is agreed by both firms, while a takeover is one firm buying another, and it can be hostile.
  • Remember that external economies of scale come from the growth of the whole industry or area, not from the firm itself.

Model answers

AO2 Explain two internal economies of scale Starbucks gains from its size. [4]

K Purchasing economies arise when larger firms buy inputs in bulk at a discount. App E With thousands of stores, Starbucks buys enormous volumes of coffee, milk and cups, so it can negotiate lower prices per unit and lower its cost per drink, which smaller coffee chains cannot match.

K Technical economies come from using larger or better machinery more intensively. E Starbucks roasts coffee in a small number of large plants that supply thousands of stores, spreading the fixed cost of roasting equipment over more output and lowering average cost.

AO3 Evaluate acquisitions and joint ventures as growth methods, using Starbucks's Teavana and Tata deals. [10]

K An acquisition means buying a controlling interest in another firm; a joint venture creates a new business jointly owned with a partner, sharing costs, risks and profits.

App E Acquisition: buying Teavana in 2012 for about $620 million quickly added hundreds of tea shops and a known tea brand. But many of the shops were in shopping malls with falling visitor numbers, and Starbucks closed all 379 of them by 2018. The deal shows the main risk of acquisitions: the buyer pays upfront, and the target's problems become its problems.

App E Joint venture: entering India in 2012 through a 50:50 venture with Tata gave Starbucks local knowledge, property contacts and a trusted local partner, while sharing costs and risks. This is market development, a medium-risk Ansoff strategy. But profits and control are shared, and the partners must agree on prices and how fast to open stores.

Ev Overall, Starbucks's experience suggests the method should fit the market: organic growth where it already knows customers, a joint venture where local knowledge matters (India), and licensing where a partner controls the site (airports) or the channel (supermarket shelves through Nestlé). Acquisition is fastest but riskiest: Teavana added shops, not lasting demand. A firm should only acquire after checking that customers, not just capacity, come with the deal.

Practice questions (tap to reveal the marking points)

AO1 Define external economies of scale. [2]
Falling average costs (1) resulting from growth of the industry or location, available to all firms (1).
AO2 Distinguish between a joint venture and a strategic alliance. [4]
JV creates a new jointly owned legal entity (2); alliance is cooperation without a new entity, firms stay independent (2).
AO2 Explain two diseconomies of scale Starbucks might face as it grows. [4]
Communication across thousands of stores; slower decisions; staff feeling like a number, lowering motivation; inconsistent quality. Applied.
AO3 Discuss whether Starbucks should slow its store openings and focus on improving existing stores. [10]
Service speed and quality, staff workload, brand experience vs economies of scale, competition from cheaper chains, investor pressure for growth. Judgement on objectives.
AO3 Evaluate franchising as a growth method for Starbucks, compared with McDonald's, which franchises about 95% of its restaurants. [10]
Low capital, rapid growth, local franchisee knowledge vs quality control and the "third place" experience, brand risk, royalties only. Starbucks prefers licensing and own stores to control quality. Conditions: proven format, strong training.
1.6

Multinational companies (MNCs)

Real company case
CATL battery plant, Debrecen (Hungary)

CATL, the Chinese company that is the world's largest maker of electric-vehicle batteries, announced in 2022 a plant in Debrecen, Hungary, worth about €7.3 billion, its largest investment in Europe. It is planned to make 100 GWh of batteries a year and create up to about 9,000 jobs. European car makers need batteries close to their factories, and BMW is building a car plant in the same city.

The Hungarian government welcomed the investment and offered state support and tax incentives. Some local residents protested over the plant's water use, possible pollution and the speed of approval. Hungary already had low unemployment, so filling thousands of jobs may mean recruiting workers from other regions or abroad.

Read more: CATL (Wikipedia)

Syllabus map

Syllabus pointHighest AOYou must be able toTypical command terms
Impact of MNCs on host countriesAO3
  • Weigh benefits and costs for a named host country and its stakeholders
  • Judge overall impact
Discuss, evaluate, to what extent
Focus of the syllabusThe guide asks about the impact on host countries, not on the MNC itself. Know why firms go multinational as context, but spend your evaluation on the host: its economy, workers, local firms, government, environment and culture.

Key terms AO1

Multinational company (MNC)
A business with its headquarters in one country and production or service operations in at least one other country.
Host country
The country in which an MNC sets up operations. The home country is where it is headquartered.
Foreign direct investment (FDI)
Investment by a firm in productive assets in another country (factories, offices, acquisitions).
Globalisation
The growing integration of the world's economies through trade, investment, technology and the movement of people and ideas.
Transfer pricing
Setting prices for trade between parts of the same MNC, which can shift profits to low-tax countries.
Repatriation of profits
Sending profits earned in the host country back to the MNC's home country.
Technology transfer
The spread of skills, knowledge and processes from the MNC to local workers and firms.
Multiplier effect
An initial injection of spending leads to a larger total rise in income as money is re-spent locally.
Free trade
International trade without barriers such as tariffs, quotas or subsidies.
Brain drain
The emigration of highly skilled or educated people from a country, reducing its supply of skilled labour.

Why firms become multinationals
  • The home market is saturated, so they need new customers.
  • Larger scale brings economies of scale.
  • Producing inside a market avoids tariffs and cuts transport costs.
  • They gain cheaper labour, materials or skills.
  • Operating in many economies spreads risk.

Key points
  • Foreign direct investment (FDI) is when an MNC builds or buys operations in another country.
  • Technology transfer: local workers and suppliers learn new skills and standards.
  • Transfer pricing can shift profit to low-tax countries, which cuts the host's tax revenue.
  • Ethical risks include low pay, poor safety and pollution where laws are weak.

Evaluating the impact: "it depends on…" AO3

Factors that decide whether impact is positive

  • The host country's level of development matters: a poorer country may gain more from the jobs and foreign investment, but it may also have weaker regulation.
  • The strength of the host's laws, and how well they are enforced, matters for the environment, workers and tax.
  • The type of operation matters: a research centre brings more skills and better jobs than an assembly plant.
  • Local linkages matter: the impact is better if the MNC buys from local suppliers and hires local staff.
  • The size of the incentives the government offers should be compared with the benefits it receives.
  • The time frame matters: a construction boom now is different from a long-term commitment to the country.
  • The MNC's own ethics and CSR record affect how it behaves in the host country.

How host governments manage MNCs

  • Governments attach conditions to incentives, such as a minimum number of local hires or rules on using local suppliers.
  • They require environmental impact assessments and monitor the site.
  • They include clawback clauses, so that the MNC must repay incentives if the promised jobs are not delivered.
  • They use international tax rules, such as the OECD global minimum corporate tax rate of 15%.
  • They encourage joint ventures with local firms so that know-how is shared.
Common mistakes
  • Don't write about the benefits to the multinational when the question asks about the host country. Keep the host country's stakeholders, such as its workers, local firms and government, at the centre of your answer.
  • Avoid sweeping claims such as "MNCs exploit poor countries." Evaluate instead: say when the impact is positive or negative, and support each point with evidence from the case.
The case in brief: CATL in Hungary
  • Scale: €7.3 billion of FDI to create up to 9,000 jobs, helped by state incentives.
  • It depends: with low unemployment, many jobs may not go to local people.
  • Costs to the host: water use and pollution concerns.

Exam corner: 1.6

Exam tips

  • Organise your answer by stakeholder: workers, local firms, the government, the community and the environment.
  • Use numbers from the case: about €7.3 billion invested for up to 9,000 jobs is roughly €800,000 per job.
  • Separate the short-term impact from the long-term impact.
  • End with the conditions under which the host country benefits.

Common pitfalls

  • Don't write a one-sided answer that is all good or all bad.
  • Don't ignore the cost of the incentives to taxpayers.
  • Remember the multiplier effect, which works upwards when the MNC arrives and downwards if it leaves.

Model answer

AO3 Discuss the impact of CATL's Debrecen plant on Hungary. [10]

K An MNC operates in more than one country; its foreign direct investment can bring benefits and costs to the host country.

App E CATL's €7.3 billion plant could create up to 9,000 jobs. Through the multiplier effect, workers' spending supports shops and services, and local firms may win supply and construction contracts. The government gains income tax and VAT, and workers gain skills in battery technology, a growth industry. However, with unemployment already low, many jobs may be filled by workers from elsewhere, so local benefits may be smaller than the headline number.

E However, state support and tax incentives cost public money that could fund schools or hospitals, and some profits may be repatriated to China. Residents' concerns about water use and pollution are serious: battery production uses hazardous materials, and damage to water supplies would harm farming and health for decades.

Ev Overall, the impact is likely to be positive for growth and exports, because the plant links Hungary to Europe's electric-car supply chain. But the benefit depends on conditions: strict and transparent environmental monitoring, real local supply contracts, and training that gives local people the better-paid jobs. Without these, the long-term environmental and fiscal costs could outweigh the gains, especially if demand for this battery technology falls.

Practice questions (tap to reveal the marking points)

AO1 Define multinational company. [2]
Business with headquarters in one country (1) and operations in at least one other (1).
AO2 Explain two ways an MNC could benefit local suppliers in a host country. [4]
New contracts; higher standards and technology transfer; bigger orders giving economies of scale. Applied.
AO3 To what extent should a host government offer large subsidies to attract MNCs? [10]
Cost per job, multiplier, tax revenue, footloose risk, opportunity cost of subsidy, conditions/clawbacks. Judgement.
AO3 Evaluate the impact of a global fast-food MNC opening in a small town. [10]
Jobs, training, investment vs local restaurants closing, culture, health, profits leaving. Conditions.
Unit 2 · Human resource management
2.1

Introduction to Human Resource Management

Real company case
Royal Mail (UK): automation and a two-year dispute

Royal Mail has delivered the UK's post for over 500 years and was privatised in 2013. Letter volumes have fallen for years while parcels have boomed, so it now competes with parcel firms such as Amazon Logistics, Evri and DPD. Several rivals use self-employed couriers paid per parcel, which keeps their fixed costs low.

To cut costs, Royal Mail invested in automated parcel hubs and wanted to change working practices, such as later start times and more Sunday work. The Communication Workers Union (CWU), which represents most of its postal workers, said the changes were being imposed without agreement. Staff held 18 days of strikes in 2022, the company reported losses of hundreds of millions of pounds and announced thousands of job cuts. A deal was finally agreed in 2023: a 10% pay rise over three years and a share of future profits, in return for changes to working practices.

Read more: Royal Mail (Wikipedia)

Syllabus map: what each point lets examiners ask

Syllabus pointHighest AOYou must be able toTypical command terms
Role of HRMAO2Explain how HR activities help a named business reach its objectivesOutline, explain, suggest
Internal and external factors influencing HR planningAO2Explain how one factor changes the number, skills, cost or location of staff a firm needsExplain, analyse, distinguish
Reasons for resistance to changeAO2Explain why a named group in the case resists a specific changeExplain, analyse
HR strategies to reduce the impact of change and resistanceAO3Weigh strategies against each other and recommend one, with conditionsDiscuss, evaluate, recommend, to what extent
Force field analysis (HL toolkit)AO2AO4Complete, score and interpret a force field using case evidenceComplete, construct, analyse
What the AO ceiling means for youFactors and reasons are AO2, so questions on them ask you to explain, not evaluate. Build cause → effect → consequence chains there and don't waste time on a judgement. The AO3 marks in 2.1 sit on strategies for managing change, so that is where your balanced, justified conclusions go. Any point can also be asked at AO1 (define, outline, state).

Key terms AO1

Human resource management (HRM)
Managing the people in an organisation, from planning and recruitment to training, appraisal, reward and exit, so that the business reaches its objectives.
Human resource (workforce) planning
Forecasting the number and type of employees a business will need, comparing this with the staff likely to be available, and planning how to close the gap.
Demographic change
Change in the size or structure of a population: age profile, birth and death rates, gender balance, migration.
Labour mobility
How easily workers move between jobs. Occupational mobility is movement between types of job, and geographical mobility is movement between places.
Immigration
People moving into a country to live and work. Emigration is people leaving.
Flexi-time
Employees choose their start and finish times within limits, usually around fixed core hours (e.g. 10:00–15:00), while working an agreed total.
Gig economy
A labour market of short-term, task-based work ("gigs"), often arranged through digital platforms, where workers are usually self-employed with no guaranteed hours.
Change management
Planning, communicating and supporting a change so that it is accepted and its benefits are achieved.
Resistance to change
Reluctance or refusal by employees or managers to accept a change, shown passively (low effort, absence) or actively (complaints, industrial action).
Redeployment
Moving an employee to a different role inside the business instead of making them redundant.
Redundancy
Ending employment because the job is no longer needed. Dismissal is ending employment because of the employee's conduct or capability.
Natural wastage
Reducing staff numbers by not replacing people who retire or leave voluntarily.
Full-time work
Employment for the standard number of hours in a working week, often around 35 to 40 hours.
Permanent contract
A contract of employment with no fixed end date, which continues until the employee resigns, retires or is dismissed.
Homeworking
Working from home instead of the employer's premises, usually using digital technology to communicate.
Resignation
When an employee chooses to leave a job, usually after giving the notice set out in the contract.
Retirement
When an employee permanently stops working, usually at or near the end of a career.
Manipulation and co-optation
A strategy for managing resistance to change that involves selectively sharing information or giving key resisters a token role in the change so that they support it.
Kotter and Schlesinger
Researchers who identified six strategies for overcoming resistance to change: education and communication; participation and involvement; facilitation and support; negotiation and agreement; manipulation and co-optation; and explicit and implicit coercion.
Cultural diversity
The range of different cultures, nationalities, languages and backgrounds within a workforce or a market.

Role of HRM AO2

HRM makes sure the business has the right number of people with the right skills, in the right place, at the right time and at the right cost. It works as a cycle: decisions at each stage feed the next.
