AO2 analysis chain: how the role of HRM affects Royal Mail

HRM plans and trains the workforce. Royal Mail needs staff who can run automated parcel hubs. If HR plans retraining early, the hubs run at full speed and productivity rises; if not, the firm pays for machines that sit underused while it searches for scarce technicians, worsening its losses.

Human resource planning AO2

Demand for labour depends on

  • Sales forecasts and growth objectives show how many staff the business will need.
  • New technology and automation usually mean fewer staff are needed, but with higher skills.
  • If productivity rises, the same output needs fewer workers.
  • Changes to products, locations or opening hours change the number and type of staff needed.
  • The budget available for wages limits how many people the firm can employ.

Supply of labour depends on

  • Inside the firm, supply depends on retirements, promotions, labour turnover, absence and the skills of current staff.
  • Outside the firm, supply depends on the unemployment rate, local wages, how many people schools and colleges train, demographics, immigration and how many staff competitors are hiring.
Gap foundHR optionsTrade-off to mention
Shortage (demand > supply)
  • Recruit externally
  • Promote and train internally
  • Overtime
  • Temporary or gig workers
  • Outsource
  • Automate
Cost and time of recruiting vs quality and loyalty of flexible labour
Surplus (supply > demand)
  • Natural wastage
  • Hiring freeze
  • Early retirement
  • Redeployment and retraining
  • Reduced hours or job sharing
  • Redundancy as last resort
Speed of savings vs morale, reputation, redundancy pay and lost skills
Skills mismatchRetraining, job rotation, targeted recruitment, partnerships with collegesTraining cost and the risk that trained staff leave
Gap foundHR optionsTrade-off to mention
Shortage (demand > supply)
  • Recruit externally.
  • Promote and train existing staff.
  • Use overtime.
  • Hire temporary or gig workers.
  • Outsource the work.
  • Automate tasks.
Recruiting takes time and money, while flexible labour may be less skilled and less loyal.
Surplus (supply > demand)
  • Let natural wastage reduce numbers.
  • Freeze hiring.
  • Offer early retirement.
  • Redeploy and retrain staff.
  • Reduce hours or share jobs.
  • Make redundancies only as a last resort.
Fast savings must be weighed against morale, reputation, redundancy pay and lost skills.
Skills mismatch

  • Rotate jobs.

Training costs money, and trained staff may leave.
Exam tipWhen a question says "HR planning", always say what changes: the number of staff, their skills, their cost or their location/hours. That single phrase turns a vague point into an applied one.

Internal factors
  • The firm's objectives set how many staff it needs.
  • Its budget limits spending on wages and training.
  • Its organisational structure, culture and leadership style shape the roles it needs and how attractive it is to work for.
  • Its labour turnover shows how many people must be replaced each year.

External factors that influence HR planning AO2

The guide names five. Learn each as meaning → effect on HR planning → example → what it depends on.

Demographic change

Changes in the size and age structure of the population.

Effect on HR planning
  • An ageing population means more retirements and fewer young workers, so firms need policies for older workers, such as phased retirement and ergonomic workplaces.
  • A young, growing population supplies plenty of entry-level workers, but they need more training.
  • Demographic change also changes what customers buy, and so changes the jobs firms need: an ageing population needs more care workers, for example.

Example: Japan, where about 29% of people are over 65, has firms raising retirement ages and investing in robots for care and logistics.

It depends on: industry (physical vs knowledge work), whether jobs can be automated, immigration policy.

Labour mobility

How easily workers move between jobs (occupational) or between places (geographical).

Effect on HR planning
  • When labour mobility is high, recruiting is easier but keeping staff is harder, so the firm may need better pay or benefits to retain them.
  • When labour mobility is low, local skills shortages appear, so the firm must train its own staff or move the work elsewhere.
  • Workers can be held back by housing costs, family ties, language barriers and qualifications that are not recognised in another country.

Example: EU free movement lets firms in Germany recruit across the EU, while high housing costs in cities such as London reduce geographical mobility.

It depends on: how specialised the skills are; remote working, which reduces the need for physical moves.

Immigration

Workers entering a country from abroad.

Effect on HR planning
  • Immigration fills skills gaps and labour shortages, often at a lower recruitment cost.
  • Immigrant workers bring a wider range of ideas, languages and knowledge of other markets.
  • The firm must check visas and may need to provide language training, cultural training and support with settling in.
  • Immigration policy, such as quotas and visa rules, can change quickly, which makes the supply of labour uncertain.

Example: Germany's Skilled Immigration Act (2020) made it easier to hire non-EU skilled workers to fill shortages in IT and healthcare.

It depends on: government policy, ethics of pay and conditions, ability to integrate staff.

Flexi-time

Staff choose start and finish times around core hours.

Effect on HR planning
  • Flexi-time attracts and keeps staff who have caring duties or long commutes, and it lowers absence.
  • It makes planning shifts and cover harder, and meetings must fit into the core hours when everyone is at work.
  • It needs trust between managers and staff, a system for recording hours, and management that judges output rather than hours at a desk.

Example: since April 2024, UK employees can ask for flexible working, including flexi-time, from their first day in a job, so employers there must plan rotas around more varied start and finish times.

It depends on: the job. Flexi-time suits office work; it is hard for a warehouse shift or a hospital ward.

Gig economy

Short-term, task-based work, often via apps, by self-employed workers.

Effect on HR planning
  • Using gig workers lets the firm match labour exactly to demand, which cuts its fixed wage costs.
  • Gig workers tend to be less loyal and less trained, quality is harder to control, and turnover is high.
  • There is a legal and ethical risk if the gig workers are really employees in all but name.
  • Permanent staff may feel insecure when they see work moving to gig workers, which can reduce their motivation.

Example: in 2021 the UK Supreme Court ruled that Uber drivers are "workers" entitled to minimum wage and holiday pay, raising costs for gig-based models.

It depends on: how important consistent service is, the law in that country, brand reputation.

Other external factors to use

  • Technology such as automation, AI and remote-working tools changes the skills firms need and where people work.
  • The state of the economy matters: high unemployment makes recruiting easier and cheaper, while a boom creates shortages and pushes wages up.
  • Laws on the minimum wage, working time and discrimination raise costs and shape the contracts firms can offer.
  • Competitors that pay more can draw staff away.
  • Social attitudes are changing, and more workers now look for work-life balance, purpose and diversity.

Use STEEPLE in the exam to come up with external factors quickly.

Common mistakes in factor questions
  • A weak answer says, "The gig economy is growing, so this affects HR planning." A strong answer applies the point to the business: "Using self-employed couriers would let Royal Mail match labour to daily parcel volumes and cut fixed wage costs, but it would reduce control over delivery quality and provoke the union."
  • Don't treat flexi-time as working from home. Flexi-time is about when people work, while remote working (teleworking) is about where they work.
  • Don't confuse labour mobility with labour turnover. Labour mobility describes how easily workers move between jobs and places in the labour market, while labour turnover is the percentage of a firm's staff who leave in a year.
  • Don't call all part-time work "gig work". Gig work is paid task by task, the worker is usually self-employed, and there are no guaranteed hours.

Change in the workplace AO2

Change is the key concept of Unit 2. Triggers can be internal (new leader, new objectives, poor results) or external (technology, competition, law, the economy, a merger). The guide does not name a change model, but the two below help you explain resistance and justify strategies.

Lewin's three steps (useful extra)

  1. Unfreeze: managers explain why the current way of working must change and create a sense of urgency.
  2. Change: the new system is introduced, with training and support.
  3. Refreeze: the change is made normal through new procedures, rewards and culture.

Lewin also created force field analysis, which HL students use to plan the unfreeze stage.

The change curve (useful extra)

Staff typically pass through shock and denial, then frustration and a dip in morale, before experimenting and accepting the change. HR's job is to make the dip shallower and shorter.

Exam tipAlways name who resists and why that group in particular. "Employees dislike change" earns little; "older warehouse staff fear that automation will make their manual skills obsolete close to retirement" earns application and explanation marks.
Why people resist change (Kotter and Schlesinger)
  • Self-interest: they expect to lose pay, status or their job.
  • Misunderstanding and lack of trust: they do not see why the change is needed, or do not believe management.
  • Different assessments: they think the change is a mistake, and they may be right.
  • Low tolerance for change: they fear they cannot learn the new skills.

ApproachWhat HR doesBest whenAdvantagesDrawbacks
1. Education and communication
  • HR explains why, what, when and how.

It works when resistance comes from misunderstanding or rumours.
  • It builds trust.
  • People who understand often help.

It works when a powerful group will clearly lose out.

Match cause to strategy

  • If staff resist because they misunderstand the change, the answer is education and communication.
  • If they fear losing their jobs, the firm can guarantee redeployment and offer retraining.
  • If they are anxious about new skills, the firm should provide training and support.
  • If a trade union opposes the change, the firm should negotiate and consult.
  • If staff fear losing status, the firm can involve them in the change and offer new roles.
  • In a crisis with no time to consult, managers may have to force the change through, but they should explain it afterwards.

Evaluation checklist (AO3)

  • Urgency: is there enough time to consult staff?
  • Power of the resisters: could they stop the change?
  • Cost: can the firm afford training or a deal with the union?
  • Culture: how much do staff trust management, given what has happened before?
  • Scale: is the change a small adjustment, or does it involve job losses?
  • Time frame: does the firm need speed now, or commitment from staff later?
  • Other stakeholders: how will customers, the union and the firm's reputation be affected?
Judgement that scoresMost good answers recommend a combination: communicate early and honestly, involve staff in the design, support with training, and negotiate where people genuinely lose out. Coercion is a last resort for genuine crises. Always state the condition: "this works best if…".
The case in brief: Royal Mail
  • Reason for change: letters falling, parcels booming, and rivals use cheaper couriers.
  • Poor process: change was imposed without agreement, which led to 18 strike days.
  • Negotiation and agreement: it settled with a pay rise and profit share.

Force field analysis HL AO2AO4

A planning tool that lists the forces for a change (driving) and against it (restraining), scores each one, and compares the totals so managers can decide whether and how to change. You must be able to complete one from a case and analyse the result. It is also used in Unit 5 (e.g. a new production method).

StepActionTip
1Define the change in one sentence"Introduce more automated parcel sorting at Royal Mail"
2List driving forcesCosts, competitors, technology, law, customers, objectives
3List restraining forcesFear, cost, culture, skills, union, contracts, time
4Score each force (usually 1 = weak to 5 = strong)Justify each score with a fact from the case
5Total, compare and planGo / don't go / go but weaken the biggest restrainers first
StepActionTip
1Define the change in one sentence.For example: "Introduce more automated parcel sorting at Royal Mail."
2List the driving forces.Look for costs, competitors, technology, law, customers and objectives.
3List the restraining forces.Look for fear, cost, culture, skills, unions, contracts and time.
4Score each force, usually from 1 (weak) to 5 (strong).Justify each score with a fact from the case.
5Total the scores, compare them and plan.Decide whether to go ahead, not go ahead, or go ahead after weakening the biggest restraining forces.
Worked example 1: Royal Mail automated parcel sorting

Net score = 11 − 12 = −1, so restraining forces are slightly stronger. Abandoning automation would leave Royal Mail with higher costs than its parcel rivals. A better response is to weaken the largest restrainer first: offer retraining and redeployment (reducing fear of job losses from 5 to perhaps 2), consult the union early, and phase the change in. Re-scored, drivers would then exceed restrainers.

Worked example 2: hybrid working in an office

Net score = +3, so go ahead, but manage the restrainers: train managers to lead remote teams, fix in-office days for collaboration, and invest in secure systems.

Strengths

  • Force field analysis is structured and visual, so it is easy to explain to staff.
  • When a team scores the forces together, it encourages staff to take part.
  • It shows where to act, which is usually on the restraining forces.
  • It links the change to the stakeholders and to the reasons for resistance.

Limitations

  • The scores are subjective and depend on who gives them.
  • The forces affect each other and change over time.
  • The totals can hide one force that decides the outcome on its own, such as a legal ban.
  • It does not produce solutions on its own.
Five-step analysis to write under any force field(1) State the totals. (2) Say which side is stronger. (3) Name the single most powerful force. (4) Recommend reducing restraining forces first, because pushing harder on drivers often raises resistance. (5) Note that the scores are subjective.

Exam corner: 2.1

Exam tips

  • Open with a one-line definition, then go straight to the case.
  • Use facts and numbers from the case, such as "18 strike days in 2022" or "10% over three years".
  • For factor questions (AO2), explain how the factor changes the number, skills, cost or location of staff.
  • For strategy questions (AO3), give at least two strategies, a trade-off for each, and a recommendation with conditions.
  • Link to other topics: the cost of training (Unit 3), motivation theories (2.4), communication (2.6) and leadership style (2.3).
  • End your evaluation by comparing the short term with the long term and saying what extra information you would need.

Common pitfalls

  • Don't list many factors without explaining them. Depth earns more marks than breadth.
  • Don't evaluate in an AO2 "explain" question: it earns no extra marks and loses time.
  • Don't just write "communicate better". Say what should be communicated, when, how and by whom.
  • Don't ignore cost. Recommending expensive retraining for a loss-making firm without discussing how to pay for it is weak.
  • Don't treat all employees as one group. Managers, older staff and the union resist change for different reasons.
  • In force field analysis, don't give scores without justifying them, add up the totals carefully, and always draw a conclusion.

Model answers

AO1 Define the term gig economy. [2]

The gig economy is a labour market in which people do short-term, task-based work, often found through digital platforms, and are usually self-employed with no guaranteed hours or employment benefits, for example app-based delivery riders.

Mark scheme: 1 mark for short-term/task-based work; 1 mark for a second feature (platform-based, self-employed, no guaranteed hours) or a clear example.

AO2 Explain two external factors that could influence HR planning at Royal Mail. [4]

K Demographic change, such as an ageing population, affects the supply of labour. App The UK workforce is ageing, and sorting and delivery work is physically demanding, E so Royal Mail must plan to recruit and train younger replacements as experienced staff retire, and may use phased retirement to keep their knowledge long enough to pass it on.

K The gig economy lets firms hire workers for individual tasks rather than on contracts. App Rivals such as Evri use self-employed couriers paid per parcel, E which lets them match courier numbers to daily volumes and cut fixed wage costs, putting price pressure on Royal Mail. However, gig models carry risks: less control over quality, high turnover, and possible legal changes, such as the 2021 UK Supreme Court ruling that Uber drivers are workers.

Mark scheme: for each factor, 1 mark for identifying a relevant external factor with brief explanation, 1 mark for applying its effect to Royal Mail. Internal factors (e.g. finance) earn 0.

AO3 Discuss HR strategies Royal Mail could use to reduce resistance to automation and new working practices. [10]

K Resistance to change is the reluctance of employees to accept new working practices. Kotter and Schlesinger suggest strategies ranging from education and participation to negotiation and coercion. App At Royal Mail, resistance was likely because the changes affected start times, Sunday work and job numbers, most postal workers belong to the CWU, and trust was low because the union said changes were being imposed.

K E First, Royal Mail could use education and communication combined with participation. Managers could hold face-to-face briefings explaining why change is needed (falling letter volumes, competition from parcel rivals, losses) and invite delivery staff to help redesign rounds and parcel processes. Because the main cause of distrust was the way changes were introduced, two-way communication tackles it directly, and staff who help design changes are more likely to accept them. Ev However, participation is slow while losses mount, so consultation needs a clear deadline.

K E Second, facilitation and support through retraining and redeployment guarantees. Training staff for automated hubs and parcel roles removes the strongest cause of resistance, fear of job loss, and keeps experienced people. This links to Maslow's safety needs: job security must be met before staff will engage with new tasks. Ev The drawback is cost: Royal Mail was making losses, and not every role can be protected.

K E Third, negotiation with the trade union. With most postal workers in the CWU, the union could call strikes that hit the busiest season, as it did in 2022. The 2023 deal traded a 10% pay rise over three years and a share of profits for changes to working practices, reducing the risk of further disruption. Ev This added costs, but coercion, such as imposing changes, would confirm staff distrust and prolong strikes.

Ev Overall, the most effective approach is a combination: early, honest communication and participation to rebuild trust, retraining and redeployment for those who want it, and negotiation with the union on pay and working practices. Communication is cheap and fast, so it should come first; negotiation was in the end unavoidable, as the 2023 deal shows. Earlier communication and participation might have avoided 18 days of strikes. Before deciding, managers should cost each option, because the case does not give the cost of retraining compared with redundancy pay.

Why this reaches 9–10
  • It focuses clearly on the question.
  • It uses theory accurately (Kotter and Schlesinger, Maslow).
  • It integrates case facts throughout.
  • It weighs each strategy against a limitation.
  • Its conclusion is justified, with conditions, time frames and the limits of the case information.
AO4 HL Complete a force field analysis for Royal Mail's automation using information from the case. [4]
Answer approach
  • Draw the change in the middle.
  • Add at least three driving forces: lower cost per parcel (4), competitor pressure (4) and faster processing (3).
  • Add at least three restraining forces: fear of job losses (5), union opposition (4) and the cost of training after last year's loss (3).
  • Justify each score with the case. The totals are 11 for the change and 12 against it.
Mark scheme
  • [1] for the correct format.
  • [1] for relevant driving forces.
  • [1] for relevant restraining forces.
  • [1] for reasonable scores and correct totals.

Practice questions (tap to reveal the marking points)

AO1 Define human resource planning. [2]
Forecasting the number and type (skills) of employees needed in the future (1), comparing with expected supply and planning how to close any gap (1).
AO1 Outline one reason employees might resist change. [2]
Identify a reason (fear of job loss, uncertainty, loss of status, lack of trust, extra workload) (1); outline why it causes resistance (1).
AO2 Explain how flexi-time could affect HR planning in a call centre. [4]
Define flexi-time with core hours (1). Benefit: easier recruitment and retention of staff with caring duties, lower absence (1–2). Problem: harder to guarantee enough agents at peak call times; needs rota and time-recording systems (1–2). Must be applied to a call centre.
AO2 Distinguish between geographical and occupational labour mobility. [4]
Geographical = ability to move between places for work (1), with a barrier or example such as housing costs (1). Occupational = ability to move between types of job (1), limited by skills/qualifications (1). Clear contrast needed for full marks.
AO2 Analyse why the trade union at Royal Mail resisted the changes. [6]
Up to 2 per developed reason: protecting members' jobs (thousands of cuts announced); later start times and Sunday work affecting work–life balance; fear that self-employed models would replace contracts; distrust because changes were said to be imposed. Each must use case evidence and explain the consequence.
AO3 Evaluate whether Royal Mail should use self-employed couriers, as some rivals do. [10]
For: flexibility matched to parcel volumes, lower fixed costs, quick scaling, matching rivals' costs. Against: quality and reliability, brand risk, legal reclassification risk (Uber ruling), low loyalty, ethical concerns, union reaction and strikes. Judgement: perhaps for peak periods only, alongside a core of employed staff; depends on the union agreement and the law.
AO3 Recommend whether Royal Mail's managers should have imposed changes without union agreement (coercion). [10]
Coercion is fast and losses were mounting, but the case shows a strong union and low trust, so strikes followed. Compare with communication, participation and negotiation, which produced the 2023 deal. Recommend against coercion except as a last resort; justify with short- vs long-term effects and stakeholder reactions.
AO4 HL Using your force field, analyse whether Royal Mail should push ahead with automation. [4]
State totals and net score (1); identify strongest force (1); recommend weakening restrainers, e.g. redeployment guarantees (1); comment on subjectivity of scores (1).
2.2

Organisational Structure

Real company case
Zappos (USA): removing the managers

Zappos, the US online shoe and clothing retailer owned by Amazon since 2009, is famous for an unusual experiment. From 2014 its chief executive, Tony Hsieh, replaced the traditional hierarchy with holacracy: manager titles were removed, and staff worked in self-organising "circles", each with its own roles and rules for making decisions.

In 2015 Hsieh offered a buyout of at least three months' pay to anyone who did not want to work this way. About 18% of staff took it and left. Supporters said the flatter structure made Zappos faster and more creative; critics said it caused confusion about who decides what. Most large firms sit between the extremes: McDonald's, for example, keeps its brand and core recipes centralised but lets national teams adapt menus, such as serving no beef in India.

Read more: Zappos (Wikipedia) · Holacracy (Wikipedia)

Key terms AO1 AO2

Organisational structure
The formal way roles, authority and communication are arranged, shown on an organisation chart.
Levels of hierarchy
The number of layers of authority from the top of the organisation to the bottom.
Span of control
The number of subordinates who report directly to one manager.
Chain of command
The formal line through which authority and instructions pass down, and accountability passes up.
Delegation
Passing authority to make a decision or complete a task to a subordinate. The manager stays accountable.
Centralisation
Decision-making is concentrated at the top of the hierarchy or at head office.
Decentralisation
Decision-making authority is spread to lower levels or to branches and regions.
Delayering
Removing one or more levels of hierarchy, usually middle management.
Bureaucracy
An organisation run by formal rules, procedures and a fixed hierarchy, in which decisions follow set processes.
Matrix structure
Staff report to two managers at once: a functional manager and a project or product manager.
Tall (vertical) structure
Many levels and narrow spans of control.
Flat (horizontal) structure
Few levels and wide spans of control.
Line manager
A manager who has direct authority over employees below them in the hierarchy and is responsible for their work and performance.
Subordinate
An employee who works under the authority of a manager and reports to them.
Superior
A person with authority over others in the hierarchy, to whom subordinates report.
Line function
A department or role directly involved in producing and selling the main product, such as production or sales, with authority passing down the chain of command.
Staff function
A department or role that supports and advises line managers without direct authority over the core work, such as human resources, legal or IT.
Informal organisation
The network of personal relationships and unofficial communication in a business that exists alongside the formal structure.
Formal organisation
The official structure of a business, showing roles, authority and lines of communication, as set out in an organisation chart.
Chief executive officer (CEO)
The most senior manager in a company, responsible for running the business and putting the board's strategy into practice.
Senior management
The top level of managers, who set the strategy and long-term objectives of the organisation.
Middle management
Managers below senior management who turn strategy into departmental plans and supervise junior managers or team leaders.
Junior management
The lowest level of managers, who organise day-to-day work and supervise operational staff.
Supervisor
An employee responsible for overseeing the daily work of a group of staff, usually at the lowest level of management.
Team leader
An employee who leads and coordinates a small team, often while also doing the same work as its members.
Organisation by function
A structure in which the business is divided into departments according to their activity, such as marketing, finance, operations and human resources.
Organisation by product
A structure in which the business is divided into divisions for each product or product range, each with its own functions.
Organisation by region
A structure in which the business is divided into divisions for each geographical area.
Flat organisation
An organisational structure with few levels of hierarchy and wide spans of control.

Authority, responsibility, accountability

  • Authority is the right to make decisions and give instructions. A manager can delegate it.
  • Responsibility is the duty to complete a task. When a task is delegated, the responsibility is shared.
  • Accountability means answering for the result. It stays with the manager who delegated the task.

Delegation vs empowerment

Delegation: the manager hands over a specific task and the authority to do it, often within limits.

Empowerment: staff are given the authority and resources to decide how to do their own work and solve problems. Empowerment goes further and links to Herzberg's motivators.

Tall vs flat structures AO2

The inverse relationshipFor the same number of people, wider spans mean fewer levels and a shorter chain of command. Narrow spans mean more levels. Use this logic in any question about delayering or flattening.

The culture is built on trust and empowerment.
  • The culture is built on control.

Benefits of delegation

  • Delegation frees senior managers to work on strategy.
  • Decisions are made faster, by people who are closer to the problem.
  • It develops staff and tests whether they are ready for promotion.
  • Being given responsibility motivates staff, which links to Herzberg's motivators and Maslow's esteem needs.

Barriers and risks

  • Some managers fear losing control, or being outshone by their staff.
  • The subordinates may lack the skills or the confidence to do the task.
  • Mistakes can be costly, and the manager remains accountable for them.
  • Giving staff extra work without the authority or reward to go with it demotivates them.

CentralisedDecentralised
Who decidesSenior managers at head office decide.Branch, regional or team managers decide.
Strengths
  • The brand, prices and quality are consistent.
  • Costs are tightly controlled.
  • Coordination is easier.
  • Experienced senior managers decide.
  • Central buying wins bulk discounts.
  • Local decisions are faster.
  • Managers use local knowledge of tastes, laws and language.
  • Responsibility motivates and develops managers.
  • Senior staff are free to focus on strategy.
Weaknesses
  • Responses are slow.

Don't mix these upDelegation is one manager passing a task down. Decentralisation is the whole organisation spreading decision-making away from the centre. A firm can delegate tasks while staying centralised.
The case in brief: Zappos
  • Extreme decentralisation: it replaced the hierarchy and removed manager titles.
  • Cost: 18% of staff left, and others reported confusion over decisions.
  • Middle way: McDonald's centralises the brand but gives franchisees local freedom.

Delayering AO2

Advantages

  • Delayering lowers salary costs, because middle managers are expensive.
  • The chain of command becomes shorter, so communication and decisions are faster.
  • Wider spans of control encourage managers to delegate and empower staff.
  • Senior managers become closer to customers and front-line staff.

Disadvantages

  • The firm must pay redundancy costs, and it loses experienced managers.
  • The managers who remain take on more work and stress, and their spans of control may become too wide.
  • With fewer levels, there are fewer chances of promotion, which can reduce motivation.
  • Fear and low morale during the process can cause resistance (link to resistance to change in 2.1).
Common mistake
  • Don't write that delayering means making staff redundant. Delayering removes levels of the hierarchy. It often involves redundancies, but cutting staff numbers in general is called downsizing. Say which levels are removed and how the spans of control change.

Bureaucracy and the matrix structure AO2

Bureaucracy

Strengths
  • It treats people fairly and consistently.
  • Roles are clear and decisions are predictable.
  • It makes legal compliance easier.
  • It suits routine and regulated work, as in banks, government and hospitals.
Weaknesses
  • "Red tape" slows decisions down.
  • The structure is rigid when markets change.
  • It discourages initiative and creativity.
  • It can frustrate customers.

Matrix structure

Strengths
  • It brings specialists from different functions together.
  • Expertise is used flexibly.
  • It is good for innovation and projects.
  • Staff develop wider skills.
Weaknesses
  • Two bosses can give conflicting instructions.
  • It can be unclear who is accountable.
  • There are more meetings, so decisions are slower.
  • Project and functional managers compete for staff.

Organisation charts AO2AO4

An organisation chart shows roles, levels, spans, chains of command and departments. Businesses group roles in three main ways.

International firms, e.g. Nestlé, which groups its markets into regional zones
GroupingAdvantagesDisadvantagesSuits
By function

  • Roles are clear.

It suits firms with one main product or market.
By product
  • Managers focus on one product and are accountable for it.
  • Profit per product is easy to measure.
  • Functions such as marketing and HR are duplicated in every division.
  • Divisions may compete with each other.
It suits diversified firms, such as a group with food and clothing brands.

  • Functions are duplicated.
  • The global brand is less consistent.
  • Central control is harder.
It suits international firms, such as Nestlé, which groups its markets into regional zones.

What charts show

  • An organisation chart shows the levels of hierarchy and each manager's span of control.
  • It shows the chain of command and who reports to whom.
  • It shows the departments and how the work is grouped.
  • It shows the formal lines of communication.

Limitations of charts

  • A chart ignores the informal organisation, such as friendships, personal influence and the grapevine.
  • Charts go out of date quickly.
  • A chart shows each person's position, but not their real power or skill.
  • It does not show how well communication actually works.

How to construct a chart from a description (AO4)

1
List every role and who each one reports to.
2
Draw one row per level. Every role on the same level sits on the same row.
3
Connect with straight lines from each manager down to each direct subordinate only.
4
Label every box with a job title, and add a title for the chart.
5
Check: count levels, spans and total headcount against the text.
AO4 common mistakes
  • Don't count everyone below the chief executive as part of their span of control. A span of control counts only the people who report directly to that manager.
  • Don't count the levels of hierarchy by counting the lines on a chart. Count the rows of roles instead. The chain of command is the number of steps from the top of the chart down to a given role.
  • Don't put two roles of the same rank on different rows of an organisation chart. Line them up so that the chart can be read at a glance.

  • It can decentralise.
It gains responsiveness but weakens brand consistency and duplicates functions.
Tight labour marketThe firm must attract and keep talent.
  • It can flatten and give staff autonomy.
  • It can create development roles.
Jobs become more attractive, but there are fewer promotion steps.
Judgement frameworkAsk: (1) size and growth of the business, (2) skills of staff and managers, (3) how important consistency is to the brand, (4) speed of change in the market, (5) cost and finance available, (6) culture and resistance to restructuring. Then recommend, give the condition, and compare short term vs long term.

Changes in organisational structure HL AO3

HL students must evaluate newer, flexible structures. These respond to technology, globalisation, the gig economy, flexi-time and cost pressure (the 2.1 external factors).

1. Project-based organisation

Work is organised into temporary teams built for a specific project (a building, a film, a software release, a campaign). A project manager leads; people come from different functions or are hired for the project; the team disbands when it ends. It often sits within a matrix and matches Handy's Task culture (2.5).

Advantages

  • A project-based organisation is flexible, because each project gets the right mix of skills.
  • Each team focuses clearly on what it must deliver and by when.
  • Staff from different functions work together, which encourages new ideas.
  • The responsibility and the sense of achievement motivate staff (Herzberg).
  • The firm avoids paying for permanent teams between projects.

Disadvantages

  • Staff may report to two bosses, which can create conflicting loyalties.
  • Staff may feel insecure about their jobs between projects.
  • Knowledge is lost when a team breaks up at the end of a project.
  • Different projects may compete for the same specialists.
  • It is harder to appraise staff and develop their careers over the long term.
Suits
  • It suits work organised in projects, such as construction, consultancy, film, software, events and R&D.
Needs
  • It needs strong project management and clear goals.
  • Teams need good communication.
  • The firm needs a way to record lessons learned before each team breaks up.

Exam corner: 2.2

Exam tips

  • Use the vocabulary precisely: span of control, levels of hierarchy, chain of command, delegation and decentralisation. Examiners reward accurate terminology.
  • Whenever the structure changes, describe what happens to the spans of control, the number of levels and the length of the chain of command.
  • Link structure to communication (2.6), motivation (2.4), leadership (2.3) and, at HL, culture (2.5).
  • For AO3 questions, start from the external change in the stimulus and finish with a recommendation and a condition.
  • In calculations, show your working, for example: 1 + 3 + (3 × 2) + (6 × 4) = 34.
  • Draw a quick chart in your answer if it helps, because a labelled diagram can earn AO4 marks.

Common pitfalls

  • Don't write that delegation passes on accountability. It does not: the manager stays accountable.
  • Don't say that a flat structure has no managers. It has fewer levels of managers, each with a wider span of control.
  • Don't describe a matrix structure only as "having two bosses". Explain the benefit too: specialists from different functions share their expertise on a project.
  • Don't recommend "making the structure flatter" without saying which level to remove and what it would cost.
  • In Handy's shamrock, don't call seasonal staff the fringe. The contractual fringe is outsourced and paid fees, while seasonal staff belong to the flexible workforce.

Model answers

AO1 Define the term span of control. [2]

Span of control is the number of subordinates who report directly to one manager. For example, a café manager supervising eight baristas has a span of control of eight.

Mark scheme: 1 mark for "number of subordinates", 1 for "directly" or a clear example.

AO2 Explain two disadvantages for Zappos of the traditional tall structure it had before 2014. [4]

K A tall structure has a long chain of command, so communication is slow. App Before 2014, Zappos had a conventional hierarchy of managers, E so ideas and customer problems had to pass through several layers before anyone acted, which Hsieh believed would slow innovation as the firm grew.

K Tall structures also have high management costs because there are many managers on each level. App Removing manager roles was one aim of holacracy, E freeing money and decision-making power for frontline staff. However, the saving is smaller than it looks if staff spend more time in meetings deciding who does what.

Mark scheme: per disadvantage, 1 mark for a relevant point about tall structures, 1 for application to Zappos.

AO3 Discuss whether Zappos was right to decentralise decision-making through holacracy. [10]

K Decentralisation means passing decision-making authority from head office to lower levels, such as teams or country managers. App Holacracy was extreme decentralisation: authority moved from managers to self-organising circles of staff.

E For: staff closest to customers can decide quickly. Zappos's brand is built on customer service, so letting service staff solve problems without asking permission fits its strategy, and wider participation can raise motivation through responsibility (Herzberg). Fewer layers also mean faster communication.

E Against: without clear managers, staff may not know who decides what, which slows decisions and causes conflict. Coordinating a large firm is harder, and some employees lose the promotion ladder they valued. About 18% of Zappos staff took the 2015 buyout rather than work this way, taking skills and knowledge with them.

Ev Overall, most firms do better with partial decentralisation than with Zappos's extreme version: keep a few clear decision-makers and company-wide standards, while giving frontline staff authority over customer problems and local choices. McDonald's shows the balance: central control of brand and core recipes, local control of menus. The right degree depends on the firm's size, its staff's skills and how much consistency customers expect.

Why this reaches 9–10
  • It gives an accurate definition.
  • It develops both sides with case evidence.
  • It links to motivation theory.
  • It makes a nuanced recommendation (partial decentralisation) with conditions and time frames.
  • It states a limitation of the information.

Practice questions (tap to reveal the marking points)

AO1 Define delayering. [2]
Removing one or more levels of hierarchy (1), usually layers of middle management, which widens spans of control (1).
AO2 Distinguish between centralisation and decentralisation. [4]
Centralisation: decisions concentrated at the top/head office (1) + effect or example (1). Decentralisation: authority spread to lower levels or branches (1) + effect or example (1). Needs an explicit contrast.
AO2 Explain two benefits of a matrix structure for a software firm. [4]
Shared expertise across functions on each project (1+1 applied); flexibility to move developers between projects (1+1 applied). Alternatives: innovation, staff skill development.
AO4 A business has a managing director, 4 heads of department, each with 3 supervisors, each supervising 7 workers. Construct the chart and calculate total employees. [4]
Correct 4-level chart with labelled rows (2). Total = 1 + 4 + 12 + 84 = 101 (1). Spans stated correctly: 4, 3, 7 (1).
AO2 Explain how delayering could affect employee motivation. [4]
Positive: wider spans lead to more delegation and responsibility (Herzberg motivators). Negative: fewer promotion steps, job insecurity (Maslow safety), heavier workloads. 2 marks per developed, applied point.
AO3 To what extent should a hospital adopt a flatter structure? [10]
For: faster communication, empowered staff, lower admin costs. Against: patient safety requires clear chains of command and supervision of junior staff; regulation and accountability; specialist hierarchy. Judgement: limited flattening of administration, but keep clear clinical hierarchy. Conditions and stakeholders.
AO3 HL Evaluate the use of Handy's Shamrock by a seasonal hotel group. [10]
Explain the three leaves applied to the hotel. For: matches labour to seasonal demand, lower fixed costs, specialist outsourced services. Against: service quality and brand risk from flexible staff, loss of control over fringe, ethics and turnover, overworked core. Judgement: suitable if the core is large enough to train and supervise seasonal staff and service standards are monitored.
AO3 HL Recommend whether a film studio should use a project-based structure. [10]
Films are one-off projects with clear deadlines, so project teams fit; specialists can be hired per film. Weigh job insecurity, knowledge loss between films, competition for key specialists. Recommend with conditions, e.g. a small permanent core plus project teams.
2.3

Leadership and management

Real company case
Microsoft (USA): a change of leader

When Satya Nadella became chief executive of Microsoft in 2014, the company was seen as slow and inward-looking. Under his predecessor, Steve Ballmer, staff had been rated against each other through "stack ranking", in which a fixed share of every team had to be graded as weak performers. Many employees said this made colleagues compete rather than cooperate, and Microsoft dropped it in 2013.

Nadella promoted a "growth mindset" culture, based on psychologist Carol Dweck's work: learn from mistakes, listen more, and collaborate across teams. He shifted Microsoft's focus to cloud computing and partnerships, even with rivals. Microsoft's stock-market value rose from around $300 billion in 2014 to over $3 trillion by 2024.

Read more: Satya Nadella (Wikipedia) · Microsoft (Wikipedia)

Syllabus map

Syllabus pointHighest AOYou must be able toTypical command terms

Key terms AO1

Management
Getting things done through others by planning, organising, commanding, coordinating and controlling resources to achieve objectives.
Leadership
Influencing and inspiring people to work willingly towards a vision or goal.
Leadership style
The way a leader makes decisions, communicates and relates to followers.
Autocratic
The leader makes decisions alone and expects them to be followed. Communication is one-way, from the leader to the staff.
Paternalistic
The leader decides but acts in what they believe are employees' best interests, explaining decisions and caring for welfare.
Democratic
The leader involves employees in decisions through consultation or voting. Communication is two-way.
Laissez-faire
The leader gives employees freedom to make their own decisions with little direction.
Situational leadership
Adapting the style to the task, the team's competence and commitment, and the urgency of the situation.
Planning (management function)
Setting objectives and deciding the strategies and resources needed to achieve them.
Organising (management function)
Arranging people, tasks and resources so that plans can be carried out efficiently.
Commanding (management function)
Giving clear instructions to employees so that tasks are carried out as planned.
Coordinating (management function)
Making sure the work of different people and departments fits together towards the same objectives.
Controlling (management function)
Monitoring performance against the plan and taking corrective action when results fall short.
Emotional intelligence
The ability to recognise, understand and manage one's own emotions and those of others, which helps leaders communicate and motivate.

Link to motivation (2.4)

  • An autocratic style fits Taylor's view that workers are motivated mainly by money and need close control.
  • Democratic and laissez-faire styles meet Herzberg's motivators and Maslow's esteem and self-actualisation needs.
  • A paternalistic style meets Maslow's safety and social needs.

Link to structure and culture

  • Tall, centralised structures suit autocratic leaders.
  • Flat, decentralised structures need democratic or laissez-faire leaders.
  • At HL, Hofstede's power distance affects which style staff will accept.

FactorPoints towards autocraticPoints towards democratic / laissez-faire
UrgencyA crisis, an emergency or a tight deadline points towards autocratic leadership.Time to consult points towards a democratic or laissez-faire style.
Staff skills and experienceNew or unskilled staff need direction.Expert, experienced staff can be trusted with decisions.
Nature of taskRoutine, safety-critical or standardised tasks need firm control.Creative, complex or problem-solving tasks benefit from staff ideas.
Size of groupA very large group is hard to consult.Small teams are easy to consult.

Leader's personality and skillsA confident decision-maker tends towards autocratic leadership.A good listener and coach tends towards democratic leadership.
Common mistakes
  • Don't write that autocratic leadership is bad and democratic leadership is good. No style is always best, so judge each one against the situation: how urgent the decision is, how skilled the staff are and what kind of task it is.
  • Don't confuse paternalistic leadership with democratic leadership. A paternalistic leader still makes the decision. Staff are consulted about their welfare, but they do not get a vote.
  • Don't describe laissez-faire leadership as "no leadership". The leader still sets the goals and provides the resources, and then steps back to let staff decide how to reach them.
What decides the right style
  • The task: emergencies need direction, and creative problems need ideas.
  • The people: skilled staff suit democratic or laissez-faire styles, and new staff need guidance.
  • The time available: consultation takes time.
  • The culture: in high power-distance cultures, staff expect leaders to decide.
The case in brief: Microsoft
  • Old style: slow and inward-looking, with stack ranking that set colleagues against each other.
  • New style: Nadella's growth mindset and listening and collaboration are more democratic.
  • Careful evidence: value rose to over $3 trillion, but the cloud boom also helped.

Exam corner: 2.3

Exam tips

  • Always link the leadership style to the specific situation: who is being led, what the task is and how urgent it is.
  • Use evidence from the case: dropping stack ranking and the later rise in market value suggest that the change of style mattered.
  • Only recommend situational leadership if you say which style suits which situation.
  • Connect leadership to motivation theory to earn analysis marks.

Common pitfalls

  • Don't describe the styles without applying them to the case.
  • Don't treat management and leadership as the same thing.
  • Don't ignore the cost of slower decisions under democratic leadership.

Model answers

AO2 Distinguish between management and leadership. [4]

Management is achieving objectives through planning, organising and controlling resources, based on formal authority, such as Microsoft's managers setting budgets and targets for each division. Leadership is influencing and inspiring people towards a vision, based on trust and credibility, such as Satya Nadella persuading staff to adopt a growth mindset. Managers focus on systems and stability, while leaders focus on people and change.

AO3 Discuss whether Microsoft was right to move from a competitive, top-down style to a more democratic, collaborative one. [10]

K An autocratic leader makes decisions alone, while a democratic leader involves staff through consultation.

App E Under Ballmer, stack ranking set staff against each other, and many said colleagues competed rather than cooperated. Software engineers are highly skilled professionals; a more democratic, collaborative style lets them contribute ideas, meeting Herzberg's motivators such as responsibility and recognition and improving innovation. Nadella's growth-mindset culture aimed at exactly this.

E However, democratic decision-making is slower. In a crisis, such as a major security breach or a global outage, a firm needs fast, clear instructions, and consultation in those moments could be costly. It also needs leaders with strong listening skills.

Ev Overall, a firm like Microsoft should use situational leadership: democratic and coaching styles for innovation and long-term projects, where staff expertise matters and time allows, and clear, directive leadership in crises. Nadella's results suggest leadership style can change performance, but success also came from strategy (the move to cloud computing), so leadership was not the only cause.

2.4

Motivation and demotivation

Real company case
Amazon warehouses vs Costco (USA)

Amazon runs huge warehouses where staff pick and pack orders against productivity targets. Software tracks each worker's rate and records "time off task". In 2024 France's data-protection regulator fined Amazon's French warehouse business €32 million, saying its monitoring of staff was excessively intrusive. Staff turnover in Amazon warehouses has been very high: a 2021 New York Times investigation reported about 150% a year. Amazon also offers Career Choice, which pays tuition for courses that help staff move into better-paid jobs.

Costco, the US warehouse-club retailer, takes a different approach: it pays more than most rivals, offers health insurance to most staff and promotes from within. Its chief executive, Ron Vachris, started at the company as a forklift driver. Costco's staff turnover is far below the retail average.

Read more: Criticism of Amazon (Wikipedia) · Costco (Wikipedia)

What the AO ceiling means for youTheories are AO3: you must judge how useful a theory is for the business, not just describe it. Rewards and training are AO2, but they are the tools you recommend in AO3 answers ("Using Herzberg, the firm should use job enrichment because…").

Key terms AO1

Motivation
The internal and external factors that drive people to work towards goals with effort and commitment.
Demotivation
A loss of drive, caused by factors such as poor pay, unfair treatment, boring work or poor management.
Intrinsic motivation
Motivation that comes from the work itself, such as interest, challenge and achievement.
Extrinsic motivation
Motivation that comes from outside rewards, such as pay, bonuses, praise and promotion.
Hygiene factors (Herzberg)
Factors that cause dissatisfaction if absent but do not motivate when present (pay, conditions, policy, supervision, security).
Motivators (Herzberg)
Factors that create satisfaction and motivate (achievement, recognition, the work itself, responsibility, advancement, growth).
Job enrichment
Giving employees more responsibility, challenge and decision-making (vertical loading).
Job enlargement
Adding more tasks of a similar level (horizontal loading).
Empowerment
Giving employees authority and resources to make decisions about their own work.
Labour turnover
The percentage of a workforce that leaves over a period.
Overtime
Hours worked beyond the normal contracted hours, usually paid at a higher rate.
Recognition
Acknowledging an employee's effort or achievement, for example through praise, awards or public thanks, which Herzberg classed as a motivator.
Job advertisement
A notice that tells potential applicants about a vacancy, the main duties and the skills required, and how to apply.
Shortlisting
Selecting the most suitable applicants from all those who applied, to be invited for interview or testing.
Selection
The stage of recruitment in which the business chooses the best candidate, using methods such as interviews, tests and references.
Headhunting
Directly approaching people who already work for other organisations to persuade them to apply for a senior or specialist post.
Recruitment agency
A business that finds and screens suitable candidates for employers in return for a fee.
Contract of employment
A legal agreement between employer and employee setting out the terms of the job, such as duties, pay, hours, holidays and notice period.
Job analysis
The process of identifying the tasks, responsibilities and skills a job involves, used as the first step of recruitment to write the job description and person specification.
Aptitude test
A selection test that measures whether a candidate has the ability to learn or carry out the skills a job needs, such as numerical, verbal or problem-solving skills.
Psychometric test
A selection test that assesses a candidate's personality, attitudes and ways of thinking, to judge whether they suit the job and the organisation's culture.
References
Statements from a candidate's previous employers or teachers that confirm their experience, skills and reliability, usually checked before a job offer is confirmed.
Job interview
A formal meeting in which managers question shortlisted candidates to judge whether they can do the job and would fit in with the team.
Pink's drive theory
A theory by Daniel Pink that people doing creative, non-routine work are motivated mainly by three intrinsic drivers, autonomy, mastery and purpose, and that rewards such as bonuses can reduce performance on these tasks.
Autonomy
Having control over what you do, when and how you do it, and who you do it with; a key driver of intrinsic motivation in Deci and Ryan's and Pink's theories.
Mastery
The desire to get better at something that matters to you; one of Pink's three drivers of motivation, supported by challenging but achievable tasks and quick feedback.
Goldilocks tasks
Tasks that are neither too easy nor too hard, so they stretch an employee's skills without overwhelming them, helping to build mastery.
Signs of demotivationConsequences for the business
Absenteeism, lateness, low productivity, poor quality, complaints, conflict, grievances, high turnoverHigher recruitment and training costs, lost output, poor customer service, damaged reputation, lower profit
Signs of demotivationConsequences for the business
  • Absence, lateness and labour turnover rise.
  • Productivity and quality fall.
  • Complaints, conflict and grievances increase.
  • Recruitment and training costs rise.
  • Output is lost and customer service suffers.
  • The firm's reputation and profit fall.

Taylor, Maslow and Herzberg AO3

Frederick Taylor: scientific management (1911)

Key ideas

  • Taylor believed that workers are motivated mainly by money, a view called "economic man".
  • Time-and-motion studies find the "one best way" to do each task.
  • Work is divided into simple, specialised tasks, and workers are trained to do them precisely.
  • Workers are closely supervised and paid by output, using a piece rate.

Evaluation

  • In favour: Taylor's methods raise productivity in routine, measurable work and set clear standards. They are still visible today in fast-food kitchens, warehouses and call-centre targets.
  • Against: the theory ignores social and esteem needs, creates boring and repetitive jobs and causes conflict with unions. It does not suit skilled or creative work, and quality may fall when workers rush to earn more.

Amazon: rate targets and tracking of every task are Taylorist. They raise output per worker but are linked to stress and very high turnover.

Abraham Maslow: hierarchy of needs (1943)

Key ideas

  • Maslow described five levels of need. Lower needs must be largely met before higher needs start to motivate.
  • Once a need is satisfied, it no longer motivates.
  • Self-actualisation, at the top, means reaching one's full potential.

Evaluation

  • In favour: the theory is easy to understand, it reminds managers that people want more than money, and it helps them target rewards.
  • Against: needs differ between individuals and cultures, people can pursue several levels at once, it is hard to tell which level someone has reached, and there is little evidence for a strict order.

Frederick Herzberg: two-factor theory (1959)

Key ideas

  • Herzberg found that satisfaction and dissatisfaction are not opposites, because different factors cause each one.
  • Managers should fix the hygiene factors first, such as pay, conditions and supervision, to remove dissatisfaction.
  • They should then motivate through job enrichment: giving staff whole tasks, responsibility, recognition and chances to develop.

Evaluation

  • In favour: the theory is practical for designing jobs, and it explains why the effect of a pay rise does not last.
  • Against: it was based on interviews with about 200 engineers and accountants in Pittsburgh, so it may not apply to lower-paid workers. Pay can motivate some people, and interviewees may have credited themselves for successes and blamed others for failures, which biases the results.

The case in brief: Amazon and Costco
  • Taylor: Amazon sets productivity targets and tracks time off task.
  • Result: 150% turnover and a €32 million fine.
  • Herzberg: Costco offers better pay, health cover and promotion, so its turnover is far below average.

Additional theories HL AO3

McClelland: acquired needs

People develop one dominant need through life experience.

  • People with a high need for achievement (nAch) want challenging goals, feedback and personal responsibility, so they respond to stretching targets.
  • People with a high need for affiliation (nAff) want to belong and to keep good relationships, so they suit teamwork and supportive roles.
  • People with a high need for power (nPow) want influence and status, so they suit leadership roles.
Evaluation
  • It helps managers match people to roles and rewards.
  • Needs are hard to measure.
  • Most people have a mixture of all three needs.

Deci and Ryan: self-determination theory

Intrinsic motivation grows when three needs are met.

  • Autonomy means having choice and control over one's work.
  • Competence means feeling capable and mastering new skills.
  • Relatedness means feeling connected to other people.
  • Extrinsic rewards that feel controlling, such as tight bonuses, can crowd out intrinsic motivation.
Evaluation
  • It has a strong research base.
  • It is harder to apply in routine jobs.
  • Managers may still need extrinsic incentives.

Adams: equity theory

People compare their input/output ratio with others'.

  • Inputs are what a worker gives, such as effort, skill and time. Outputs are what they receive, such as pay, recognition and promotion.
  • If workers feel under-rewarded compared with others, they reduce their effort, ask for more or leave.
  • If they feel over-rewarded, they may feel guilty or work harder, but this effect does not last long.
Evaluation
  • It explains disputes when pay becomes transparent.
  • Perceptions of fairness differ between people.
  • People compare themselves with different reference groups.

Vroom: expectancy theory

Motivation depends on three beliefs multiplied together.

  • Expectancy is the belief that more effort will lead to better performance.
  • Instrumentality is the belief that better performance will lead to a reward.
  • Valence is how much the person values that reward.
Evaluation
  • It shows why badly designed bonuses fail.
  • It assumes that people calculate rationally.
  • The three elements are hard to measure.

Amazon through expectancy theory: if a rate target feels impossible on busy days (low expectancy) or rewards seem unrelated to effort (low instrumentality), extra pay will not motivate, however large it is.

Applying rewards: Amazon vs Costco

Replace pure rate targets with goals that include safety and accuracy; give experienced staff more control over how they work (Herzberg, autonomy); rotate them into training and quality roles; pay at or above the market rate (hygiene). Costco's model suggests better pay and promotion from within can cut turnover enough to pay for themselves.

Internal recruitment (AO3)

  • Internal recruitment is cheaper and faster.
  • The candidate already knows the culture, and the employer already knows their record.
  • A visible path to promotion motivates other staff.
  • Induction is shorter.
  • However, the pool of candidates is smaller, it brings no fresh ideas, it creates another vacancy, and colleagues who were not chosen may feel resentful.

External recruitment (AO3)

  • External recruitment gives a wider pool of candidates and brings in new skills.
  • Newcomers bring fresh ideas, which is useful when the firm needs to change.
  • It avoids rivalry between internal candidates.
  • However, it is costly and slow, there is a higher risk of a poor fit, induction takes longer, and internal candidates may be demotivated.

Labour turnover HL AO2AO4

Labour turnover (%) = number of staff leaving in a period ÷ average number of staff × 100LEARN IT
Worked example: Amazon warehouses

A warehouse had 310 staff at the start of the year and 290 at the end → average = (310 + 290) ÷ 2 = 300. Leavers = 114. Labour turnover = 114 ÷ 300 × 100 = 38%. If recruiting and training one worker costs $2,000, replacing 114 workers costs about $228,000 a year.

Causes of high turnover

  • Pay may be low compared with rivals, so staff feel unfairly treated (equity theory).
  • Jobs may be boring and tightly controlled, as in Taylor's approach.
  • Management may be poor, with little recognition for good work.
  • There may be few chances for promotion or training.
  • Better jobs may be available elsewhere when the labour market is tight.

Consequences and benefits

  • High turnover is costly: the firm pays for recruitment and induction, loses productivity, gives a lower quality of service and suffers from low morale.
  • Some turnover has benefits: newcomers bring fresh ideas, poor performers leave, and new staff often start on lower wages.
  • A healthy rate depends on the industry. Call centres and hospitality naturally have higher turnover than, for example, banking.

Exam corner: 2.4

Exam tips

  • Use a theory to explain the problem and to justify your solution.
  • Evaluate the theory itself, for example its sample, its cultural bias and individual differences.
  • Recommend specific rewards instead of writing "motivate staff more".
  • For labour turnover, write the formula, substitute the figures, give the answer as a percentage, interpret it and comment on the cost.

Common pitfalls

  • Don't call pay a motivator under Herzberg. He classed it as a hygiene factor.
  • Don't mix up job enrichment and job enlargement. Enrichment adds responsibility (vertical), while enlargement adds more tasks at the same level (horizontal).
  • Don't describe Maslow's pyramid without applying it to the case.
  • Remember that rewards cost money, and link this to finance.

Model answers

AO2 Explain how job enrichment could motivate Amazon warehouse staff. [4]

K Job enrichment gives employees more responsibility and challenge, which Herzberg calls motivators. App Amazon pickers follow system instructions and are tracked on every task. E Letting experienced staff train new starters, fix problems at their stations and suggest process improvements would give them achievement and responsibility, which could cut turnover and the cost of constant recruitment.

AO3 Evaluate the usefulness of Herzberg's theory in explaining high staff turnover in Amazon warehouses. [10]

K Herzberg argued that hygiene factors such as pay and supervision prevent dissatisfaction, while motivators such as responsibility, recognition and achievement create satisfaction.

App E Amazon's warehouse turnover of about 150% a year suggests deep dissatisfaction. Two hygiene factors look poor: intense monitoring of every task and physically demanding targets. Herzberg tells managers to fix these first, or no motivator will work. Costco shows the other side: good pay, benefits and promotion from within are linked to much lower turnover. Job enrichment, such as letting experienced staff train others or solve problems at their station, would add the responsibility that rate targets remove.

E However, Herzberg studied professional engineers and accountants; for warehouse staff, money may be a genuine motivator, so expectancy theory suggests a well-designed bonus can still work. Enrichment also needs training and trust, which cost money in a business that competes on low cost and speed.

Ev Overall, Herzberg is highly useful here because it explains why pay and targets alone have not cut turnover: monitoring damages hygiene, and the work offers few motivators. The best solution combines Herzberg (fair pay, less intrusive monitoring, enriched roles) with expectancy theory (achievable targets with rewards that clearly follow effort). Costco shows the approach can work in low-margin retail, although its business model differs from Amazon's.

Practice questions (tap to reveal the marking points)

AO1 Define piece rate. [2]
Payment per unit produced (1); pay rises with output / example (1).
AO2 Explain one advantage and one disadvantage of off-the-job training, such as Amazon's Career Choice courses. [4]
Advantage: recognised skills and qualifications, motivation and retention, no disruption to the warehouse floor. Disadvantage: cost, staff away from work, staff may leave once qualified (Career Choice is partly designed for this). Applied.
AO3 Compare and contrast Maslow's and Herzberg's theories. [10]
Similarities (lower/hygiene vs higher/motivators; money limited). Differences (hierarchy vs two independent factors; sequence; evidence base). Apply and judge usefulness.
AO4 HL A firm had 120 staff at the start and 140 at the end of the year; 26 left. Calculate labour turnover. [2]
Average = 130 (1); 26 ÷ 130 × 100 = 20% (1).
AO3 HL Recommend whether Costco should keep filling manager vacancies internally rather than externally. [10]
Internal: motivates staff (visible promotion path; the CEO started as a forklift driver), knows systems and culture, cheaper, retention. External: fresh ideas and new skills (e.g. e-commerce), wider pool. Likely recommend mainly internal with selective external hires; conditions.
2.5

Organisational (corporate) culture

HL
Real company case
Disney and Pixar (USA): protecting a culture

In 2006 Disney bought the animation studio Pixar, maker of Toy Story, for about $7.4 billion. Pixar's culture was built on small creative teams, daily reviews of unfinished work, blunt feedback through its "Braintrust" meetings and freedom to experiment. Disney was a huge, more formal corporation, and many feared its processes would crush Pixar's creativity.

Instead, Disney kept Pixar as a separate studio on its own California campus, with its own name and ways of working, and put Pixar's leaders, Ed Catmull and John Lasseter, in charge of Disney's own animation studio too. Pixar kept making hits, and Disney Animation recovered with films such as Frozen (2013). Compare the 1998 merger of Daimler-Benz and Chrysler: German and American managers clashed over pay, decision-making and working styles, and Daimler sold Chrysler in 2007 for a fraction of what it had paid.

Read more: Pixar (Wikipedia) · DaimlerChrysler (Wikipedia)

Key terms AO1

Organisational culture
The shared values, beliefs, norms and attitudes that shape how people in an organisation behave: "the way we do things around here".
Strong culture
Values are widely shared and deeply held, guiding behaviour without many rules.
Cultural clash
Conflict that arises when two different cultures meet, e.g. after a merger or a new leader.
Cultural integration
The process of combining cultures after organisational change.
National culture
The shared values of a country's people, which influence what they expect at work (Hofstede).
Values
The beliefs about what is important and right that guide how people in an organisation behave and make decisions.
Norms
The unwritten rules about what is normal and acceptable behaviour in an organisation.

Power (Zeus)It is a spider's web, with power at the centre.

  • There are few rules.
  • The centre makes the decisions.
  • Decisions are fast.
  • Direction is strong.
  • It depends on one person.
  • Favouritism can grow.
  • Talented staff may leave.
It is common in start-ups and small owner-led firms.
Role (Apollo)It is a Greek temple, whose pillars are the functions.Rules, procedures, job descriptions and hierarchy shape the work.
  • It is stable and efficient.
  • Roles are clear and secure.
  • It is slow to change.
  • It is bureaucratic.
  • It stifles initiative.
It is common in banks, government and large corporations, such as Disney's corporate side.
Task (Athena)It is a net or matrix.
  • Teams form around projects.
  • Expertise matters more than rank.
  • It is flexible and creative.
  • It adapts quickly.
  • It is costly.
  • It is harder to control.
  • Teams compete for resources.
It is common in consultancies, agencies and studios such as Pixar.
Person (Dionysus)It is a cluster of stars.The organisation exists to serve talented individuals.
  • Individuals have autonomy.
  • It attracts experts.
  • It is hard to manage.
  • Loyalty to the organisation is weak.
It is common in law firms, medical partnerships and universities.

Strengths of Hofstede

  • Hofstede's country scores are simple and easy to compare.
  • They help prepare managers for operating abroad, for international mergers and for international marketing (4.6).
  • They explain why a leadership style that works at home can fail in another country.

Limitations

  • National averages hide differences between individuals and regions.
  • The original data came from IBM staff in the 1960s and 1970s, and cultures have changed since then.
  • Using the scores carelessly risks stereotyping people.
  • A firm's organisational culture may differ from the national culture around it.

Evaluating culture change (AO3)Culture is slow to change because it lives in people's habits and beliefs. Forcing it fast creates resistance (link to 2.1); allowing two cultures to coexist (e.g. keeping a creative subsidiary semi-independent) can preserve value. Judge by the size of the clash, the value of the people at risk, and the time available.
The case in brief: Disney and Pixar
  • Task culture: Disney paid $7.4 billion for Pixar's small teams and blunt feedback.
  • Clash risk: Disney was a formal role culture, and many feared it would crush Pixar.
  • Solution: it kept Pixar separate, unlike DaimlerChrysler, which sold at a huge loss.

Exam corner: 2.5

Exam tips

  • Identify the type of culture using evidence from the case.
  • Explain the consequences of a culture clash, such as higher staff turnover, delays and extra cost.
  • Use Hofstede only when national culture is relevant to the question.
  • Link culture to resistance to change (2.1), structure (2.2) and leadership (2.3).

Common pitfalls

  • Don't confuse organisational culture with national culture.
  • Don't label a culture without justifying the label with evidence.
  • Don't assume that one culture is better than another. The best culture depends on the firm's strategy and environment.

Model answer

AO3 Discuss how Disney should have managed the risk of a cultural clash after buying Pixar. [10]

K A cultural clash occurs when organisations with different values and ways of working are combined. Using Handy, Pixar had a task culture built around project teams, while Disney's corporate side was closer to a role culture.

App E The main risk in 2006 was that Pixar's directors and animators would leave. Formal approvals and reporting would have slowed creative work and removed the autonomy that motivated Pixar staff (Deci and Ryan). Losing key creative people would have destroyed the very knowledge Disney paid $7.4 billion for.

E Option 1: keep Pixar semi-independent, with Disney controlling only budgets and release dates. This protects creativity and retention, but Disney gets less control and fewer economies of scale. Option 2: fully integrate Pixar into Disney's systems. This gives consistency and control, but risks resignations and weaker films, as the DaimlerChrysler clash suggests.

Ev Overall, Disney chose light-touch integration, and the results suggest it was right: Pixar kept its campus, name and ways of working, and its leaders even helped revive Disney Animation. The value of a creative studio lies in its people, so protecting their culture mattered more than standardising processes. This depends on the buyer's leaders accepting that a role culture does not suit creative work, which Daimler's managers did not accept with Chrysler.

Shared values, beliefs and norms (1) that shape how people behave in an organisation (1).
AO2 Explain one strength and one weakness of a role culture for a bank. [4]
Strength: consistency, compliance, security. Weakness: slow to adapt to fintech competition. Applied.
AO3 Evaluate the usefulness of Hofstede's dimensions for a firm opening offices in Japan. [10]

2.6

Communication

Real company case
Better.com (USA): 900 jobs cut on one video call

In December 2021 Vishal Garg, chief executive of the US online mortgage lender Better.com, laid off about 900 employees, roughly 9% of staff, on a three-minute Zoom call, weeks before the holidays. He told them: "If you're on this call, you are part of the unlucky group that is being laid off." Many found their access to work systems cut off straight away. A recording spread on social media within hours.

The announcement caused a public backlash. Garg apologised and took time off, and several senior managers resigned. The case is now a standard example of how the channel, timing and tone of a message matter as much as its content.

Syllabus pointHighest AOYou must be able to

Key terms AO1

Communication
The transfer of information, ideas or feelings from a sender to a receiver, so that it is understood.
Formal communication
Official, recorded communication through approved channels and the chain of command.
Informal communication
Unofficial communication outside formal channels, e.g. the grapevine, chats, social messaging.
Grapevine
The informal network through which rumours and information spread.
One-way vs two-way
One-way: no response expected. Two-way: the receiver responds, allowing feedback.
Barrier (noise)
Anything that stops the message being received or understood as intended.
Information overload
Receiving more information than can be processed, so key messages are missed.
Sender
The person or group that starts the communication by putting a message into words, images or other form.
Receiver
The person or group for whom a message is intended and who must interpret it.
Channel of communication
The route or path through which a message passes between sender and receiver, such as formal lines in the hierarchy.
Medium of communication
The method used to send a message, such as email, meeting, phone call, letter or video.
Noise (communication)
Anything that interferes with a message as it passes from sender to receiver, such as distractions, technical problems or misunderstanding.
Jargon
Technical or specialist language that people outside a particular group may not understand.
Verbal communication
Communication using spoken words, such as meetings, phone calls and presentations.
Written communication
Communication using written words, such as emails, letters, reports and notices.
Visual communication
Communication using images, such as charts, graphs, diagrams, signs and video.
Non-verbal communication
Communication without words, through body language, facial expressions, gestures and tone of voice.
