The case in brief: Better.com
  • Wrong method: it cut 900 jobs in a three-minute Zoom call.
  • No respect or questions: system access was cut at once.
  • Consequences: the news went viral, and senior managers resigned.

Exam corner: 2.6

Exam tips

  • Match the method to the message, the audience and the situation, and justify each choice.
  • Recommend a combination of methods, such as a meeting followed by a written record.
  • Show the consequence of a barrier in terms of money or customers.

Common pitfalls

  • Don't say that informal communication is always bad. The grapevine can spread information quickly and build team spirit.
  • Don't recommend face-to-face meetings for hundreds of staff without saying how, for example by cascading the message through team leaders in small groups.
  • Don't list barriers without suggesting how to overcome them.

Model answer

AO3 Recommend how Better.com should have communicated its job cuts. [10]

K Formal communication passes through official channels, while two-way methods allow feedback; the right method depends on urgency, sensitivity, complexity and audience.

App E The mass Zoom call failed because it gave personal, life-changing news to 900 people at once, with no chance to ask questions, and it came weeks before the holidays. Staff who stayed also lost trust, and the recording spread on social media, turning an internal decision into a reputation crisis.

E First, the company should have told people individually or in small groups, led by their own managers, with a common script to explain the reason and answer questions on pay and notice. This two-way method shows respect and limits rumours, though it takes managers' time.

E Second, written follow-up, with clear information on severance pay, benefits and next steps, would give everyone a record to refer back to and reduce confusion and fear.

Ev Recommendation: combine individual or small-group conversations (for respect and trust) with clear written follow-up (for detail and record), plus a named contact for questions. Mass video calls or email alone should never be used for sensitive news such as job losses, because the channel itself sends a message about how the company values its people.

Practice questions (tap to reveal the marking points)

Wrong channel (mass video call for personal news); no chance for questions or feedback; emotional barriers (shock, fear); poor timing before the holidays; distrust of management. 2 each, applied.
AO2 Explain one benefit and one risk of informal communication. [4]
Benefit: speed, relationships, honest feedback. Risk: rumours, inaccuracy, undermines management.
AO3 Discuss the use of instant messaging apps for workplace communication. [10]
Speed, mobility, team coordination vs overload, privacy, out-of-hours pressure, no formal record. Conditions and policy.
2.7

Industrial / employee relations

HL
Real company case
British Airways cabin crew dispute (UK, 2009–2011)

In 2009 British Airways, facing heavy losses in the global recession, cut the number of cabin crew on many long-haul flights and planned a pay freeze. The union Unite, which represented most BA cabin crew, said the changes were imposed without agreement and balloted for strikes over Christmas 2009. A court blocked that strike because of problems with the ballot, but crew walked out on 22 days in 2010.

BA trained other staff as emergency cabin crew and leased planes and crews from other airlines to keep flying. It also removed travel perks from staff who went on strike, which deepened the anger. The dispute cost BA well over £100 million and damaged trust before a deal was agreed in 2011. Strikes timed for peak travel periods give a union strong bargaining power, because an empty airline seat cannot be stored and sold later.

Read more: British Airways (Wikipedia)

Syllabus map

Syllabus pointHighest AOYou must be able to
Sources of conflictAO2Explain why conflict arises in a case
Employee and employer approaches to conflictAO3Evaluate the effectiveness and consequences of each action

Key terms AO1

Employee (industrial) relations
The relationship between employers and employees, often through trade unions, covering pay, conditions and how disputes are handled.
Trade union
An organisation of workers that represents members' interests in pay, conditions and job security.
Collective bargaining
Negotiation between employers and union representatives on behalf of a group of workers.
Work-to-rule
Employees do exactly what their contract requires and no more (no overtime, no flexibility).
Strike
A collective refusal to work.
Lockout
An employer prevents workers from entering the workplace during a dispute.
Conciliation
A neutral third party helps both sides reach their own agreement. The outcome is not binding.
Arbitration
A neutral third party hears both sides and decides the outcome, usually binding.
Industrial democracy
Employees share in decision-making, for example through works councils or worker directors on the board.
No-strike agreement
A union agrees not to strike, usually in return for binding arbitration or other guarantees.
Single-union agreement
An employer recognises and negotiates with only one union for all its workers.
Employer
A person or organisation that employs people and pays them wages or salaries.
Sit-in
A form of industrial action in which employees occupy their workplace and refuse to leave.
Change of contract
An employer tactic in a dispute that alters employees' terms and conditions, such as hours or pay, sometimes by dismissing and re-hiring staff on new contracts.
Binding arbitration
Arbitration in which both sides agree in advance to accept the arbitrator's decision as final.
Worker director
An employee representative who sits on the board of directors, giving the workforce a voice in major decisions.
Grievance
A formal complaint by an employee about their treatment at work.
Industrial dispute
A disagreement between employers and employees, often represented by a trade union, over pay, conditions or other issues.
Employers' association
An organisation that represents the interests of employers in an industry, for example in negotiations with trade unions.

No-strike agreement
  • Operations are stable.
  • Relations are predictable.
  • The union loses its main weapon.
  • Members may resent it.
Single-union agreement
  • Negotiations are simpler and faster.
  • There are fewer disputes between unions.
  • Workers have less choice.
  • The single union gains bargaining power.
Evaluation checklistCost of the dispute vs cost of concessions · timing (peak season) · power of each side · legal framework · long-term relationship and reputation · whether prevention (participation, communication) is cheaper than cure.
The case in brief: British Airways
  • Cause: heavy losses led BA to cut crew and freeze pay, imposed without agreement.
  • Escalation: 22 strike days, and BA removed strikers' travel perks.
  • Union power: an empty seat cannot be stored, and the dispute cost over £100 million.

Exam corner: 2.7

Exam tips

  • Quantify the cost of the conflict, for example 22 strike days and losses of well over £100 million.
  • Consider the power and the costs of both sides.
  • Recommend a sequence of steps: negotiation first, then conciliation, then arbitration.

Common pitfalls

  • Don't confuse conciliation with arbitration. A conciliator helps the two sides reach an agreement, while an arbitrator decides the outcome.
  • Don't treat strikes as the only action employees can take. They can also work to rule, ban overtime or go slow.
  • Don't ignore the long-term relationship between managers and staff after the dispute ends.

Model answer

AO3 Recommend how British Airways could have resolved its dispute with cabin crew sooner. [10]

K Disputes can be resolved by collective bargaining, conciliation or arbitration, or prevented by greater employee participation.

App E Strikes at Christmas or Easter hit the busiest travel periods, and Unite represented most BA cabin crew, giving it strong bargaining power. Imposing contract changes, as BA did in 2009, triggered strikes and damaged trust for years.

E BA could have returned to collective bargaining earlier with a package: a shorter pay freeze plus job-security guarantees and agreed crewing levels. If talks stalled, conciliation (as through Acas) keeps both sides in control and is quicker to arrange than a strike is to end. Arbitration gives certainty, but management might be forced to accept a higher settlement.

Ev Recommendation: negotiate a compromise before peak periods, using conciliation if needed, and set up a joint working group with crew to find other savings (fuel, scheduling), which builds participation and reduces future conflict. Accepting slightly smaller cost savings is better than losing well over £100 million to strikes and years of damaged trust, as BA did.

Practice questions (tap to reveal the marking points)

AO1 Distinguish between conciliation and arbitration. [2]
Conciliation: third party helps sides agree, non-binding (1). Arbitration: third party decides, usually binding (1).
AO2 Explain two sources of conflict at British Airways in 2009–2011. [4]
Pay freeze; fewer crew per flight and heavier workloads; changes imposed without agreement; removal of travel perks from strikers. Applied.
AO3 Evaluate a no-strike agreement for an airline. [10]
Stability in peak seasons, customer trust vs union concession, need for binding arbitration, member resentment. Judgement.
Unit 3 · Finance and accounts
3.1/3.2

Introduction to finance and sources of finance

Real company case
BrewDog (UK): raising finance from fans

BrewDog was founded in Scotland in 2007 by James Watt and Martin Dickie, using their savings and a bank loan. Banks were cautious about lending more, so from 2009 BrewDog raised money through "Equity for Punks", a crowdfunding scheme that sold small numbers of shares directly to fans, who also got discounts in its bars. Over the next decade it raised tens of millions of pounds from well over 100,000 small investors.

In 2017 it sold about 22% of the company to the private-equity firm TSG Consumer Partners for about £213 million, which paid for new breweries abroad. Selling shares avoids interest payments, but every sale dilutes the founders' ownership, and TSG's shares carried rights that ranked ahead of the crowd investors' ordinary shares.

Apply it: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for BrewDog of crowdfunding compared with a bank loan.

Read more: BrewDog (Wikipedia)

Practice firm for the worked answers · made-up numbers

Sunrise Bakery Ltd has three shops. It wants (a) a $90,000 oven line that will last 10 years, and (b) $15,000 to cover the gap each December, when it buys extra ingredients for Christmas before customers pay corporate orders in January. Retained profit available is $30,000. The two owners hold all the shares and do not want to lose control. Gearing is currently 25%.

Syllabus map

Syllabus pointHighest AOYou must be able to
Role of finance: capital and revenue expenditureAO2Classify spending and explain why the distinction matters
Internal and external sourcesAO2Explain how each source works and its pros and cons for a named firm
Appropriateness of short- or long-term sourcesAO3Recommend sources for a specific need and justify the choice

Key terms AO1

Capital expenditure
Spending on non-current assets that will be used for more than a year (machinery, buildings, vehicles).
Revenue expenditure
Spending on day-to-day running costs, used up within a year (wages, rent, ingredients, utilities).
Internal finance
Money raised from within the business or its owner.
External finance
Money raised from outside the business: investors, lenders, suppliers.
Equity (share) capital
Money raised by selling ownership (shares). No repayment, but ownership is diluted.
Loan (debt) capital
Money borrowed for a fixed term at interest, repaid in instalments, often secured on assets (collateral).
Overdraft
A bank agreement that lets an account go below zero up to a set limit. Interest is charged only on the amount used.
Trade credit
Buying from suppliers now and paying later (typically 30–90 days).
Gearing
The proportion of capital employed financed by long-term debt (HL ratio, 3.6).
Sources of finance
The ways in which a business obtains the money it needs, classified as internal or external and short, medium or long term.
Private equity
Investment in companies that are not listed on a stock exchange, usually by firms that buy a large stake, aim to improve performance and later sell at a profit.
Interest
The price paid for borrowing money, or the reward received for saving or lending it.
Interest rate
The cost of borrowing expressed as a percentage of the amount borrowed per year.
Dilution of control
The reduction in existing owners' percentage ownership and voting power when new shares are issued to other investors.
Share issue
The sale of new shares by an existing company to raise finance, which brings in permanent capital but dilutes the ownership of existing shareholders.
Rights issue
An offer of new shares to existing shareholders, in proportion to the shares they already own and usually at a discount, so they can keep their share of ownership.

The role of finance AO2

Capital expenditureRevenue expenditure
What it buysLong-lasting assetsDay-to-day costs

Where it appearsBalance sheet (non-current assets), then depreciatedProfit and loss account as an expense
Usual financeLong-term: loans, shares, leasing, retained profitShort-term: overdraft, trade credit, cash flow
Capital expenditureRevenue expenditure
What it buysIt buys long-lasting assets.It pays day-to-day costs.
Sunrise exampleSunrise buys a $90,000 oven line.Sunrise pays for flour, wages, electricity and December's ingredients.
Where it appearsIt appears on the balance sheet as a non-current asset and is then depreciated.It appears in the profit and loss account as an expense.
Usual financeIt is usually financed long term, through loans, shares, leasing or retained profit.It is usually financed short term, through an overdraft, trade credit or cash flow.

Businesses need finance to start up, to run day to day (working capital), to grow (expansion, new products) and to survive shocks (a cash-flow crisis).

What finance pays for
  • Start-up costs, before any revenue arrives.
  • Day-to-day running, such as wages, stock and bills.
  • Growth, such as new premises, machinery or acquisitions.

Key points
  • Grants and subsidies usually do not have to be repaid, but they come with conditions.
  • Debt factoring sells money owed by customers to a specialist firm for immediate cash, minus a fee.
The case in brief: BrewDog
  • Internal and debt first: savings and a bank loan, until banks grew cautious.
  • Crowdfunding: Equity for Punks created 100,000+ investors who were also loyal fans.
  • Trade-off: selling 22% to private equity gave new owners shares ranking ahead.

Short-, medium- and long-term finance

TermUsual periodUsed forSources
Short termUnder 1 yearWorking capital, seasonal gaps, cash-flow problemsOverdraft, trade credit, short-term loans
Medium term1–5 yearsVehicles, equipment, ITBank loans, leasing, microfinance

TermUsual periodUsed forSources
Short termIt lasts under one year.It pays for working capital, seasonal gaps and cash-flow problems.Overdrafts, trade credit and short-term loans provide it.

The matching principleMatch the life of the finance to the life of what it pays for. Short-term needs → short-term finance; long-lasting assets → long-term finance. Funding a 10-year oven with an overdraft is risky because the bank can withdraw it; funding December ingredients with a 10-year loan means paying interest on money you only needed for a month.

Applying it to Sunrise Bakery

Oven line ($90,000, capital expenditure, long term): $30,000 retained profit plus a $60,000 bank loan over 7–10 years, or leasing the line. Both keep control. Gearing would rise from 25% but stay moderate. December gap ($15,000, revenue expenditure, short term): an arranged overdraft or extended trade credit from flour suppliers, repaid when January corporate payments arrive.

Exam corner: 3.1/3.2

Exam tips

  • Classify the need first: is it capital or revenue expenditure, and is it short term or long term?
  • Recommend a mix of sources and say why each one fits the need.
  • Use the owners' objectives, such as keeping control, and the firm's gearing to choose between debt and equity.
  • Mention interest rates and the state of the economy as external factors.

Common pitfalls

  • Don't recommend selling shares to owners who want to keep control of the business.
  • Don't call retained profit free. It has an opportunity cost, because that money could have been paid out as dividends.
  • Don't say that an overdraft is suitable for buying buildings. An overdraft is short-term finance, while buildings are a long-term asset.
  • Don't confuse leasing with a loan. When a firm leases an asset, it does not own it.

Model answers

AO2 Distinguish between capital expenditure and revenue expenditure. [4]

Capital expenditure is spending on non-current assets that last more than a year, such as Sunrise's $90,000 oven line. Revenue expenditure is spending on day-to-day costs used up within a year, such as flour and wages. Capital expenditure appears on the balance sheet and is depreciated; revenue expenditure is charged to the profit and loss account in the year it occurs.

AO3 Recommend appropriate sources of finance for Sunrise Bakery's two needs. [10]

K Finance should match the purpose and time period of the need: long-term finance for long-lasting assets and short-term finance for temporary working-capital gaps.

App E The $90,000 oven line is capital expenditure lasting 10 years. Using the $30,000 of retained profit avoids interest and keeps control, but is not enough. A $60,000 bank loan over 7–10 years spreads repayments over the oven's life and keeps the owners' 100% ownership. With gearing at 25%, Sunrise can take on this debt, although rising interest rates would increase costs. Leasing is an alternative that avoids a large upfront payment and may include maintenance, but costs more over 10 years and Sunrise would not own the asset.

App E The $15,000 December gap lasts about a month. An overdraft is ideal: interest is paid only on the amount used and only for the weeks needed, and it is repaid when January payments arrive. Negotiating 60-day trade credit with flour suppliers would reduce the gap further at no interest cost, but may lose early-payment discounts.

Ev Recommendation: retained profit plus a long-term bank loan for the oven, and an overdraft plus extended trade credit for December. Share capital should be avoided because the owners want to keep control. This plan depends on the bank agreeing the loan at an affordable rate; if rates are high, leasing becomes more attractive.

Practice questions (tap to reveal the marking points)

AO1 Define trade credit. [2]
Buying goods now from suppliers (1) and paying at a later agreed date, e.g. 30–90 days (1).
AO2 Explain two advantages of crowdfunding for a start-up. [4]
Tests demand; marketing exposure; no bank or collateral; early customer community. Applied.
AO2 Explain why retained profit may not be suitable for a fast-growing firm. [4]
Profit too small relative to needs; shareholders want dividends; profit may be tied up in stock/debtors, not cash.
AO3 Discuss whether a start-up should use a business angel or a bank loan. [10]
Angel: equity, expertise, no repayment vs loss of control. Loan: control kept vs interest, collateral, risk for a firm with no track record. Judgement.
3.3

Costs and revenues

Real company case
Lime (USA): making shared scooters pay

Lime hires out e-scooters and e-bikes in hundreds of cities. Riders pay an unlock fee plus a charge per minute, so revenue rises with every ride; it also sells passes and subscriptions as extra revenue streams. Some costs vary with use, such as charging batteries and card-payment fees. Others are fixed or indirect, such as software, city licences, warehouses and head-office salaries.

For years Lime made heavy losses, because early scooters wore out or were vandalised within months. It cut cost per ride with sturdier vehicles and swappable batteries, and reported its first full year of positive adjusted earnings in 2022.

Apply it: Classify three of Lime's costs as fixed or variable, and as direct or indirect.

Read more: Lime (Wikipedia)

Practice firm for the worked answers · made-up numbers

CycleCo rents e-bikes to tourists in a seaside resort. Monthly costs: shop rent $2,400, manager's salary $2,100, insurance $500, charging electricity $1.20 per rental, cleaning $0.80 per rental, and part-time staff paid $0.90 per rental. Each rental is $25. It also earns money from guided tours, advertising local cafés on its maps, and selling helmets. Last month it had 600 rentals.

Syllabus map

Syllabus pointHighest AOYou must be able to
Fixed, variable, direct and indirect/overhead costsAO2Classify costs in a case and explain why classification matters
Total revenue and revenue streamsAO2
  • Calculate total revenue
  • Explain different revenue streams and their value
Why this topic mattersCost classification is the foundation for break-even (5.5), contribution (HL toolkit), final accounts (3.4), ratios (3.5) and budgets (3.9). A mistake here spreads through every calculation.

Key terms AO1

Fixed costs (FC)
Costs that do not change with the level of output in the short run, such as rent, salaries and insurance.
Variable costs (VC)
Costs that change in direct proportion to output, such as materials, packaging and piece-rate pay.
Semi-variable costs
Costs with a fixed element and a variable element, such as a phone contract with a fixed fee plus a charge for usage. This is a useful extra term.
Direct costs
Costs that can be clearly traced to a specific product or activity.
Indirect costs (overheads)
Costs that cannot be traced to one product and are shared by the whole business, such as head-office rent and administration.
Total cost (TC)
TC = FC + VC, where total VC = variable cost per unit × quantity.
Average cost (unit cost)
Total cost ÷ quantity produced.
Total revenue (TR)
Price × quantity sold.
Revenue stream
A distinct source of income for a business (sales, subscriptions, advertising, licensing, commission).
Profit
Total revenue − total costs.
Total variable cost
Variable cost per unit multiplied by the number of units produced.

Types of cost AO2

CycleCo costFixed or variable?Direct or indirect?Reason
Shop rent $2,400FixedIndirect
  • Same whatever the rentals
  • Shared by rentals, tours and sales
Manager's salary $2,100FixedIndirect
  • Paid regardless
  • Supports the whole business

Electricity $1.20 per rentalVariableDirectRises with each rental and traceable to it

Part-time staff $0.90 per rentalVariableDirectPaid per rental handled
CycleCo costFixed or variable?Direct or indirect?Reason
Shop rent $2,400It is fixed.It is indirect.
  • It stays the same however many bikes are rented.
  • Rentals, tours and sales all share it.
Manager's salary $2,100It is fixed.It is indirect.
  • It is paid whatever the level of activity.
  • It supports the whole business.
Insurance $500It is fixed.It is indirect.It is an annual policy.
Electricity $1.20 per rentalIt is variable.It is direct.It rises with each rental and can be traced to it.
Cleaning $0.80 per rentalIt is variable.It is direct.Each bike is cleaned after use.
Part-time staff $0.90 per rentalIt is variable.It is direct.Staff are paid for each rental they handle.

Fixed vs variable (behaviour)

This approach classifies costs by how they change with output. It is used for break-even, contribution and pricing decisions.

Direct vs indirect (traceability)

This approach classifies costs by whether they can be traced to one product. It is used for product costing, cost-plus pricing and judging which products are profitable.

Common mistakes
  • Don't write that fixed costs never change. They do not change with output in the short run, but rent can still rise next year, and in the long run all costs are variable.
  • Don't assume that fixed costs are always indirect and variable costs are always direct. This is usually true, but not always: a machine used for only one product is both a fixed cost and a direct cost.
  • Don't write that fixed cost per unit stays the same. Total fixed cost stays the same, but fixed cost per unit falls as output rises, because the overheads are spread over more units.
The case in brief: Lime
  • Revenue streams: unlock fee plus per-minute charge, and passes.
  • Variable costs: charging and payment fees. Fixed and indirect costs: software, licences, warehouses and salaries.
  • Fix: after heavy losses, sturdier scooters and swappable batteries cut the variable cost per ride.

Calculations AO4

Total revenue = price × quantity soldLEARN IT
Total cost = fixed costs + (variable cost per unit × quantity)LEARN IT
Profit = total revenue − total costLEARN IT
Average cost = total cost ÷ quantityLEARN IT
Worked example: CycleCo last month (600 rentals)

Total cost5,000 + 1,740$6,740

Average cost at 1,000 rentals(5,000 + 2,900) ÷ 1,000$7.90 (fixed costs spread further)

Why multiple revenue streams help

  • Several revenue streams spread risk, because the firm still earns money if one stream falls, for example when the tourist season ends.
  • They make fuller use of the firm's existing assets and customers.
  • They smooth cash flow across the seasons, for example when subscriptions bring in money during winter.
  • Streams with higher profit margins raise the firm's overall profitability.

Risks

  • New streams can distract managers from the core business.
  • They add extra costs and complexity.
  • Too many different offers can confuse customers about what the brand stands for.
  • Some streams depend on partners that the firm does not control.

Exam corner: 3.3

Exam tips

  • Show every step: write the formula, substitute the figures, and give the answer with $ or units.
  • Justify each cost classification briefly.
  • Link the fall in average cost as output rises to economies of scale (1.5).

Common pitfalls

  • Don't forget to multiply the variable cost per unit by the quantity.
  • Don't mix up revenue, which is the money coming in from sales, with profit, which is what is left after costs.
  • Don't leave out units and currency.

Model answers

AO2 Distinguish between direct and indirect costs, using CycleCo. [4]

Direct costs can be traced to a particular product or activity, such as the $1.20 electricity for charging each e-bike rental. Indirect costs are overheads that cannot be traced to one product, such as the $2,400 shop rent shared by rentals, tours and helmet sales. This matters because indirect costs must be allocated when CycleCo judges which service is most profitable.

AO2 Explain two benefits for CycleCo of having several revenue streams. [4]

K Several revenue streams spread risk. App E Tourist rentals fall sharply in winter, so advertising income from cafés and a resident subscription pass keep cash coming in and help cover the $5,000 monthly fixed costs.

K They also use existing assets and customers more fully. E Guided tours use the same bikes and customers, adding revenue with little extra fixed cost, so average cost per euro of revenue falls and profit rises.

Practice questions (tap to reveal the marking points)

AO4 Calculate CycleCo's profit if rentals fall to 300 in a month. [3]
TR = 25 × 300 = $7,500 (1). TC = 5,000 + 2.90 × 300 = $5,870 (1). Profit = $1,630 (1).
AO2 Explain why average cost falls as output rises. [4]
Fixed costs spread over more units (2); possible economies of scale (2). Use numbers.
AO2 Explain why classifying costs as direct or indirect matters when CycleCo sets its prices. [4]
Direct costs can be traced to each rental or tour, so they set the minimum price for that service (1–2). Indirect costs such as rent must be shared out, and the way they are allocated changes how profitable each service looks, so a price may not cover the full cost (1–2).
3.4

Final accounts

Real company case
Apple (USA): the final accounts of a giant

Apple's accounts for the year to September 2024 show the same statements you prepare, at a huge scale. Its income statement reported revenue of about $391 billion, gross profit of about $181 billion and profit for the year of about $94 billion. Its statement of financial position showed total assets of about $365 billion. Apple returned most of its profit to shareholders through dividends and by buying back its own shares.

Apply it: Explain why Apple's gross profit is so much larger than its profit for the year.

Read more: Apple Inc. (Wikipedia)

Practice firm for the worked answers · made-up numbers

Sunrise Bakery Ltd (all figures in $). Year to 31 December: sales revenue 400,000; opening stock 36,000; purchases 244,000; closing stock 40,000; expenses including depreciation 100,000 (depreciation 15,000); interest 10,000; tax 20% of profit before tax; dividends 15,000. These figures are reused in 3.5 and 3.6.

Syllabus map

Syllabus pointHighest AOYou must be able to

Key terms AO1

Profit and loss account (income statement)
A statement that shows revenue, costs and profit over a period, usually a year.
Balance sheet (statement of financial position)
A statement that shows assets, liabilities and equity at one point in time.
Cost of goods sold (COGS)
The direct cost of the goods sold: opening stock + purchases − closing stock.
Gross profit
Sales revenue − cost of goods sold.
Profit before interest and tax (operating profit)
Gross profit − expenses (overheads).
Retained profit
Profit after tax and dividends that is kept in the business. It is added to the reserves on the balance sheet.
Non-current assets
Assets held for more than a year: property, plant, equipment, intangibles.
Current assets
Assets likely to be turned into cash within a year: cash, debtors (receivables), stock (inventory).
Current liabilities
Debts due within a year: creditors (payables), overdraft, short-term loans.
Non-current liabilities
Debts due after more than a year: long-term loans, mortgages, debentures.
Equity
Owners' funds: share capital + retained profit (reserves).
Depreciation
The fall in value of a non-current asset over its useful life, charged as an expense.
Net profit
Another name for profit after all costs have been deducted; in the IB syllabus the terms profit before interest and tax and profit for the period are used.
Cash
Money held by the business in notes, coins and bank accounts, shown as a current asset on the statement of financial position.
Tangible assets
Physical assets that can be seen and touched, such as land, buildings, machinery and vehicles.

The case in brief: Apple
  • Gross profit: $391 billion revenue minus cost of sales gives $181 billion.
  • Profit for the year: $94 billion after expenses, interest and tax.
  • Use of profit: dividends and share buybacks instead of retained profit.

Balance sheet AO2AO4

Sunrise Bakery Ltd: balance sheet as at 31 December$$
  • Non-current assets: property, plant and equipment 270,000
  • Intangible assets 30,000
300,000

Checks

  • Net assets equal equity: 240,000 = 240,000, so the balance sheet balances.
  • Working capital is current assets minus current liabilities: 90,000 − 50,000 = 40,000.
  • Capital employed is non-current liabilities plus equity: 100,000 + 240,000 = 340,000.

How the statements link

  • The retained profit for the year (25,000) is added to the reserves in equity.
  • Closing stock appears in both statements: in the cost of sales and in current assets.
  • Depreciation is an expense in the profit and loss account, and it lowers the value of the assets on the balance sheet.

Intangible assets AO2

TypeMeaning
Goodwill
  • Value of reputation, customer base and brand above the value of net assets
  • Usually recorded only when a business is bought
PatentsExclusive right to make and sell an invention for a period
Trademarks and brand namesProtected names, logos and slogans
CopyrightProtection of original creative work (software, music, text)
TypeMeaning
Goodwill
  • Goodwill is the value of reputation, customers and brand above the value of net assets.
  • It is usually recorded only when a business is bought.
PatentsA patent gives the exclusive right to make and sell an invention for a period.
Trademarks and brand namesTrademarks protect names, logos and slogans.
CopyrightCopyright protects original creative work, such as software, music and text.

Why they matter

  • Intangible assets, such as brands and technology, are often the main source of a firm's competitive advantage.
  • They raise the value of the firm when it is sold.
  • They can earn licensing revenue from other firms.

Problems

  • They are hard to value objectively.
  • Their value can collapse quickly: a scandal can destroy goodwill.
  • Brands that a firm creates itself are usually not shown on its balance sheet, so the accounts may undervalue it.

Depreciation HL AO2AO4AO3

Depreciation spreads the cost of a non-current asset over its useful life. It is an expense that reduces profit but is not a cash outflow. Causes: wear and tear, age, obsolescence, usage.

Straight line: annual depreciation = (cost − residual value) ÷ useful life (years)LEARN IT
Units of production: depreciation per unit = (cost − residual value) ÷ expected lifetime units; annual = per unit × units producedLEARN IT
Net book value (NBV) = cost − accumulated depreciationLEARN IT
Worked example: oven costing $60,000, residual value $10,000, life 5 years or 250,000 batches
YearBatchesStraight lineNBV (SL)Units of production ($0.20 × batches)NBV (UoP)
140,00010,00050,0008,00052,000
270,00010,00040,00014,00038,000
360,00010,00030,00012,00026,000
450,00010,00020,00010,00016,000
530,00010,00010,0006,00010,000

Per-unit rate = (60,000 − 10,000) ÷ 250,000 = $0.20 per batch. Both methods end at the $10,000 residual value; only the timing differs.

Straight lineUnits of production
Strengths
  • Simple
  • Same charge each year
  • Easy to compare and budget
  • Matches expense to actual use
  • More accurate for machines
Weaknesses
  • Ignores how much the asset is used
  • Many assets lose more value early
  • Needs reliable output forecasts and records
  • Uneven profit
Best forAssets that lose value with time: buildings, furniture, office equipmentAssets that wear with use: machinery, vehicles (by km), ovens
Straight lineUnits of production
Strengths
  • It is simple.
  • The charge is the same each year.
  • It is easy to compare and budget.
  • The expense matches actual use.
  • It is more accurate for machines.
Weaknesses
  • It ignores how much the asset is used.
  • Many assets lose more value early on.
  • It needs reliable output forecasts and records.
  • Profit becomes uneven.
Best forIt suits assets that lose value with time, such as buildings, furniture and office equipment.It suits assets that wear with use, such as machinery, vehicles (by distance) and ovens.

Exam corner: 3.4

Exam tips

  • Lay out the statements in the standard order, with labelled subtotals.
  • Show your workings beside each figure.
  • Always check that net assets equal equity.
  • When asked to amend the accounts, trace every knock-on effect. For example, higher depreciation lowers profit, which lowers retained profit, which lowers equity and the net book value of the assets.

Common pitfalls

  • Don't put the cost of sales among the expenses, or an overdraft among the non-current liabilities.
  • Don't treat depreciation as cash. It is an accounting cost, and no money leaves the business when it is recorded.
  • Remember that dividends are paid out of profit after tax.
  • Don't call debtors a liability. Debtors are an asset, because they are money owed to the firm.

Model answers

AO4 Sunrise Bakery's expenses rise by $12,000. Calculate the new retained profit. [3]

PBIT = 160,000 − 112,000 = 48,000. PBT = 48,000 − 10,000 = 38,000. Tax = 20% × 38,000 = 7,600. PAT = 30,400. Retained profit = 30,400 − 15,000 = $15,400.

Mark scheme: 1 for PBIT/PBT, 1 for tax, 1 for correct final answer with working.

AO2 Explain why a bank lender would look at Sunrise Bakery's balance sheet. [4]

K The balance sheet shows assets that could secure a loan and existing debts. App E Sunrise has $270,000 of property and equipment, which could act as collateral, reducing the lender's risk. It also has a $100,000 loan and a $15,000 overdraft, so the bank can judge whether extra borrowing would make the firm too highly geared to repay.

AO3 HL Discuss which depreciation method Sunrise should use for its delivery vans. [6]

Vans wear out mainly through use (kilometres driven), so units of production matches depreciation to actual wear. If deliveries vary a lot between years, this gives a truer profit figure. However, it needs accurate mileage records and forecasts, and makes profit uneven. Straight line is simpler and adequate if annual mileage is fairly steady. If Sunrise's delivery volumes are seasonal or growing, units of production is more appropriate; otherwise straight line is acceptable for its simplicity.

Intangible value of reputation, customers and brand (1) above the value of net assets, usually recorded when a business is bought (1).
AO4 Construct a profit and loss account: revenue 250,000; COGS 140,000; expenses 70,000; interest 5,000; tax 25%; dividends 10,000. [4]
GP 110,000; PBIT 40,000; PBT 35,000; tax 8,750; PAT 26,250; retained 16,250.
AO4 HL A van costs $32,000, residual $4,000, life 4 years. Calculate straight-line depreciation and NBV after 2 years. [2]
(32,000 − 4,000) ÷ 4 = $7,000 a year (1); NBV = 32,000 − 14,000 = $18,000 (1).
3.5

Profitability and liquidity ratio analysis

Real company case
Tesco and Apple: why margins differ

Profit margins vary hugely between industries. Tesco, the UK's largest supermarket, keeps only a few pence of profit from every £1 of sales, because grocery is fiercely competitive; it makes money through enormous volume. Apple kept about 24 cents of profit from every $1 of sales in 2024, because customers pay premium prices for its brand. This is why ratios should be compared with the firm's own past and with direct rivals, not across industries.

Apply it: Explain why comparing Tesco's profit margin with Apple's would be misleading.

Read more: Tesco (Wikipedia)

Practice firm for the worked answers · made-up numbers

Sunrise Bakery Ltd (from 3.4): revenue $400,000; gross profit $160,000; profit before interest and tax $60,000; capital employed $340,000; current assets $90,000 (stock $40,000); current liabilities $50,000. Last year: GPM 44%, profit margin 18%, ROCE 21%, current ratio 1.4:1. A rival bakery chain has GPM 42%, profit margin 12%, ROCE 15%.

Syllabus map

Syllabus pointHighest AOYou must be able to
Gross profit margin, profit margin, ROCEAO2AO4Calculate, interpret and compare over time and with rivals
Strategies to improve profitability ratiosAO3Evaluate strategies and their trade-offs
Current ratio, acid-test ratioAO2AO4Calculate and interpret liquidity
Strategies to improve liquidity ratiosAO3Evaluate strategies and their trade-offs

Key terms AO1

Ratio analysis
Comparing figures from the accounts to judge performance, over time and against other firms.
Profitability
The ability to generate profit from sales or from the capital invested.
Liquidity
The ability to pay short-term debts as they fall due.
Capital employed
Total long-term finance: non-current liabilities + equity.
Window dressing
Presenting accounts to look better than reality at the balance sheet date.
Solvency
The ability of a business to meet all its financial obligations, especially its long-term debts.

Profitability ratios AO2AO4

Gross profit margin (GPM) = gross profit ÷ sales revenue × 100ON THE SHEET
Profit margin = profit before interest and tax ÷ sales revenue × 100ON THE SHEET
ROCE = profit before interest and tax ÷ capital employed × 100ON THE SHEET
RatioCalculationThis yearLast yearRivalInterpretation
GPM160,000 ÷ 400,000 × 10040%44%42%Each $1 of sales leaves 40¢ after direct costs. Falling: ingredient costs rising faster than prices
Profit margin60,000 ÷ 400,000 × 10015%18%12%Still beats the rival, so overheads are well controlled, but the fall in GPM feeds through
ROCE60,000 ÷ 340,000 × 10017.6%21%15%
  • Good return on capital, above typical loan interest rates
  • But falling
How the exam formulae sheet shows theseThe sheet lists gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE together, all using profit before interest and tax where profit is needed, and defines capital employed = non-current liabilities + equity. You are given these formulas in the exam, but you still have to choose the right figures from the accounts.
Reading GPM and profit margin togetherThe gap between GPM and profit margin shows overheads as a % of sales: 40% − 15% = 25%. If GPM is steady but profit margin falls, overheads are the problem. If both fall equally, direct costs or prices are the problem.
The case in brief: Tesco and Apple
  • Low margin, high volume: Tesco keeps a few pence per £1 because grocery is fiercely competitive, but it sells in enormous volume.
  • High margin: Apple keeps about 24 cents per $1 thanks to premium prices.
  • Lesson: compare ratios within an industry, not across industries.

Liquidity ratios AO2AO4

Current ratio = current assets ÷ current liabilitiesON THE SHEET
Acid-test (quick) ratio = (current assets − stock) ÷ current liabilitiesON THE SHEET
RatioCalculationResultRule of thumbInterpretation
Current ratio90,000 ÷ 50,0001.8 : 1About 1.5–2 : 1
  • Comfortable
  • Improved from 1.4
Acid test(90,000 − 40,000) ÷ 50,0001.0 : 1About 1 : 1Can just pay short-term debts without selling stock

Too low

The firm risks being unable to pay its suppliers, its wages or its overdraft. It may need emergency finance, and it risks becoming insolvent.

Too high

Cash or stock sitting idle; could be invested; stock may go out of date (bread!). Liquidity and profitability trade off.

Why acid test? Stock is the least liquid current asset; it may be slow to sell or perishable. Acceptable levels differ by industry: supermarkets often run acid-test ratios well below 1 because they sell stock for cash before paying suppliers.

Strategies to improve the ratios AO3

RatioStrategyTrade-off to evaluate
GPMRaise pricesVolume may fall if demand is price elastic
Cheaper suppliers, bulk buying, reduce waste
  • Quality and reputation risk
  • Supplier relations
Shift sales mix towards higher-margin productsMay lose customers who want the cheaper items
Profit marginCut overheads: energy, rent renegotiation, admin, marketingCuts may harm service or growth
Improve GPM (all of the above)As above
ROCEIncrease PBIT (as above)As above
Reduce capital employed: sell unused assets, repay long-term debt
  • Less capacity for growth
  • One-off effect
Current / acid testIncrease cash: collect debts faster, sale and leaseback, inject capital
  • Customers may go elsewhere
  • Leaseback adds rent
Reduce current liabilities: convert overdraft into a long-term loanRaises gearing and interest
Reduce stock (raises acid test relative to current)Stock-out risk
RatioStrategyTrade-off to evaluate
GPMRaise prices.Sales volume may fall if demand is price elastic.
Use cheaper suppliers, buy in bulk and reduce waste.
  • Quality and reputation may suffer.
  • Supplier relations may be strained.
Shift the sales mix towards higher-margin products.Customers who want the cheaper items may go elsewhere.
Profit marginCut overheads, such as energy, rent, administration and marketing.Cuts may harm service or growth.
Improve the gross profit margin in the ways above.The same trade-offs apply.
ROCEIncrease profit before interest and tax in the ways above.The same trade-offs apply.
Reduce capital employed by selling unused assets or repaying long-term debt.
  • Less capacity is left for growth.
  • The effect is one-off.
Current / acid testIncrease cash by collecting debts faster, using a sale and leaseback or asking owners to inject capital.
  • Customers may go elsewhere.
  • A leaseback adds rent.
Reduce current liabilities by turning an overdraft into a long-term loan.Gearing and interest costs rise.
Reduce stock, which raises the acid test relative to the current ratio.The firm risks running out of stock.

Limitations of ratio analysis AO3

  • Ratios are based on past data, so they are not a forecast.
  • The balance sheet is a snapshot of one day, and firms can "window dress" it to look better.
  • Comparisons can be distorted by different accounting policies, year-ends, sizes and industries.
  • Inflation can distort trends over time.
  • Ratios ignore qualitative factors such as staff morale, the brand, customer satisfaction, ethics and the state of the economy.
  • A ratio shows what has changed, but not why, so the causes must be investigated.

Exam corner: 3.5

Exam tips

  • Write the formula, substitute the figures and give the answer with units (a percentage, or x : 1). Two decimal places is plenty.
  • Compare each ratio with a benchmark: last year, a rival or the industry average.
  • For each ratio, explain one cause and one implication.
  • When you suggest an improvement, always give its trade-off.

Common pitfalls

  • Don't use profit after tax in ROCE or the profit margin. Use profit before interest and tax.
  • Don't write the current ratio as a percentage. It is written as x : 1.
  • Don't say that a higher liquidity ratio is always better. Too much cash or stock is idle money that earns nothing.
  • Don't forget to subtract stock in the acid-test ratio.

Model answer

AO3 Evaluate strategies Sunrise Bakery could use to improve its gross profit margin. [10]

K Gross profit margin shows gross profit as a percentage of revenue. Sunrise's GPM fell from 44% to 40%, below the rival's 42%.

E Raise prices: a 5% price rise on bread with loyal local customers could restore margin quickly. But if demand is price elastic, or the rival keeps prices low, volume could fall, reducing total gross profit despite a higher margin.

E Reduce cost of sales: negotiating bulk flour contracts across three shops, or cutting waste of unsold bread through better forecasting, lowers COGS without customers noticing. Cheaper ingredients, however, could damage the quality that justifies Sunrise's prices.

E Change the sales mix: promoting higher-margin products such as cakes and coffee raises average margin, but depends on demand for those items.

Ev Overall, reducing waste and negotiating supplier prices is the best first step because it raises margin without risking customers. A small price rise on premium lines could follow. Sunrise should first find out why GPM fell (ingredient inflation or waste?), since the right strategy depends on the cause, which the ratio alone does not show.

GPM = 100,000 ÷ 250,000 × 100 = 40% (1). Profit margin = 40,000 ÷ 250,000 × 100 = 16% (1).
AO4 Current assets $72,000 (stock $30,000); current liabilities $48,000. Calculate both liquidity ratios. [2]
Current ratio 1.5 : 1; acid test (72,000 − 30,000) ÷ 48,000 = 0.875 : 1.

Faster debt collection, sale of assets, equity injection, refinancing overdraft long term, reduce stock; trade-offs; depends on industry norms.
3.6

Debt/equity ratio analysis

HL
Real company case
Tesco and Zara: efficiency in practice

Supermarkets sell most food within days but often pay suppliers weeks later, so suppliers help finance them. In 2016 the UK's Groceries Code Adjudicator found that Tesco had delayed payments to suppliers to improve its own financial position. Long creditor days help a retailer's cash flow, but abusing them damages supplier relationships and reputation.

Fashion retailer Zara shows fast stock turnover: it makes small batches and restocks stores twice a week, so little money is tied up in unsold clothes.

Apply it: Explain how long creditor days affect both a supermarket and its suppliers.

Read more: Groceries Code Adjudicator (Wikipedia)

Practice firm for the worked answers · made-up numbers

Sunrise Bakery Ltd: COGS $240,000; opening stock $36,000; closing stock $40,000; revenue $400,000 (of which $120,000 is credit sales to cafés and offices); debtors $30,000; creditors $35,000; non-current liabilities $100,000; capital employed $340,000.

Syllabus map

Syllabus pointHighest AOYou must be able to
Stock turnover, debtor days, creditor days, gearingAO2AO4Calculate and interpret, compare with benchmarks
Strategies to improve efficiency ratiosAO3Evaluate strategies and trade-offs
Insolvency vs bankruptcyAO2Distinguish and explain causes

The efficiency ratios AO2AO4

Stock turnover (times) = cost of goods sold ÷ average stockON THE SHEET
Stock turnover (days) = average stock ÷ cost of goods sold × 365ON THE SHEET
Average stock = (opening stock + closing stock) ÷ 2ON THE SHEET
Debtor days = debtors ÷ total sales revenue × 365ON THE SHEET
Creditor days = creditors ÷ cost of goods sold × 365ON THE SHEET
Gearing ratio = non-current liabilities ÷ capital employed × 100ON THE SHEET
RatioCalculationResultInterpretation for a bakery
Stock turnover (times)240,000 ÷ 38,0006.3 times
  • Low for a bakery: fresh goods should turn over far faster
  • Stock may include slow non-food lines or waste
Stock turnover (days)38,000 ÷ 240,000 × 36557.8 daysIngredients held for nearly two months: cash tied up and spoilage risk
Debtor days30,000 ÷ 400,000 × 36527.4 days
  • On average customers pay within a month
  • Reasonable for corporate orders
Creditor days35,000 ÷ 240,000 × 36553.2 daysSunrise pays suppliers after ~53 days, longer than it waits for customers: good for cash flow, but suppliers may object
Gearing100,000 ÷ 340,000 × 10029.4%
  • Low to moderate (below 25% low, above 50% high)
  • Room to borrow
Debtor days and credit salesThe IB formula uses total sales revenue. If only $120,000 is credit sales, using total sales understates how long credit customers really take (30,000 ÷ 120,000 × 365 = 91 days). Mention this as a limitation if the case gives credit sales.

Strategies to improve efficiency AO3

RatioStrategyTrade-off
Stock turnoverJIT ordering, better demand forecasting, clear slow-moving lines with discounts, reduce product range
  • Stock-out risk
  • Supplier reliability
  • Lost sales
Debtor days (reduce)Shorter credit terms, early-payment discounts, credit checks, chasing late payers
  • Customers may switch to rivals
  • Discounts cut revenue
  • Collection takes staff time
Creditor days (increase)Negotiate longer credit terms, pay on the last allowed day
  • Lose early-payment discounts
  • Damage supplier relations
Gearing (reduce)Issue shares, use retained profit to repay loans, sell assets
  • Dilutes control
  • Less cash for investment
Gearing (increase, if low)Borrow to invest when ROCE exceeds the interest rateHigher interest burden and risk if rates or sales change
RatioStrategyTrade-off
Stock turnoverUse JIT ordering, forecast demand better, clear slow-moving lines with discounts and reduce the product range.
  • The firm may run out of stock.
  • It depends on reliable suppliers.
  • Sales may be lost.
Debtor days (reduce)Shorten credit terms, offer early-payment discounts, check customers' credit and chase late payers.
  • Customers may switch to rivals.
  • Discounts cut revenue.
  • Chasing debts takes staff time.
Creditor days (increase)Negotiate longer credit terms and pay on the last allowed day.
  • The firm loses early-payment discounts.
  • Supplier relations may suffer.
Gearing (reduce)Issue shares, use retained profit to repay loans or sell assets.
  • Control is diluted.
  • Less cash is left for investment.
Gearing (increase, if low)Borrow to invest when ROCE is higher than the interest rate.The interest burden and risk rise if rates rise or sales fall.
The case in brief: Supermarkets and Zara
  • Creditor days: supermarkets pay suppliers weeks later, but delayed payments damage relationships.
  • Stock turnover: Zara restocks twice a week, so little cash is tied up in stock.

Insolvency vs bankruptcy AO2

InsolvencyBankruptcy
MeaningA financial state: unable to pay debts as they fall due (or liabilities exceed assets)A legal process declared by a court, usually for individuals (sole traders, partners), to deal with debts they cannot pay
Applies toIndividuals and companies
  • Individuals
  • Companies go into liquidation or administration
Possible outcomesRescue (refinancing, restructuring), administration or liquidation
  • Assets sold to repay creditors
  • Restrictions on the person
InsolvencyBankruptcy
MeaningIt is a financial state: the firm cannot pay its debts as they fall due, or its liabilities exceed its assets.It is a legal process, declared by a court, usually for individuals such as sole traders and partners who cannot pay their debts.
Applies toIt applies to individuals and companies.
  • It applies to individuals.
  • Companies instead go into liquidation or administration.
Possible outcomesThe firm may be rescued by refinancing or restructuring, or it may go into administration or liquidation.
  • Assets are sold to repay creditors.
  • Restrictions are placed on the person.

A profitable firm can still become insolvent if cash runs out: poor liquidity, overtrading, long debtor days and high stock levels are warning signs (link to 3.7).

Exam corner: 3.6

Exam tips

  • Compare debtor days with creditor days to see whether cash comes in before it has to go out.
  • Judge stock turnover against the product: fresh food should turn over far faster than furniture.
  • Gearing above 50% means the firm is highly geared, so explain the risk if interest rates rise.

Common pitfalls

  • Don't use closing stock instead of average stock in stock turnover.
  • Don't use revenue in creditor days. Use the cost of sales.
  • Don't say that insolvency and bankruptcy are the same. Insolvency means being unable to pay debts on time, while bankruptcy is the legal process that follows for an individual.

Practice questions (tap to reveal the marking points)

AO4 Opening stock $20,000, closing $30,000, COGS $200,000. Calculate stock turnover in times and days. [2]
Average 25,000; 200,000 ÷ 25,000 = 8 times; 25,000 ÷ 200,000 × 365 = 45.6 days.
AO2 Explain why high gearing increases risk for a business. [4]
Interest must be paid regardless of profit; rising rates raise costs; lenders may refuse more credit; shareholders' returns more volatile.
AO3 Evaluate strategies Sunrise could use to improve its stock turnover. [10]
JIT for flour, daily forecasting, fewer product lines, discounting near-expiry goods vs stock-outs, supplier reliability, lost sales. Judgement.
3.7

Cash flow

Real company case
Carillion (UK): profitable on paper, out of cash

Carillion, one of the UK's largest construction and services firms with about 43,000 staff worldwide, collapsed in January 2018. It had reported profits and paid dividends for years, but much of that profit sat in long contracts where the cash would arrive later, if at all. It protected its cash by paying suppliers slowly, with terms of up to 120 days, while its debts grew.

When it admitted large losses on contracts in 2017, lenders refused further credit and it ran out of cash. Thousands of small suppliers were left unpaid. Profit depends on accounting judgements; cash is what pays the bills.

Apply it: Explain how Carillion could report a profit while running out of cash.

Read more: Carillion (Wikipedia)

Practice firm for the worked answers · made-up numbers

BlueWave Kayaks rents kayaks and sells tours at a beach resort from April to October. It made a profit of $48,000 last year, yet in March it could not pay its insurance bill. It buys 10 new kayaks ($12,000) every March, pays staff from April, and most tour revenue comes through a booking platform that pays 45 days after each tour.

Syllabus map

Syllabus pointHighest AOYou must be able to
Profit vs cash flowAO2Explain why a profitable firm can run out of cash
  • Working capital
  • Cash-flow forecasts
AO2AO4
  • Construct, complete and interpret a cash-flow forecast
  • Calculate working capital
Investment, profit and cash flowAO2Explain how investment affects cash now and profit later
Strategies for cash-flow problemsAO3Evaluate and recommend strategies

Key terms AO1

Cash flow
The movement of money into (inflows) and out of (outflows) a business over a period.
Net cash flow
Cash inflows − cash outflows for a period.
Opening / closing balance
The cash held at the start or the end of a period. The closing balance equals the opening balance plus the net cash flow, and it becomes the next period's opening balance.
Cash-flow forecast
A prediction of future cash inflows and outflows, usually month by month.
Working capital
Current assets − current liabilities: the funds available for day-to-day operations.
Working capital cycle
The time between paying for inputs and receiving cash from customers.
Liquidity position
How easily a firm can meet short-term obligations.
Overtrading
Expanding too quickly without enough working capital to fund it.
Credit terms
The period a business allows customers to pay for goods or services bought on credit, or that suppliers allow it.
Bad debt
Money owed by a customer that will not be paid, so the business must write it off as a loss.

Profit vs cash flow AO2

ProfitCash flow
MeasuresRevenue − costs over a period (accounting)Actual money in and out (timing)
Credit salesCounted when the sale is madeCounted when the customer pays (45 days later for BlueWave)
Buying an assetSpread over years as depreciationFull $12,000 leaves in March
DepreciationReduces profitNo cash movement
Loans and capital injectionsNot revenueCash inflow
Loan repayments, owner drawingsNot expenses (only interest is)Cash outflow
ProfitCash flow
MeasuresProfit is revenue minus costs over a period, an accounting measure.Cash flow is the actual money in and out, so timing matters.
Credit salesA credit sale counts when the sale is made.A credit sale counts when the customer pays, 45 days later for BlueWave.
Buying an assetThe cost of an asset is spread over several years as depreciation.The full $12,000 leaves the bank in March.
DepreciationDepreciation reduces profit.Depreciation involves no cash.
Loans and capital injectionsLoans and capital injections are not revenue.Loans and capital injections are cash inflows.
Loan repayments, owner drawingsLoan repayments and owner drawings are not expenses; only interest is.Loan repayments and owner drawings are cash outflows.
Why it mattersProfit is needed in the long run; cash is needed every day. Firms usually fail because they run out of cash, not because they are unprofitable. BlueWave is profitable over the year but cash-poor in March, before the season starts.
The case in brief: Carillion
  • Profit is not cash: it reported profits and paid dividends, but cash would arrive later, if at all.
  • Hidden problem: it paid suppliers in up to 120 days.
  • Collapse: lenders refused credit, and thousands of suppliers went unpaid.

Working capital AO2AO4

Working capital = current assets − current liabilitiesLEARN IT

Too little working capital means bills can't be paid; too much means cash is idle. Shortening the cycle (selling stock faster, collecting debts sooner) and lengthening supplier credit both free cash.

Investment, profit and cash flow: investing (new kayaks, a new shop) causes a large cash outflow now, may reduce profit in the short term through depreciation and interest, and should raise revenue and profit later. Rapid growth needs more stock and more debtors, so a growing firm can run short of cash: overtrading.

Cash-flow forecasts AO2AO4

BlueWave Kayaks ($)MarchAprilMayJune
Opening balance6,000−9,500−11,700−3,900
Cash inflows: walk-in rentals04,0007,00010,000
Platform tour revenue (paid 45 days later)006,00012,000
Total inflows04,00013,00022,000
Cash outflows: new kayaks12,000000
Wages04,0004,0006,000

Interpretation: BlueWave needs an overdraft of at least $12,000 for March to May. The problem is timing, not profitability: by June the balance is positive and rising.

How to complete a forecast (AO4)

1
Total the inflows for each month.
2
Total the outflows for each month.
3
Net cash flow = inflows − outflows (keep the sign).
4
Closing balance = opening + net cash flow.
5
Carry forward: closing balance becomes next month's opening balance.

Benefits of forecasts

  • A forecast shows shortfalls early, so the firm can arrange finance in advance.
  • Banks usually ask for one before they lend.
  • It helps the firm time its investment and spending.
  • Comparing actual cash flow with the forecast helps managers control spending.

Limitations

  • A forecast is based on estimates, and the weather, demand and prices can all change.
  • New firms have little past data to base their forecasts on.
  • Customers may pay late, and unexpected costs can arise.
  • A forecast is only as good as the assumptions behind it.

Causes of cash-flow problems AO2

Long credit given to customersPlatform pays 45 days after tours
Large capital expenditure$12,000 of kayaks bought in one month

Choosing a strategyMatch it to the cause and duration: a seasonal timing gap suits an overdraft and winter deposits; a permanent gap (costs exceed revenue) needs a structural fix (pricing, costs), not more borrowing.

Exam corner: 3.7

Exam tips

  • In forecast questions, show every subtotal and carry each closing balance forward correctly.
  • Identify the month or months with a shortage, and the amount of finance needed.
  • Separate timing problems, where cash arrives too late, from profitability problems, where costs are too high.

Common pitfalls

  • Don't include depreciation as a cash outflow.
  • Don't record credit sales in the month of the sale. Record them in the month the customer pays.
  • Don't recommend "increase sales" as a cash-flow fix without discussing when that money would actually arrive.
  • Don't confuse cash with profit.

Model answer

AO2 Explain why BlueWave could not pay its insurance bill despite making a profit. [4]

K Profit measures revenue minus costs over a year, while cash flow depends on when money actually moves. App E BlueWave earns almost all revenue from April to October and the platform pays 45 days late, so by March its cash from last season has been used up. In the same month it pays $12,000 for kayaks and its insurance, so outflows exceed the cash available even though the year as a whole is profitable.

AO3 Recommend how BlueWave should solve its cash-flow problem. [10]

App The forecast shows a shortfall from March to May, peaking at $11,700 in April, before turning positive in June. E Because the gap is seasonal and temporary, an arranged overdraft of around $12,000 is suitable: interest is paid only for three months, and June inflows repay it. The risk is that a poor season (bad weather) delays repayment.

E BlueWave could also cut the peak need: leasing kayaks instead of buying $12,000 in March removes the largest outflow, though it costs more over time; paying insurance monthly spreads $2,500 across the year. Selling season passes with a deposit in February would bring cash forward, at the cost of a discount.

Ev Recommendation: combine a small overdraft with monthly insurance payments and early-season deposits. This tackles the timing problem cheaply without giving up ownership. Leasing makes sense only if the kayaks are replaced frequently. Because forecasts depend on the weather and bookings, BlueWave should agree the overdraft limit with headroom (e.g. $15,000) and review the forecast monthly.

Practice questions (tap to reveal the marking points)

AO4 Opening balance $2,000; inflows $9,000; outflows $12,500. Calculate the closing balance. [2]
Net = −3,500 (1); closing = −$1,500 (1).
AO2 Explain the relationship between investment, profit and cash flow. [4]
Investment = immediate outflow; profit affected over time via depreciation and extra revenue; cash recovers later; overtrading risk.
AO3 Evaluate the use of an overdraft to solve BlueWave's cash-flow problem. [10]
Flexible, interest only on what is used, matches a seasonal gap, quick to arrange vs high interest, can be withdrawn, does not fix a permanent gap between costs and revenue. Compare with deposits, leasing, monthly insurance. Judgement on the size and length of the gap.
3.8

Investment appraisal

Real company case
TSMC (Taiwan): a $165 billion investment decision

TSMC makes most of the world's most advanced computer chips. It announced its first Arizona factory in 2020 at about $12 billion, later raised its US plans to $65 billion, and in 2025 added a further $100 billion, for about $165 billion in total. Building in the USA costs more than in Taiwan, but it puts TSMC closer to customers such as Apple and Nvidia and earned about $6.6 billion of US government grants.

Decisions like this rely on investment appraisal: estimating cash flows many years ahead, then judging payback, average rate of return and net present value, while costs, demand and politics all remain uncertain.

Apply it: Explain why net present value is more useful than the payback period for an investment like this.

Read more: TSMC (Wikipedia)

Practice firm for the worked answers · made-up numbers

Olive Grove Hotel has $60,000 to invest and two options over 4 years. Project A: a rooftop restaurant, net cash inflows $20,000, $25,000, $30,000, $30,000. Project B: solar panels, $40,000, $30,000, $20,000, $5,000 (savings fall as panels age and electricity prices are expected to drop). The bank charges 10% interest.

Syllabus map

Syllabus pointHighest AOYou must be able to
Payback and ARRAO3AO4Calculate both, interpret and use them to recommend a project
NPV (HL)AO3AO4Calculate with given discount factors and evaluate

Key terms AO1

Investment appraisal
Quantitative and qualitative methods used to judge whether an investment is worthwhile, or to choose between projects.
Net cash flow
Cash inflows minus cash outflows from the project each year.
Payback period
The time it takes for cumulative net cash inflows to repay the initial investment.
Average rate of return (ARR)
The average annual profit from a project as a percentage of the initial investment.
Time value of money
$1 today is worth more than $1 in the future, because it could be invested or earn interest now.
Discount factor
A multiplier (given in tables) that converts a future cash flow into its present value at a chosen interest rate.
Net present value (NPV)
The sum of discounted future net cash flows minus the initial investment.
Investment
Spending on capital assets, such as machinery, buildings or technology, that are expected to bring returns in the future.

Payback period AO4

YearA: net cash flowA: cumulativeB: net cash flowB: cumulative
0(60,000)(60,000)(60,000)(60,000)
120,000(40,000)40,000(20,000)
225,000(15,000)30,00010,000
330,00015,00020,00030,000
430,00045,0005,00035,000
Payback in the final part-year = amount still needed ÷ cash flow in that year × 12 monthsLEARN IT
Workings

A: after year 2, $15,000 still needed; year 3 earns $30,000 → 15,000 ÷ 30,000 × 12 = 6 months. Payback = 2 years 6 months.
B: after year 1, $20,000 still needed; year 2 earns $30,000 → 20,000 ÷ 30,000 × 12 = 8 months. Payback = 1 year 8 months.

Average rate of return AO4

ARR = (total returns − capital cost) ÷ years of use ÷ capital cost × 100ON THE SHEET
Project AProject B
Total returns20 + 25 + 30 + 30 = $105,00040 + 30 + 20 + 5 = $95,000
Total profit (returns − cost)$45,000$35,000
Average annual profit (÷ 4)$11,250$8,750
ARR (÷ 60,000 × 100)18.75%14.58%

Both beat the 10% bank rate, so both earn more than the cost of borrowing.

Net present value HL AO4

NPV = sum of (net cash flow × discount factor) − initial investmentON THE SHEET
YearDiscount factor at 10%A: present valueB: present value

20.82620,65024,780
30.75122,53015,020
40.68320,4903,415
Total PV81,85079,575
NPV (− 60,000)+21,850+19,575

Decision rule: accept if NPV > 0; choose the project with the higher NPV. A wins, but by less than ARR suggests, because B's cash arrives earlier and is discounted less.

Comparing the methods AO3

MethodStrengthsWeaknessesOlive Grove result
Payback

  • Focuses on liquidity and risk
  • Good when the future is uncertain or technology changes fast
  • Ignores cash after payback
  • Ignores profitability
  • Ignores the time value of money (within payback)
B better (1y 8m vs 2y 6m)

  • Uses all cash flows
  • % easy to compare with interest rates and targets
  • Ignores timing of cash
  • Treats year-4 money like year-1 money
A better (18.75% vs 14.58%)

  • Accounts for the time value of money
  • Shows absolute value added
  • Choice of discount rate is subjective
  • Harder to understand

A better (+$21,850 vs +$19,575)
MethodStrengthsWeaknessesOlive Grove result
Payback
  • It is simple.
  • It focuses on liquidity and risk.
  • It helps when the future is uncertain or technology changes fast.
  • It ignores cash received after payback.
  • It ignores profitability.
  • It ignores the time value of money within the payback period.
Project B is better: it pays back in 1 year 8 months, against 2 years 6 months.
ARR
  • It uses all the cash flows.
  • Its percentage is easy to compare with interest rates and targets.
  • It ignores the timing of cash.
  • It treats money in year 4 as if it were worth the same as money in year 1.
Project A is better: 18.75%, against 14.58%.
When the methods disagreePayback favours fast, safe returns; ARR and NPV favour total profitability. Decide using the firm's priorities: a cash-strapped or risk-averse firm values payback; a firm seeking long-term returns values ARR/NPV.

The case in brief: TSMC in the US
  • Weak numbers: a $165 billion plan, where production costs more than in Taiwan.
  • Qualitative reasons: closer to Apple and Nvidia, plus $6.6 billion in grants.
  • Limitation: costs, demand and politics are uncertain, so forecasts are estimates.

Exam corner: 3.8

Exam tips

  • Lay out a table of cumulative cash flows, because it makes the payback point easy to see.
  • Convert the payback period into years and months.
  • Compare the ARR with the interest rate the firm could earn or would pay.
  • End with a decision that also uses qualitative factors.

Common pitfalls

  • Don't forget to subtract the initial cost before working out the average annual profit for ARR.
  • Don't divide by the total returns. Divide the average annual profit by the capital cost.
  • Don't write the payback as "2.5 years" when the question asks for years and months.
  • In NPV, don't multiply the year 0 cost by a discount factor. Money spent today is already in today's value.

Model answer

AO3 Recommend which project Olive Grove Hotel should choose. [10]

App Project B pays back faster (1 year 8 months vs 2 years 6 months), but Project A has a higher ARR (18.75% vs 14.58%) and a higher NPV ($21,850 vs $19,575).

E A creates more value overall, and its later cash flows grow, which suits a long-term investment. B's quick payback reduces risk, important if the hotel's cash is tight or if solar savings are uncertain, but its returns collapse in year 4 as panels age and electricity prices fall.

E Qualitative factors pull both ways: the restaurant depends on tourism and needs staff and planning permission; solar panels support a sustainability brand and protect against energy price rises if forecasts are wrong.

Ev Recommendation: choose Project A, because it is more profitable on both ARR and NPV and both projects beat the 10% cost of borrowing. However, if the hotel's priority is liquidity or reducing risk in an uncertain tourism market, B is safer. The decision depends on the reliability of the restaurant's forecasts, which should be tested with market research before committing.

Practice questions (tap to reveal the marking points)

AO4 A $50,000 machine returns $15,000, $20,000, $25,000, $10,000. Calculate payback. [2]
After year 2: $15,000 still needed; 15,000 ÷ 25,000 × 12 = 7.2 months → 2 years 7 months.
AO4 Calculate ARR for the same machine. [2]
Total returns 70,000; profit 20,000; ÷ 4 = 5,000; ÷ 50,000 × 100 = 10%.

Simple, liquidity focus, suits uncertain or fast-changing tech vs ignores later cash flows and profitability, time value. Judge alongside ARR/NPV.
3.9

Budgets

HL
Real company case
London 2012 Olympics: from £2.4bn to £9.3bn

When London bid for the 2012 Olympic Games in 2005, the public budget was about £2.4 billion. In 2007 the government replaced it with a budget of £9.3 billion, after adding security, tax, higher construction costs and a large contingency fund. The Games were finally delivered slightly under the revised budget.

The case shows why budgets need realistic assumptions and a contingency, and why variance analysis only helps when the budget was sensible in the first place.

Apply it: Calculate the variance between the two budgets and state whether it is favourable or adverse.

Read more: Cost of the 2012 Olympics (Wikipedia)

Practice firm for the worked answers · made-up numbers

Marina Sports Club has a gym, a café and a swimming school, each run as a profit centre, plus maintenance and administration as cost centres. Last quarter the café's revenue was $4,000 below budget, food costs were $2,500 over budget, and staff costs were $1,000 under budget because two staff left.

Syllabus map

Syllabus pointHighest AOYou must be able to
  • Cost vs profit centres
  • Their roles
AO2Distinguish and explain benefits and problems
  • Constructing a budget
  • Variances
AO2AO4
  • Build a budget
  • Calculate and label variances favourable/adverse
Importance of budgets and variancesAO2Explain how they support planning, control and decisions

Key terms AO1

Budget
A financial plan for a future period, setting targets for revenue, costs or profit.
Cost centre
A part of the business that incurs costs but does not directly earn revenue (maintenance, HR, IT).
Profit centre
A part of the business that earns revenue and incurs costs, so its profit can be measured (a shop, a product line).
Variance
The difference between a budgeted figure and the actual figure.
Favourable variance
A variance that makes profit higher than budgeted (revenue above, or costs below, budget).
Adverse variance
A variance that makes profit lower than budgeted (revenue below, or costs above, budget).
Zero-based budgeting
Every item must be justified from zero each period. Historical (incremental) budgeting adjusts last year's figures.
Budget holder
The manager responsible for a budget, who must keep spending within it and explain variances.
Flexible budget
A budget that is adjusted to the actual level of output, so that costs can be compared fairly with what they should have been at that output.

Cost and profit centres AO2

Benefits

  • Cost and profit centres show which parts of the business make or lose money.
  • Managers are held accountable for their centre, and the delegated responsibility can motivate them (Herzberg).
  • Costs are controlled better, and problems are spotted sooner.
  • They help managers decide on pricing, investment or closing a part of the business.

Problems

  • Dividing shared overheads, such as the rent for a building, between centres is arbitrary and can distort the results.
  • Centres may compete with each other instead of cooperating.
  • They create extra administration and reporting.
  • A centre's results may be affected by factors outside its manager's control.

Constructing a budget AO4

Steps

1
Set objectives for the period (e.g. café profit $15,000 per quarter).
2
Forecast sales using past data, market research and trends (HL: 4.3).
3
Budget costs item by item: materials, labour, overheads.
4
Agree with managers who will be responsible (involvement aids motivation).
5
Monitor actual results monthly and calculate variances.
6
Act on significant variances and revise the budget if conditions change.

Variance analysis AO4

Café ($)BudgetActualVarianceF / A
Revenue50,00046,0004,000Adverse
Food costs20,00022,5002,500Adverse
Staff costs10,0009,0001,000Favourable
Overheads5,0005,0000—
Profit15,0009,5005,500Adverse
Check the profit variance−4,000 (revenue) − 2,500 (food) + 1,000 (staff) = −5,500. Label variances in words (favourable/adverse) rather than relying on signs, since sign conventions differ between textbooks.
VariancePossible causesPossible action
Revenue adverseFewer members, poor weather, competition, prices too highPromotions, menu review, research
Food costs adverseSupplier price rises, waste, theft, more portionsRenegotiate, portion control, stock checks

  • Recruit if queues grow
VariancePossible causesPossible action
Revenue adverseThere may be fewer members, poor weather, more competition or prices that are too high.The café can run promotions, review the menu or research customers.
Food costs adverseSuppliers may have raised prices, or there may be waste, theft or larger portions.The café can renegotiate, control portions and check stock.

  • Recruit if queues grow.
The case in brief: London 2012
  • Moving budget: £2.4 billion became £9.3 billion because of security, tax and building costs.
  • Misleading variance: under the revised budget is favourable, but against the original it is hugely adverse.

Importance of budgets and variances AO2

Why they matter

  • Planning: budgets force managers to think ahead.
  • Coordination: they bring departments into line with the firm's objectives.
  • Control: variances show problems early.
  • Motivation: budgets give managers targets and delegated responsibility.
  • Accountability: managers answer for their spending, and resources are allocated better.

Limitations

  • Budgets are based on forecasts that may turn out to be wrong.
  • They can be inflexible when conditions change quickly.
  • Managers may pad their budgets ("budgetary slack"), or spend everything they have so that next year's budget is not cut.
  • Unrealistic targets demotivate staff.
  • A favourable variance is not always good news: spending less than planned on staff may mean the firm is understaffed.

Exam corner: 3.9

Exam tips

  • Always state whether each variance is favourable (F) or adverse (A), and check the profit total.
  • Investigate the causes of a variance before recommending action.
  • Comment on whether a favourable variance hides a problem.

Common pitfalls

  • Don't call a cost variance favourable just because the actual number is bigger. Higher costs than budgeted give an adverse variance.
  • Don't confuse cost centres with profit centres. A cost centre only has costs, while a profit centre has both costs and revenues.
  • Don't say that budgets guarantee results. They are plans, and the results still depend on what happens.

Model answer

AO2 Explain why the favourable staff-cost variance may not be good news for the café. [4]

K A favourable variance means costs were below budget, raising profit. App E The $1,000 saving arose because two staff left, not from better efficiency. Fewer staff may mean longer queues and poorer service, which could explain part of the $4,000 adverse revenue variance. The saving may therefore be reducing revenue by more than it saves.
