AO2 Distinguish between a cost centre and a profit centre. [4]
Cost centre: incurs costs only, e.g. maintenance (2). Profit centre: revenue and costs, profit measured, e.g. café (2).
AO4 Budgeted revenue $30,000, actual $33,000; budgeted costs $18,000, actual $20,000. Calculate the variances and profit variance. [3]
Revenue $3,000 F; costs $2,000 A; profit variance $1,000 F.

Unit 4 · Marketing
4.1

Introduction to marketing

Real company case
Innocent Drinks (UK): marketing that starts with the customer

Innocent (from 1.1) is a classic market-oriented business: before launching, its founders tested demand by asking festival customers to vote with their empty bottles. It still researches customers closely and writes its labels in a chatty voice that makes the brand feel personal.

It also shows social marketing. In its yearly "Big Knit" campaign, volunteers knit tiny woollen hats for smoothie bottles, and Innocent donates money to the charity Age UK for each hatted bottle sold. Compare Dyson, a more product-oriented firm: James Dyson built over 5,000 prototypes of his bagless vacuum cleaner before it went on sale.

Apply it: Explain one advantage and one risk of market orientation for a firm like Innocent.

Read more: Innocent Drinks (Wikipedia)

Practice firm for the worked answers · made-up numbers

Fizzwell, a small craft drinks firm, sells $420,000 of kombucha a year in a national market worth $3.5 million, which grew from $2.8 million last year. A large soft-drink firm sells $1.4 million and launched its own kombucha after market research showed growing demand for low-sugar drinks. Its founder designs new flavours mainly by experimenting with what he likes.

Syllabus map

Syllabus pointHighest AOYou must be able to
Market vs product orientationAO2Distinguish and explain the implications for a named firm
  • Market share
  • Market growth
AO2AO4Calculate and interpret both
Importance of market share and leadership (HL)AO3Evaluate the benefits and costs of pursuing market leadership

Key terms AO1

Marketing
The management process of identifying, anticipating and satisfying customer needs profitably.
Market
A place where buyers and sellers exchange goods or services. It can be physical or online.
Market orientation
The business researches customer needs first and designs products to meet them.
Product orientation
The business focuses on making a product it believes is good, then looks for customers.
Market size
The total sales of all firms in a market, by value or volume.
Market share
A firm's sales as a percentage of total market sales.
Market growth
The percentage change in market size over a period.
Market leader
The firm with the largest market share.
Social marketing
Marketing that aims to change people's behaviour for the benefit of society, not just to increase sales, such as campaigns to encourage healthy eating or reduce smoking.
Commercial marketing
Marketing that aims to sell products to earn a profit for the business.
Ethical marketing
Marketing that is honest, fair and socially responsible, avoiding practices such as misleading claims, hidden charges or targeting vulnerable groups.
Pester power
The pressure children put on their parents to buy products they have seen advertised; marketing that deliberately uses it is widely seen as unethical.
Bait and switch
An unethical sales tactic in which a business advertises a very cheap offer to attract customers, then says it is unavailable and pushes a more expensive alternative.
Confusion marketing
Making prices or tariffs so complicated that customers cannot easily compare offers, which discourages them from switching to rivals.

Market vs product orientation AO2

Market orientationProduct orientation
Starting pointCustomer needs and market researchThe product and technical excellence
Strengths
  • Products people want
  • Less risk of failure
  • Responds to change
  • Customer loyalty
  • Innovation and quality
  • Can create new markets customers did not know they wanted
  • Lower research cost
Weaknesses
  • Research is costly and slow
  • May chase trends
  • May not create radical innovation
  • Risk of no demand
  • Ignores changing tastes
  • Competitors may overtake
SuitsCompetitive consumer markets (food, fashion)
  • Technical, scientific or luxury products
  • Inventions
ExampleInnocent tested demand at a festival before launchingDyson built over 5,000 prototypes before selling one vacuum cleaner
Market orientationProduct orientation
Starting pointIt starts with customer needs and market research.It starts with the product and technical excellence.
Strengths
  • It makes products people want.
  • The risk of failure is lower.
  • It responds to change.
  • Customers become loyal.
  • It drives innovation and quality.
  • It can create markets customers did not know they wanted.
  • It spends less on research.
Weaknesses
  • Research is costly and slow.
  • The firm may chase short-lived trends.
  • It may not produce radical innovation.
  • There may be no demand.
  • It can ignore changing tastes.
  • Competitors may overtake it.
SuitsIt suits competitive consumer markets, such as food and fashion.
  • It suits technical, scientific and luxury products.
  • It suits genuine inventions.
ExampleInnocent let customers vote with their empty bottles before launching.Dyson built over 5,000 prototypes before selling one vacuum cleaner.
Exam tipMost firms combine both. A good answer says which approach suits the market: Fizzwell's competitive drinks market rewards a shift towards market orientation (e.g. tasting panels), while keeping the craft identity that makes it different.
The case in brief: Innocent and Dyson
  • Market orientation: Innocent let customers vote with bottles and uses a chatty voice and the Big Knit.
  • Product orientation: Dyson built 5,000+ prototypes first.
  • Lesson: both can work, depending on where the advantage comes from.

Market share and market growth AO2AO4

Market share (%) = firm's sales ÷ total market sales × 100LEARN IT
Market growth (%) = (this year's market size − last year's) ÷ last year's × 100LEARN IT
Worked example

Fizzwell's share = 420,000 ÷ 3,500,000 × 100 = 12%. Rival's share = 1,400,000 ÷ 3,500,000 × 100 = 40%. Market growth = (3.5m − 2.8m) ÷ 2.8m × 100 = 25%.
If Fizzwell's sales were $380,000 last year, its share was 380,000 ÷ 2,800,000 = 13.6%. Fizzwell's sales grew, but its share fell because the market grew faster.

Common mistake
  • Don't assume that rising sales mean a rising market share. Market share depends on how fast the whole market grows, so always compare the firm's sales growth with the market's growth.

Importance of market share and market leadership HL AO3

Benefits of high share / leadership

  • A large market share brings economies of scale, which lower unit costs (1.5).
  • It gives the firm bargaining power with retailers and suppliers.
  • The brand is well known, and customers see the market leader as the safe choice.
  • The leader can set prices that rivals follow, which is called price leadership.
  • Higher profits can be reinvested in research and marketing.
  • A market leader attracts investors and talented staff.

Costs and risks

  • Winning and defending market share is expensive, because it needs price cuts and advertising.
  • Regulators may investigate a firm that dominates its market.
  • A leader can become complacent and slow to innovate.
  • It becomes a target for competitors and critics.
  • A large share of a shrinking market is worth less than it seems.
JudgementLeadership matters most in mass markets with economies of scale. In niche markets (Fizzwell's craft segment), profitability, loyalty and brand distinctiveness can matter more than overall share.

Exam corner: 4.1

Exam tips

  • Show your working for market share and market growth, and give percentages to one decimal place.
  • Interpret the result: explain what the change means for the firm.
  • Link market or product orientation to market research (4.4).

Common pitfalls

  • Don't use sales volume for one figure and sales value for another in the same calculation.
  • Don't call product orientation bad. It works well for firms whose strength is innovation, such as technology or luxury brands.

Model answers

AO2 Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for Fizzwell of becoming more market-oriented. [4]

K Market orientation means researching customer needs before developing products. E Testing flavours with tasting panels would reduce the risk of launching drinks only the founder likes, helping Fizzwell compete with the rival that already uses research. E However, research costs time and money that a small firm with cash-flow problems may not have, and following trends could weaken the craft identity that differentiates Fizzwell.

AO3 HL To what extent should Fizzwell aim to become market leader? [10]

App Fizzwell has 12% of a market growing 25% a year; the leader has 40%. E Leadership would bring economies of scale and bargaining power with supermarkets, but winning it would mean matching a rival with far more money for advertising and lower prices, which could destroy Fizzwell's margins. Ev Fizzwell should instead aim to lead the premium craft niche, where its organic, small-batch brand gives it an advantage, and grow share steadily as the market expands. Overall leadership is unrealistic and unnecessary for profitability, unless Fizzwell secures major investment.

Practice questions (tap to reveal the marking points)

AO4 A market grows from $8m to $9.2m. A firm's sales rise from $1.2m to $1.3m. Calculate market growth and the change in the firm's share. [3]
Growth = 1.2 ÷ 8 × 100 = 15%. Share 15% → 14.1%: share fell by 0.9 percentage points.

4.2

Marketing planning

Real company case
Pret A Manger (UK): a clear position in a crowded market

Pret A Manger opened in London in 1986 and competes with global coffee chains, supermarket meal deals, independent cafés and fast food. It targets busy office workers, commuters and students in city centres, stations and airports. It positions itself on freshness: sandwiches and salads are made in each shop's kitchen every day, unsold food is given to charities, and its coffee is organic.

In 2020, when the pandemic emptied city centres, Pret launched a coffee subscription, Club Pret, to bring customers back regularly; it has changed the price and terms since. It also began selling through supermarkets and delivery apps to reach customers working from home.

Read more: Pret A Manger (Wikipedia)

Syllabus map

Syllabus pointHighest AOYou must be able to
Role of marketing planningAO2Explain the purpose and contents of a marketing plan
  • Segmentation, targeting, positioning
  • Position maps
AO2AO4Segment a market, choose targets, construct and interpret a position map
  • Niche vs mass
  • USP
AO2Distinguish markets and explain the importance of a USP
How organisations differentiateAO3Evaluate differentiation strategies for a named firm

Key terms AO1

Marketing plan
A document setting out marketing objectives, research findings, target markets, the marketing mix, budget and how success will be measured.
Market segmentation
Dividing a market into groups of customers with similar characteristics or needs.
Targeting
Choosing which segment(s) to serve.
Positioning
How a product is perceived by customers relative to competitors.
Position (perception) map
A diagram plotting brands on two attributes (e.g. price and quality) to show competitors and gaps.
Niche market
A small, specialised segment with particular needs.
Mass market
A large market with broadly similar needs, served by standardised products.
USP
A unique selling point/proposition: a feature that makes a product different from and preferable to competitors.
Differentiation
Making a product or firm distinct from rivals in ways customers value.
Four Ps
The traditional marketing mix for goods: product, price, promotion and place.
Marketing objectives
The targets the marketing department sets to help the business reach its aims, such as higher sales, a larger market share or greater brand awareness; they should be SMART.

The role of marketing planning AO2

Marketing objectives→Market research & audit (SWOT, STEEPLE)→Segment, target, position→Marketing mix (7 Ps)→Budget & timeline→Monitor & evaluate

Benefits

  • A marketing plan gives clear objectives and direction, and it coordinates the marketing mix.
  • It helps the firm spend its marketing budget efficiently.
  • It links marketing with finance and operations.
  • It helps the firm raise finance, because it forms part of the business plan.
  • It sets targets against which success can be measured.

Limitations

  • A plan takes time and money to produce.
  • It is based on research and forecasts that may be wrong.
  • It can become too rigid in a market that changes quickly.
  • It is only useful if the firm actually carries it out and reviews it.

Segmentation AO2

BasisExamples of variablesPret A Manger example
DemographicAge, gender, income, occupation, education, family stage, religion, ethnicityOffice workers, commuters and students
GeographicCountry, region, urban/rural, climateCity centres, train stations and airports
PsychographicLifestyle, values, personality, interests
  • Values fresh, natural food
  • Short of time
BehaviouralUsage rate, loyalty, benefits sought, occasion
  • Weekday lunch and coffee buyers
  • Subscription regulars
BasisExamples of variablesPret A Manger example
DemographicFirms group customers by age, gender, income, occupation, education, family stage, religion or ethnicity.Pret targets busy office workers, commuters and students.
GeographicFirms group customers by country, region, urban or rural area, or climate.Pret opens in city centres, train stations and airports.
PsychographicFirms group customers by lifestyle, values, personality and interests.
  • Pret's customers value fresh, natural food.
  • They are short of time.
BehaviouralFirms group customers by how often they buy, their loyalty, the benefits they seek and the occasion.
  • Pret serves weekday lunch and coffee buyers.
  • It rewards subscription regulars.

Benefits of segmentation

  • Segmentation lets the firm design products and messages that fit each group's needs.
  • Marketing money is spent more efficiently, because it reaches the right customers.
  • It reveals gaps in the market and new opportunities.
  • Customers who feel understood are more loyal and may pay higher prices.

Limitations

  • The research needed to segment a market costs money.
  • Some segments may be too small to be profitable, or they may overlap.
  • Grouping customers can lead to stereotyping them.
  • Customer behaviour changes over time, so segments must be reviewed.

Targeting and positioning AO2AO4

Targeting strategyMeaningExample
Undifferentiated (mass)One mix for the whole marketBasic bottled water
DifferentiatedDifferent mixes for several segmentsCar makers' range from budget to luxury
Concentrated (niche)One mix for one segmentGymshark, which began by targeting gym enthusiasts only
Targeting strategyMeaningExample
Undifferentiated (mass)The firm offers one marketing mix to the whole market.Basic bottled water is sold this way.
DifferentiatedThe firm offers a different mix to each of several segments.Car makers offer a range from budget to luxury.
Concentrated (niche)The firm offers one mix to one segment.Gymshark began by targeting only gym enthusiasts.

Constructing a position map (AO4)

1
Choose two attributes customers care about (price and quality; healthy vs indulgent; modern vs traditional).
2
Draw and label both axes with high and low ends.
3
Plot each brand using data from the case or research.
4
Identify clusters (intense competition) and gaps (possible opportunities).
5
Interpret: a gap is only an opportunity if research shows demand there.

Strengths of position maps

  • A position map is visual and quick to read, and it shows where competitors sit and where the gaps are.
  • It helps a firm plan how to reposition its brand.

Limitations

  • A map compares only two attributes, but real buying decisions depend on many.
  • It is based on customers' perceptions, which vary from person to person.
  • A gap on the map may exist simply because nobody wants that combination.
The case in brief: Pret
  • Target and position: office workers and commuters, with a position on freshness backed by food made in-shop daily.
  • Risk of one segment: the pandemic emptied city centres.
  • Changed the mix, not the position: a coffee subscription and supermarket and delivery sales.

Exam corner: 4.2

Exam tips

  • For segmentation, state the basis you are using and name the specific segment.
  • On a position map, label both axes, plot every competitor named in the case, and comment on the gaps and clusters.
  • For differentiation questions (AO3), weigh up the cost and how easily rivals could copy it.

Common pitfalls

  • Don't confuse segmentation with targeting. Segmentation divides the market into groups, while targeting chooses which groups to serve.
  • Don't assume that every gap on a position map is profitable.
  • Don't state a USP that rivals already offer, because then it is not unique.

Model answer

AO3 Evaluate how Pret A Manger differentiates itself from competitors. [10]

App The position map shows a gap for good-quality food at mid prices; global chains and artisan roasteries are clustered elsewhere.

E Product: making sandwiches and salads fresh in each shop every day is a point of difference that chains relying on factory-made food cannot easily copy. Kitchens in every shop raise costs, but the target segment values freshness. E Sustainability and ethics: donating unsold food and using organic coffee fit customers who care where food comes from, but such claims must be genuine to avoid greenwashing accusations. E Price: a coffee subscription locks in regular visits and data on customers, but heavy users can make it unprofitable, which is why Pret has changed the terms.

Ev Overall, the strongest differentiation is the product (fresh food made on site) supported by ethics, because together they are valued by the target segment and hard for rivals to copy credibly. Price offers such as subscriptions should support, not lead, the positioning, since rivals can match a discount overnight. A gap on a position map does not prove demand, so a firm should test a new format in a few locations before expanding.

4.3

Sales forecasting

HL
Real company case
Walmart (USA): forecasting before a hurricane

Before Hurricane Frances reached Florida in 2004, Walmart studied its sales data from earlier storms. It found that sales of strawberry Pop-Tarts rose to about seven times their normal rate before a hurricane, and that beer was the top-selling item. It rushed extra stock to stores in the storm's path, and most of it sold.

Forecasting from past data helps firms plan stock, staff and cash, but only while the patterns stay stable; unusual events such as a pandemic can break them.

Apply it: Explain one benefit and one limitation for Walmart of forecasting from past sales data.

Read more: Walmart (Wikipedia)

Practice firm for the worked answers · made-up numbers

BlueWave Kayaks (from 3.7) wants to forecast next season's sales to plan staff, kayak purchases and its overdraft. It has 8 seasons of data showing that sales rise with its online advertising spend, and sales fell sharply in one year with a heatwave warning and travel disruption.

Syllabus map

Syllabus pointHighest AOYou must be able to
Benefits and limitations of sales forecastingAO3Evaluate how useful a forecast is for a named firm's decisions
Simple linear regression (toolkit)AO2AO4Draw or interpret a scatter diagram, line of best fit, correlation and extrapolation

Key terms AO1

Sales forecasting
Predicting future sales volume or value using past data, research and judgement.
Trend
The underlying long-term direction of data.
Seasonal variation
Regular, predictable fluctuations within a year (summer peak for kayaks).
Cyclical variation
Fluctuations linked to the business (economic) cycle over several years.
Random variation
Unpredictable changes from one-off events (weather, pandemics, strikes).
Correlation
The strength and direction of a relationship between two variables.
Extrapolation
Extending a trend line beyond the data to make a forecast.
Positive correlation
A relationship in which two variables move in the same direction: as one increases, so does the other.
Negative correlation
A relationship in which two variables move in opposite directions: as one increases, the other decreases.

Why businesses forecast sales

FunctionUses the forecast to…
OperationsPlan capacity, stock and purchasing (kayaks, wetsuits)
HRPlan recruitment of seasonal staff (2.1)
Finance
  • Build budgets and cash-flow forecasts
  • Arrange overdrafts
MarketingSet targets and promotion budgets
FunctionUses the forecast to…
OperationsIt plans capacity, stock and purchasing, such as kayaks and wetsuits.
HRIt plans the recruitment of seasonal staff (2.1).
Finance
  • It builds budgets and cash-flow forecasts.
  • It arranges overdrafts in time.
MarketingIt sets sales targets and promotion budgets.

Forecasting approaches

Quantitative

  • Extrapolation extends past sales trends into the future (a time series).
  • Simple linear regression relates sales to another variable, such as advertising spending or temperature.
  • Moving averages smooth out seasonal and random variation, which makes the trend easier to see.

Qualitative

  • Market research and test marketing show how customers are likely to respond.
  • Experts and the sales team can give their own estimates.
  • In the Delphi method, a panel of experts refines its estimates over several rounds.
  • Qualitative methods are useful for new products, which have no past data.

Simple linear regression (toolkit) AO4

FeatureWhat to say
Scatter diagramPlot the independent variable (advertising) on x and the dependent variable (sales) on y
Line of best fit
  • Straight line through the middle of the points
  • Shows the trend
Correlation
  • Positive or negative
  • Strong (points close to the line) or weak
  • None
ExtrapolationExtending the line to forecast (e.g. sales at $60k advertising ≈ $119k)
Caution
  • Correlation does not prove causation
  • Extrapolation far beyond the data is unreliable
  • Outliers (heatwave year) distort the line
FeatureWhat to say
Scatter diagramPlot the independent variable, such as advertising, on the x-axis and the dependent variable, such as sales, on the y-axis.
Line of best fit
  • Draw a straight line through the middle of the points.
  • The line shows the trend.
Correlation
  • Say whether the correlation is positive, negative or absent.
  • Say whether it is strong, with points close to the line, or weak.
ExtrapolationExtend the line to make a forecast, for example sales of about $119k at $60k of advertising.
Caution
  • Correlation does not prove causation.
  • Extrapolating far beyond the data is unreliable.
  • Outliers, such as a heatwave year, distort the line.

Benefits and limitations AO3

Benefits

  • A forecast helps the firm plan its stock, staff and cash, and it reduces waste.
  • It supports budgets and applications for finance.
  • It gives an early warning that demand is falling.
  • It helps set realistic targets and coordinate departments.

Limitations

  • The past may not predict the future, because tastes, competitors and technology change.
  • Random events, such as bad weather or a pandemic, cannot be predicted.
  • The data may be poor or limited, and new products have none at all.
  • Qualitative estimates can be biased by the views of the people making them.
  • The further ahead a forecast looks, the less reliable it becomes.
JudgementA forecast is most reliable when the market is stable, data is plentiful, and the forecast is short term. Use ranges (best/worst case) and update regularly.
The case in brief: Walmart
  • Forecasting from past data: earlier storms showed some sales at seven times normal.
  • Action: it rushed extra stock to stores.
  • Limitation: it works only while patterns stay stable.

Exam corner: 4.3

Exam tips

  • Name the decision that the forecast supports, such as the size of an overdraft or the number of staff to hire.
  • Comment on the type of correlation and how strong it is.
  • Always mention a limitation of extrapolation.

Common pitfalls

  • Don't claim that a correlation proves that one thing causes the other.
  • Don't treat a forecast as certain.
  • Don't extrapolate far beyond the data without commenting on the risk.

Model answer

AO3 Evaluate the usefulness of sales forecasting for BlueWave Kayaks. [10]

E A forecast lets BlueWave decide how many kayaks to buy, how many seasonal staff to hire and how large an overdraft to arrange before the season starts. The strong positive correlation between advertising and sales over 8 seasons makes regression a reasonable tool. E However, weather and travel disruption cause random variation, as the heatwave year showed, and extrapolating to higher advertising levels assumes the relationship continues. Ev Forecasting is useful for BlueWave as a planning range rather than a single figure. It should plan for a cautious case (e.g. 15% below forecast) when setting the overdraft, and update the forecast with early bookings each spring.

Seasonal: regular, predictable within a year (2). Random: unpredictable one-off (2). Examples.
AO3 Discuss the limitations of using linear regression to forecast sales for a new product. [6]
No past data; correlation vs causation; outliers; changing conditions; better to use qualitative methods or test marketing.
4.4

Market research

Real company case
New Coke (USA, 1985): research that asked the wrong question

In the early 1980s Coca-Cola was losing market share to Pepsi, whose "Pepsi Challenge" blind taste tests showed many people preferred Pepsi's sweeter taste. Coca-Cola developed a sweeter recipe and ran about 200,000 taste tests; most tasters preferred it to both old Coke and Pepsi. In April 1985 it replaced the original with "New Coke".

Customers were furious. The company received hundreds of thousands of complaints, and after 79 days it brought the original back as "Coca-Cola Classic". The research was large and well run, but it measured taste in a sip, not how people would feel about losing a product they had grown up with. Some focus groups had shown that anger, but the numbers from the taste tests carried more weight.

Apply it: Explain one strength and one limitation of the quantitative research Coca-Cola relied on.

Read more: New Coke (Wikipedia)

Practice firm for the worked answers · made-up numbers

FitBox plans to launch a monthly subscription box of healthy snacks in two European countries at $24 a month. It has $8,000 for research. The founders have read an industry report on snack trends, and want to know whether 18–35-year-olds will pay $24 and which snacks they prefer.

Syllabus map

Syllabus pointHighest AOYou must be able to
Why and how organisations carry out market researchAO3Evaluate and recommend a research plan for a named firm
Primary and secondary methodsAO2Explain how each method works and its pros and cons
Qualitative vs quantitative dataAO2Distinguish and explain uses
Sampling: quota, random, convenienceAO2Explain each and its suitability

Key terms AO1

Market research
Collecting, analysing and interpreting information about markets, customers and competitors to support decisions.
Primary (field) research
New, first-hand data collected for a specific purpose.
Secondary (desk) research
Data that already exists, collected by others for another purpose.
Quantitative data
Numerical data that can be measured and analysed statistically.
Qualitative data
Non-numerical data about opinions, feelings and motives.
Sample
A subset of the target population selected for research.
Sampling error / bias
Results that differ from the true population because of how the sample was chosen or questions were asked.
Market analysis
A published report on a particular market, often by a research company, covering its size, growth, trends and main competitors.
Academic journals
Publications containing research by universities and experts, reviewed by other experts before publication.
Government publications
Official statistics and reports published by government agencies, such as population, income and trade data.
Media articles
Reports in newspapers, magazines and websites that may contain information about markets, firms and trends.
Sample size
The number of people or items chosen from a population to take part in research.
Bias
A distortion in research that makes results unrepresentative, for example from leading questions or an unrepresentative sample.
Open question
A question that allows the respondent to answer in their own words, producing qualitative data.
Closed question
A question with a fixed set of possible answers, producing quantitative data that is easy to analyse.

Why organisations carry out market research AO3

  • Market research reduces the risk of launching a product that nobody wants.
  • It shows what customers need and prefer, and how much they are willing to pay.
  • It measures the size and growth of the market, and it identifies segments and gaps.
  • It keeps track of competitors and of changes in the external environment.
  • It lets the firm test parts of the marketing mix, such as price, packaging and promotion, and measure the results of a campaign.
  • It supports sales forecasts, budgets and applications for finance.

Qualitative vs quantitative AO2

Quantitative

"62% of respondents would pay $24 a month." Large samples, statistical analysis, easy to compare and chart. Doesn't explain why.

Qualitative

"I'd pay more if the snacks were locally made." Explains motives and feelings, generates ideas. Small samples, hard to generalise, interpretation bias.

Sampling methods AO2

MethodHow it worksStrengthsWeaknesses
RandomEvery member of the population has an equal chance of selection
  • Least biased
  • Statistically valid
  • Needs a full list (sampling frame)
  • May miss key groups by chance
  • Costly

MethodHow it worksStrengthsWeaknesses
RandomEvery member of the population has an equal chance of selection.
  • It is the least biased method.
  • It is statistically valid.
  • It needs a full list of the population, called a sampling frame.
  • By chance it may miss key groups.
  • It can be costly.
Quota
  • The population is split into groups, such as age or gender.
  • The researcher fills a set number from each group.
  • It represents the key segments.
  • It is quick and needs no list.
The interviewer chooses whom to ask, so selection bias can creep in.
ConvenienceThe researcher asks whoever is easiest to reach, such as friends, passers-by or followers.
  • It is cheap and fast.
  • It suits pilot studies.
  • It is not representative.
  • The results may mislead.

Sample size: larger samples are more reliable but cost more; the right size depends on budget, the variety of the population and the risk of the decision.

Reliability, validity and ethics

  • Bias: results can be distorted by leading questions, samples that do not represent the market, the effect of the interviewer, and people saying what they think is expected.
  • Validity: research must measure what it claims to measure. What people say they will buy often differs from what they actually buy.
  • Ethics and privacy: researchers need informed consent, must protect personal data (under the GDPR in the EU), must use the results honestly and must take extra care with minors.
The case in brief: New Coke
  • Large but not valid: 200,000 taste tests led Coca-Cola to replace the original.
  • Failure: the old recipe returned after 79 days.
  • Why: tests measured taste in a sip, but focus groups showed anger about losing the original.

Exam corner: 4.4

Exam tips

  • Recommend a mix: start with secondary research for cheap background, then carry out targeted primary research.
  • Match the sampling method to the target market and the budget.
  • Show how the results will be used to make a decision.

Common pitfalls

  • Don't say that primary research is always better. It is more expensive and slower than secondary research.
  • Don't confuse quota sampling with random sampling. In quota sampling the researcher chooses people to fill set groups, while in random sampling everyone has an equal chance of being chosen.
  • Don't forget the limits on cost and time given in the case.

Model answer

AO3 Recommend a market research plan for FitBox. [10]

E FitBox should start with cheap secondary research: the industry report, national statistics and Eurostat data on 18–35-year-olds' income and spending, and competitors' prices and reviews online. This sizes the market quickly, but cannot show whether customers will pay $24 for this box.

E It should then run an online survey with a quota sample (for example 400 people split by age band, gender and country), producing quantitative data on willingness to pay and snack preferences. Quota sampling is cheaper than random sampling and ensures both countries and age groups are represented, although the respondents are self-selected.

E Finally, two focus groups tasting sample boxes would give qualitative insight into packaging, flavours and the price, helping explain the survey results.

Ev Recommendation: secondary research, then a quota-sampled survey, then focus groups, fits the $8,000 budget and answers both "how many?" and "why?". Because survey answers about future buying are often over-optimistic, FitBox should also run a small pre-order test before full launch to confirm real demand.

4.5

The seven Ps: product and branding

Real company case
Apple (USA): a portfolio at different life-cycle stages

The iPhone, launched in 2007, earns about half of Apple's revenue in a smartphone market that has almost stopped growing: a classic cash cow. Its services (App Store, iCloud, Apple Music) are growing fast. The Vision Pro headset (2024) has a small share of a young, uncertain market: a question mark. The iPod, once a star, declined as phones replaced music players, and Apple stopped selling the last model in 2022.

Apple extends the iPhone's life cycle with a new model every year, new colours and features, trade-in offers and a brand that keeps customers inside its ecosystem.

Apply it: Place the iPhone, Vision Pro and iPod on the BCG matrix and justify each position.

Read more: iPhone (Wikipedia) · iPod (Wikipedia)

Practice firm for the worked answers · made-up numbers

Sunsip makes three drinks: its original lemonade (sold for 20 years, sales flat for 5 years, the main source of profit), a sparkling iced tea (launched 2 years ago, sales growing 40% a year), and a canned energy drink (sales falling for 3 years in a shrinking market).

Syllabus map

Syllabus pointHighest AOYou must be able to
  • Product life cycle

  • Branding: awareness, development, loyalty, value
  • Importance

Key terms AO1

Product
A good or service that satisfies customers' needs. It includes the product's features, quality, design and packaging.
Product life cycle (PLC)
The stages a product passes through: development, introduction, growth, maturity, decline.
Extension strategy
An action to prolong the maturity stage and delay decline.
Product portfolio
The range of products a business sells.
Brand
A name, symbol, design or identity that distinguishes a product and creates associations in customers' minds.
Brand awareness
The extent to which customers recognise or recall a brand.
Brand development
Strengthening and extending a brand: improving its image, or extending it to new products and markets.
Brand loyalty
Customers repeatedly choosing a brand over rivals.
Brand value
The extra worth a brand adds: the premium customers will pay, or the financial value of the brand as an asset.
Saturation
The stage in the product life cycle when sales stop growing because most potential customers already own the product and competition is intense.
Brand extension
Using an established brand name to launch a new product in a different category.
Packaging
The container or wrapping of a product, which protects it, gives information and helps promote and differentiate it.
Own-label brand
A product sold under a retailer's own brand name instead of the manufacturer's, usually at a lower price.
Family branding
Selling several products under one brand name so that each benefits from the reputation of the others.
Corporate brand
A brand that represents the whole company rather than a single product, so the company name and reputation are used across all its products.

Strengths of BCG

  • The BCG matrix gives a simple visual picture of a firm's whole product portfolio.
  • It guides how cash should be shared between products.

Limitations

  • It uses only two variables, so it ignores profitability and the ways products support each other.
  • How the market is defined changes the result.
  • A "dog" can still be profitable, or it can support sales of other products.
The case in brief: Apple
  • Cash cow: the iPhone earns half the revenue in a market that has almost stopped growing.
  • Star: services growing fast. Question mark: Vision Pro, with a small share of a new market.
  • Dog: the iPod, dropped in 2022.

Branding AO2

AspectMeaningHow firms build it
Brand awarenessRecognition and recallAdvertising, social media, sponsorship, consistent logo and packaging

Consistent quality, loyalty schemes, customer experience, emotional connection

AspectMeaningHow firms build it
Brand awarenessCustomers recognise and remember the brand.Firms use advertising, social media, sponsorship and a consistent logo and packaging.
Brand developmentThe firm strengthens or extends the brand.Firms use brand extensions such as Sunsip iced tea, repositioning and co-branding.
Brand loyalty
  • Customers buy again and again.
  • They resist rivals' offers.
Firms offer consistent quality, loyalty schemes, a good experience and an emotional connection.
Brand value
  • Customers will pay a premium.
  • The brand becomes a valuable asset.
Firms sustain all of the above over time.

Importance of branding

  • Branding makes products stand out in crowded markets.
  • It supports premium prices and higher margins.
  • It builds loyalty, which makes customers less sensitive to price (demand becomes more price inelastic).
  • It makes new products easier to launch as brand extensions.
  • A strong brand adds to the value of the business as goodwill.

Risks

  • A brand is expensive to build and to maintain.
  • One scandal can damage every product sold under the brand.
  • A failed brand extension can harm the core brand.

Exam corner: 4.5 product

Exam tips

  • Identify the product life cycle stage using evidence, such as the sales trend and the growth of the market.
  • Link the stage of the life cycle to cash flow and investment.
  • Choose an extension strategy that fits the reason why sales are falling.

Common pitfalls

  • Don't draw the profit curve above zero at the introduction stage. Most products make a loss at launch.
  • Don't recommend an extension strategy for a product whose market is shrinking for good without also discussing withdrawing it.
  • Don't treat the BCG matrix as the same thing as the product life cycle. The matrix compares several products, while the life cycle follows one product over time.

Model answer

AO3 Discuss whether Sunsip should use an extension strategy for its energy drink or withdraw it. [10]

App The energy drink is in decline: sales have fallen for three years in a shrinking market, making it a dog on the BCG matrix. E An extension such as a low-sugar reformulation might revive sales, but because the whole market is shrinking, any gain is likely to be short-lived while R&D and promotion costs are high. Withdrawing it would free production capacity and marketing budget for the iced tea, which is growing 40% a year. E However, if the drink still covers its variable costs and contributes to overheads, or if retailers expect a full range from Sunsip, keeping it with minimal promotion (harvesting) could be sensible. Ev Sunsip should harvest the energy drink, spending little on it while it still makes a contribution, and redirect investment to the iced tea and to cash-cow lemonade extensions. It should withdraw the drink once its contribution turns negative.

4.5

The seven Ps: price

Real company case
Netflix (USA): testing how much customers will pay

Netflix has raised its prices many times while its subscriber numbers kept growing, which suggests demand is fairly price inelastic. In late 2022 it launched a cheaper plan with adverts, aimed at price-sensitive viewers. In 2023 it began charging for password sharing outside a household; many expected customers to leave, but sign-ups rose as people who had borrowed accounts started paying for their own.

Apply it: Using price elasticity of demand, explain why Netflix could raise prices without losing many subscribers.

Read more: Netflix (Wikipedia)

Practice firm for the worked answers · made-up numbers

StreamStudy is launching an online revision app for IB students. Development cost $200,000; each subscriber costs $1.50 a month to serve. Rivals charge $8–$15 a month. A large education publisher is rumoured to be planning a free app supported by advertising.

Syllabus map

Syllabus pointHighest AOYou must be able to
Cost-plus, penetration, loss leader, predatory, premiumAO3Evaluate and recommend a pricing strategy
Dynamic, competitive, contribution pricing (HL)AO3Evaluate these strategies for a named firm
Price elasticity of demand (HL)AO3Explain what PED means for revenue and use it to judge a pricing decision

Key terms AO1

Cost-plus (mark-up) pricing
Adding a percentage mark-up to the unit cost to set the price.
Penetration pricing
Setting a low initial price to gain market share quickly, then raising it.
Loss leader
Selling a product below cost to attract customers who then buy other, profitable products.
Predatory pricing
Deliberately setting prices below cost to force competitors out of the market. It is illegal in many countries.
Premium pricing
Setting a high price to reflect exclusivity and quality.
Dynamic pricing (HL)
Prices change in real time with demand, time and customer data (airlines, ride-hailing).
Competitive pricing (HL)
Setting prices with reference to competitors' prices (at, below or above).
Contribution pricing (HL)
Setting a price that covers variable cost and makes a contribution to fixed costs, often for special orders.
Price elasticity of demand (HL)
The responsiveness of quantity demanded to a change in price.
Substitutes
Products that customers can use in place of one another to satisfy the same need.
Necessity
A product that people need and will buy even when its price rises, so demand tends to be price inelastic.
Price leadership
A pricing strategy in which the dominant firm in a market sets the price and smaller rivals follow it.

Cost-plus worked example

Unit cost $40, mark-up 25% → price = 40 × 1.25 = $50. Profit per unit = $10. Note: margin on selling price = 10 ÷ 50 = 20%, not 25%.

Contribution pricing decision

A school offers to buy 2,000 StreamStudy licences at $3 a month. Variable cost $1.50 → contribution $1.50 × 2,000 = $3,000 a month towards fixed costs. Accept if spare capacity exists and it will not undercut individual subscribers.

Price elasticity of demand HL AO3

What the guide asksPED is listed at AO3, alongside dynamic, competitive and contribution pricing. You will not get a stand-alone "calculate PED" question, but you must explain what elastic or inelastic demand means for revenue and use it to judge a pricing decision. Working out the number from case data is the clearest way to back up that judgement.
PED = % change in quantity demanded ÷ % change in priceUSE TO JUDGE
|PED|MeaningEffect of a price rise on revenueEffect of a price cut on revenue
> 1 (elastic)Quantity changes proportionately more than priceRevenue fallsRevenue rises
< 1 (inelastic)Quantity changes proportionately lessRevenue risesRevenue falls
= 1 (unitary)Equal proportional changeRevenue unchangedRevenue unchanged
|PED|MeaningEffect of a price rise on revenueEffect of a price cut on revenue
> 1 (elastic)Quantity demanded changes proportionately more than price.Revenue falls.Revenue rises.
< 1 (inelastic)Quantity demanded changes proportionately less than price.Revenue rises.Revenue falls.
= 1 (unitary)Quantity demanded changes by the same proportion as price.Revenue stays the same.Revenue stays the same.
Worked example

StreamStudy raises its price from $10 to $12 (+20%); subscribers fall from 5,000 to 4,500 (−10%). PED = −10 ÷ 20 = −0.5 (inelastic). Revenue: 5,000 × $10 = $50,000 → 4,500 × $12 = $54,000. The price rise increased revenue.

Determinants of PED

  • Demand is more price elastic when there are more, and closer, substitutes.
  • Necessities, habits and strong brand loyalty make demand less price elastic, while luxuries make it more elastic.
  • The larger the share of income a product takes, the more price elastic its demand.
  • Demand becomes more elastic over time, as customers find alternatives.
  • How the market is defined matters: demand for all drinks is far less elastic than demand for one brand.

Limitations of PED

  • PED estimates rely on past data, and conditions change.
  • Other factors, such as incomes and rivals' prices, change at the same time as the price.
  • PED is only valid for small changes in price.
The case in brief: Netflix
  • Inelastic demand: it raised prices while subscribers grew.
  • Price discrimination: a cheaper plan with adverts.
  • Surprise: charging for password sharing made sign-ups rise.

Choosing a price AO3

  • Costs: in the long run, the price must at least cover costs.
  • Competition: the firm must consider rivals' prices and the threat of new firms entering the market.
  • Customers: the firm must consider how much they are willing to pay, how sensitive they are to price, and which segment they belong to.
  • Objectives: a firm aiming for market share may choose penetration pricing, while one aiming for profit and image may choose premium pricing.
  • The stage of the product life cycle and the product's place on the position map affect the price.
  • Laws and ethics set limits, for example the rules against predatory pricing and price discrimination.
  • The price must be consistent with the rest of the marketing mix.

Exam corner: 4.5 price

Exam tips

  • Name the pricing strategy and justify it with facts from the case, such as costs, rivals and objectives.
  • Show the effect on revenue with numbers where possible.
  • Check that the price fits the rest of the marketing mix and the brand.

Common pitfalls

  • Don't confuse penetration pricing with predatory pricing. They differ in intent and legality: predatory pricing aims to drive rivals out and is illegal in many countries.
  • Don't mix up mark-up and margin. Mark-up is profit as a percentage of cost, while margin is profit as a percentage of the selling price.
  • Don't forget the minus sign in PED, and judge PED by its size, not by its sign.

Model answer

AO3 Recommend a pricing strategy for StreamStudy's launch. [10]

E Penetration pricing (e.g. $5 a month, below rivals' $8–$15) would attract students quickly and build a user base before the publisher's free app arrives. With a variable cost of only $1.50, each subscriber still contributes $3.50, and a large base makes the app more valuable through reviews and word of mouth. The risk is that raising prices later causes churn. E Premium pricing ($15) would signal quality and recover the $200,000 development cost faster, but with close substitutes and price-sensitive students, demand is likely to be elastic. Ev StreamStudy should use penetration pricing with an introductory offer clearly time-limited, then move towards competitive pricing (around $8) once loyalty is established. This works only if the product quality justifies staying with it when the price rises.

Practice questions (tap to reveal the marking points)

AO4 Unit cost $16, mark-up 50%. Calculate the price. [2]
16 × 1.5 = $24.
AO3 HL A 10% price cut is expected to raise quantity demanded by 25%. Discuss whether StreamStudy should cut its price. [6]
PED = 25 ÷ −10 = −2.5: demand is price elastic (size above 1), so the cut should raise revenue (1–2). But weigh it: lower contribution per subscriber, rivals may match the cut, a lower price may signal lower quality, and the estimate comes from past data (2–3). Conditional judgement (1).
AO3 Evaluate loss-leader pricing for a supermarket. [10]
Footfall, basket size, competitive image vs losses, cherry-picking customers, supplier pressure, legality. Judgement.
4.5

The seven Ps: promotion and place

Real company case
Oatly (Sweden): baristas first, supermarkets later

Oatly, a Swedish oat-drink company, entered the USA in 2016 with an unusual distribution choice. Instead of supermarkets, it first sold its Barista Edition to independent coffee shops, because baristas wanted a plant milk that foamed well. Coffee drinkers tried it in their lattes, demand grew, and supermarkets then wanted to stock it. In 2021 Starbucks added Oatly across its US stores.

Its promotion is deliberately provocative: packaging covered in jokes, posters such as "It's like milk but made for humans", and a 2021 Super Bowl advert in which its chief executive sang "Wow, wow, no cow" in a field. Some viewers loved it and others hated it, but people talked about it.

Read more: Oatly (Wikipedia)

Syllabus map

Syllabus pointHighest AOYou must be able to
Above, below and through the line promotionAO2Explain each with examples, pros and cons
Social media marketingAO3Evaluate social media as a promotional strategy
Place: distribution channelsAO3Evaluate and recommend channels

Key terms AO1

Promotion
Communicating with customers to inform, persuade or remind them about a product.
Above the line (ATL)
Paid advertising through independent mass media: TV, radio, cinema, newspapers, billboards, mass digital ads.
Below the line (BTL)
Promotion the business controls directly, often targeted: sales promotions, direct mail, email, sponsorship, PR, trade shows, personal selling.
Through the line (TTL)
An integrated campaign combining ATL and BTL to reach the mass market and convert individuals.
Social media marketing
Using social platforms (paid ads, organic content, influencers, communities) to promote a brand.
Place
How and where the product reaches customers: channels, locations, logistics.
Distribution channel
The route a product takes from producer to consumer.
Intermediary
A business between producer and consumer: wholesaler, retailer, agent, platform.
Advertising
Paid communication through the media to inform and persuade customers to buy a product.
Sales promotion
A short-term incentive to encourage customers to buy, such as discounts, free samples, competitions or buy-one-get-one-free offers.
Public relations (PR)
Activities that build and protect a good image of the business with the public and the media, such as press releases and events.
Sponsorship
Paying to be associated with an event, team or person in order to promote the business's name and image.
Personal selling
Promotion through direct contact between a sales representative and the customer, used especially for expensive or complex products.
Direct marketing
Communicating directly with individual customers, for example by email, text or post, without using mass media.
Guerrilla marketing
Unconventional, low-cost promotion that uses surprise and creativity in public places to attract attention.
Business-to-business (B2B)
Selling goods or services from one business to another business.
Business-to-consumer (B2C)
Selling goods or services directly from a business to individual consumers.
Informative advertising
Advertising that gives customers facts about a product, such as its features, price or where to buy it, often used at launch.
Persuasive advertising
Advertising that tries to convince customers to buy a product by appealing to their emotions or showing it as better than rivals.

Above, below and through the line AO2

Cost

StrengthsIt builds awareness and brand image quickly.
  • It drives action, especially purchase.
  • Results are easy to measure.
  • It builds relationships.
Weaknesses
  • It is hard to measure.
  • Much of it is wasted on people outside the target market.
  • Many people avoid adverts.
  • Its reach is limited.
  • Frequent promotions can cheapen the brand.
  • The effect is often short-term.

Through the line: e.g. a TV advert for an oat drink (ATL) with a QR code for recipes and a discount voucher, plus free tastings in coffee shops (BTL). The combination builds awareness and converts it into sales; the challenge is coordinating the message and budget.

Social media marketing AO3

Advantages

  • Social media lets a firm target people precisely by age, interests and location.
  • It is cheap to start, and the budget can be scaled up or down.
  • It allows two-way engagement, so the firm gets feedback and can build a community.
  • Results are measurable through clicks, conversions and engagement.
  • Content can go viral, and customers create their own content, such as recipe videos.
  • Influencers can give recommendations that followers trust.

Disadvantages

  • Negative comments and crises spread fast.
  • Platforms change their algorithms, and the number of people who see unpaid posts tends to fall.
  • It needs a constant supply of fresh content and skilled staff.
  • Influencers may not be authentic, and they must disclose when they are paid.
  • Feeds are crowded and people's attention spans are short.
  • Firms must follow data-privacy rules such as the GDPR.
Evaluating social media (AO3)It works best when the target market uses the platform heavily (young adults on Instagram, TikTok and YouTube), the product is visual (latte art, bold packaging), and the firm can produce consistent content. It is weaker for older or B2B markets, and should be combined with other channels for reach and credibility.
Key points
  • Influencer marketing pays well-known users to recommend products. It builds trust fast, but fake-seeming posts backfire, and paid posts must be labelled.

Own web shop: small orders are costly to deliver

Supermarkets, once demand was proven

ChannelAdvantagesDisadvantagesOatly example
Zero-level (direct, incl. own e-commerce)
  • The firm keeps the full margin and control.
  • It collects customer data.
  • Logistics are costly.
  • Reach is limited.
Oatly's own web shop finds small orders costly to deliver.
One-level (via retailers)
  • Retailers give wide reach.
  • Retailers run the stores.
  • Retailers take a margin and have power over suppliers.
  • The producer controls the display less.
Oatly moved into supermarkets once demand was proven, when supermarkets then wanted to stock it.
Two-level (wholesaler → retailer)
  • It reaches many small shops.
  • The wholesaler holds stock.
  • Two margins are taken.
  • Control is weaker and feedback is slower.
Oatly first sold its Barista Edition to independent coffee shops through coffee wholesalers.
Agents / platforms
  • Agents bring local market knowledge.
  • Entry is quick.
  • They charge commission.
  • The firm depends on them.
Oatly uses local distributors when it enters a new country.

Choosing a channel

  • The type of product matters, for example whether it is perishable, bulky or technical.
  • The firm must consider who the target market is and where they shop.
  • Each channel has a different cost and leaves the firm a different margin.
  • Some channels give the firm more control over its brand and service than others.
  • The firm should consider which channels its competitors use.
  • When selling abroad, legal and logistics factors also matter.

Why place matters

  • A good product fails if customers cannot find it.
  • Place shapes the brand image: the same product looks different in a premium deli and in a discount store.
  • Convenience is a key part of the value customers receive.
  • Customers now expect to buy both online and in store, which is called omnichannel retailing.
The case in brief: Oatly
  • Niche channel first: it sold to coffee shops, where baristas wanted milk that foamed.
  • Pull into mass retail: supermarkets then wanted it.
  • Promotion trade-off: provocative ads win attention but divide opinion.

Exam corner: 4.5 promotion and place

Exam tips

  • Match the promotion to the target market and to the objective, which may be raising awareness or increasing sales.
  • Use the case, for example by explaining why Oatly started in coffee shops rather than supermarkets.
  • For distribution channels, weigh reach against control and margin.

Common pitfalls

  • Don't call all online promotion below-the-line. Mass online display advertising can be above-the-line, while targeted email is below-the-line.
  • Don't recommend TV advertising for a tiny niche market with a small budget.
  • Don't ignore whether the product is perishable when choosing channels.

Model answer

AO3 Evaluate social media marketing as a strategy for Oatly when it enters a new country. [10]

E Social media fits Oatly's target market of young, urban consumers, who share food and coffee content on Instagram and TikTok. Its bold packaging and humour are made to be photographed, and paid targeting reaches people interested in plant-based food rather than everyone. Results are measurable, so spending can move to the best-performing content. E However, social media alone may not build enough awareness where the brand is unknown, and provocative messages can backfire: Oatly's Super Bowl advert divided opinion. Trial matters more for a new taste, which is why putting the product in coffee shops, where people could try it in a drink they already buy, was so effective. Ev Overall, social media is a strong part of the mix for a visual, youth-focused brand, but it works best combined with sampling through coffee shops and, later, in-store promotion. It depends on the firm keeping a consistent voice and on local tastes: humour that works in Sweden may not work everywhere.

Practice questions (tap to reveal the marking points)

AO2 Distinguish between above-the-line and below-the-line promotion. [4]
ATL: paid mass media, wide reach (2). BTL: targeted, firm-controlled methods (2). Examples and contrast.
AO3 Recommend a distribution channel for Oatly when it enters a new country. [10]
Compare coffee shops (trial, credibility with baristas, small volumes), supermarket listing (reach, retailer power, needs existing demand), online direct, local distributor. Margin, reach, control. Justified choice, e.g. coffee shops first.
4.5

The seven Ps: people, processes, physical evidence and the mix

Real company case
Starbucks (USA): when the process breaks the experience

Starbucks calls its stores a "third place" between home and work, so the service experience is the product. Its app's Mobile Order & Pay became hugely popular, but by 2024 waiting orders were piling up, baristas were overloaded, and customers in the shop faced long queues: a process problem that damaged the people part of the mix.

Under chief executive Brian Niccol, appointed in 2024, the "Back to Starbucks" plan set out to fix this: changes to how orders are sequenced, more staff at busy times, and physical evidence of a coffee house again, such as ceramic mugs for customers staying in and handwritten notes on cups.

Apply it: Explain how one of the extended Ps can damage another, using Starbucks.

Read more: Starbucks (Wikipedia)

Practice firm for the worked answers · made-up numbers

Sea View Hotels is opening a boutique hotel in a coastal resort for couples aged 30–55. Online reviews of its existing hotels praise the rooms but criticise slow check-in and inconsistent staff friendliness. The new hotel will charge 30% more than its other hotels.

Syllabus map

Syllabus pointHighest AOYou must be able to
People, processes, physical evidenceAO3Evaluate how each affects customer experience and competitiveness
Appropriate marketing mixesAO3Recommend a consistent 7P mix for a named product

Why services need extra Ps

Feature of servicesMeaningWhich P addresses it
IntangibleCannot be seen or tried before purchasePhysical evidence (reviews, décor, website)
InseparableProduced and consumed at the same time, with staff presentPeople
Variable (heterogeneous)Quality depends on who delivers it and whenProcesses and people (training, standards)

Feature of servicesMeaningWhich P addresses it
IntangibleCustomers cannot see or try a service before they buy it.Physical evidence, such as reviews, décor and the website, reassures them.
InseparableThe service is produced and consumed at the same time, with staff present.People matter most.
Variable (heterogeneous)Quality depends on who delivers the service and when.Processes and people, through training and standards, keep it consistent.
PerishableA service cannot be stored: an empty room tonight is revenue lost for ever.Processes, such as booking systems and dynamic pricing, fill capacity.

People, processes and physical evidence AO3

People

Everyone who interacts with customers.

  • Recruit staff for their attitude, not only their skills.
  • Train staff and empower them to solve customers' problems.
  • Motivate and reward staff (2.4).
  • Pay attention to staff appearance and uniforms.

Sea View: inconsistent friendliness damages a premium brand; train and empower staff.

Processes

The systems and steps used to deliver the service.

  • Processes include booking, checking in, paying and handling complaints.
  • Good processes are fast, reliable and consistent.
  • Technology, such as apps and self-service, can improve processes.

Sea View: mobile check-in and pre-arrival preferences to fix slow check-in.

Physical evidence

Tangible cues that signal quality.

  • Physical evidence includes the building, its décor, its cleanliness and staff uniforms.
  • It also includes the website, brochures and packaging.
  • Online reviews, ratings and awards are physical evidence too.

Sea View: design and reviews must justify a 30% price premium.

Common mistake
  • Don't apply the extra three Ps (people, processes and physical evidence) only to services. They matter for goods too, as Apple's stores, packaging and delivery process show, but they are essential for services.
The case in brief: Starbucks
  • Brand promise: a third place.
  • Process problem: orders piled up and baristas were overloaded.
  • Fix the Ps together: more staff (people) and ceramic mugs and handwritten notes (physical evidence).

Exam corner: 4.5 service Ps and the mix

Exam tips

  • Use evidence from reviews or complaints in the case.
  • Check for consistency: a premium price needs premium people, processes and physical evidence.
  • Prioritise: say which P matters most for this firm and why.

Common pitfalls

  • Don't list all seven Ps without linking them to each other and to the case.
  • Don't give generic answers such as "train staff" without saying what training, for whom and why.
  • Don't ignore the cost of improving people and processes.

Model answer

AO3 Discuss the importance of people and processes for Sea View's new boutique hotel. [10]

App Reviews criticise slow check-in and inconsistent friendliness, and the new hotel will charge 30% more. E Hotel services are inseparable and variable, so staff behaviour directly shapes the guest's experience. Recruiting for warmth, training and empowering staff to solve problems would raise consistency and justify premium prices. Processes such as mobile check-in remove the most common complaint and free staff to focus on personal service. E These changes cost money (training, technology) and take time to show results in reviews, while competitors may already offer similar features. Ev People and processes are the most important Ps here, because guests can only judge an intangible service by how it is delivered, and reviews (physical evidence) depend on them. Without improving them, the 30% premium is unlikely to be sustained.

4.6

International marketing

HL
Real company case
IKEA in India (2018): adapt or fail

IKEA opened its first Indian store, in Hyderabad, in 2018, after India allowed foreign single-brand retailers to own their Indian business outright if they sourced a share of products locally (30% for most firms). IKEA had studied Indian homes for years. It adapted products for smaller flats and Indian cooking, priced around a thousand items very cheaply for price-conscious shoppers, and its restaurant served biryani alongside meatballs made from chicken or vegetables, not beef or pork.

Other firms entered India differently: McDonald's through local franchise partners, and Starbucks through a joint venture with Tata (1.5). Walmart shows the cost of not adapting: it left Germany in 2006 after struggling with local shopping habits, labour rules and strong discount rivals.

Read more: IKEA (Wikipedia) · Walmart (Wikipedia)

Syllabus map

Syllabus pointHighest AOYou must be able to
Methods of entry (useful extra: not a separate syllabus point)—Use entry methods to explain how a firm could reduce the threats of entering a market
Opportunities and threats of international marketsAO3Weigh opportunities and threats for a named firm

Key terms AO1

International marketing
Marketing goods or services in more than one country.
Exporting
Selling goods produced in the home country to customers abroad, directly or via agents.
Licensing
Allowing a foreign firm to produce or sell your product or use your IP in return for royalties.
Foreign direct investment (FDI)
Setting up or buying operations abroad (subsidiary, factory, acquisition).
Standardisation
Using the same marketing mix in every country.
Adaptation (glocalisation)
Changing parts of the mix to suit local tastes, culture, law and income ("think global, act local").
Direct investment
Setting up or buying production or sales operations in another country, giving the business full control.
Cultural differences
Differences between countries in language, values, customs, religion and tastes that affect how products are used and marketed.
Embargo
A government ban on trade with a particular country or in a particular product.

Opportunities and threats AO3

Opportunities

  • Selling abroad opens a larger market, which allows sales to grow when the home market is saturated.
  • Higher output brings economies of scale.
  • Selling in several economies spreads risk.
  • A new market can extend the life cycle of a mature product.
  • The firm may gain access to cheaper resources or new ideas.
  • Being an international firm adds prestige to the brand.

Threats

  • Cultural and language differences can lead the firm to misread local tastes.
  • Laws and regulations differ, for example on labelling, local sourcing and food safety.
  • Changes in exchange rates can cut the value of foreign earnings.
  • Political instability and trade barriers, such as tariffs and quotas, add risk.
  • Distance makes logistics harder, especially for perishable goods.
  • Local competitors may be strong, and the firm may lack knowledge of the market.

Methods of entry (useful extra)

The guide only lists the opportunities and threats of entering and operating in international markets. Entry methods are not a separate syllabus point, but they are the clearest way to show how a firm could cut those threats, so use them inside your evaluation.

  • May create a future competitor

The firm needs its own sales effort and logistics.

  • Agents bring local knowledge.
  • Little investment is needed.
  • Agents take commission.
  • The firm has less control and contact with customers.
Licensing / franchisingControl is low to medium.Cost and risk are low.
  • Entry is fast.

  • The local partner bears the investment.

  • A licensee may become a competitor.
Joint ventureControl is shared.Cost and risk are medium.

Trade-off to rememberMore control = more cost and risk. Firms often start with low-risk exporting, then move to joint ventures or subsidiaries once demand is proven.

Standardise or adapt?

Standardisation

  • Standardisation brings economies of scale in production and promotion.
  • It keeps the global brand consistent.
  • It fails if tastes, laws or incomes differ too much between countries.

Adaptation

  • Adaptation fits the product to local culture and law: IKEA's restaurants in India serve no beef or pork, for example.
  • Adapted products appeal more to local customers.
  • Adaptation raises costs and risks diluting the global brand.

Use Hofstede's dimensions (2.5 and the HL toolkit) to anticipate cultural differences in communication, decision-making and consumer behaviour.

The case in brief: IKEA in India
  • Research first: it studied Indian homes for years before opening in 2018.
  • Glocalisation: products for smaller flats and Indian cooking and very low prices on many items, with local sourcing.
  • Contrast: Walmart left Germany in 2006.

Exam corner: 4.6

Exam tips

  • For each method of entering a market, weigh control against risk and cost.
  • Use facts from the case, such as certification, logistics and a partner's offer.
  • Recommend a staged approach where it makes sense.

Common pitfalls

  • Don't just write that "the culture is different". Say which difference matters and how it affects the product or promotion.
  • Don't ignore the legal requirements given in the case.
  • Don't confuse licensing with franchising. Franchising includes the whole business format, not just the right to use a brand or a patent.

Model answer

AO3 Evaluate IKEA's decision to enter India through its own wholly owned stores. [10]

E Owning its stores gave IKEA full control of the store experience, prices and brand, which matter for a retailer whose format is its advantage, and it keeps all the profit. However, it carried the whole cost and risk of large stores in an unfamiliar market, and had to meet the 30% local-sourcing rule by building an Indian supplier base. E A joint venture, as Starbucks used with Tata, would have brought local knowledge and shared risk, but also shared profit and control. Franchising, as McDonald's uses, needs little capital but relies on partners to protect quality. Ev Overall, wholly owned stores suited IKEA because it had the money, years of research and a format it did not want to dilute, and the law had changed to allow it. The choice was only sound because IKEA adapted products, prices and food to local culture. For a smaller firm with less capital or knowledge, a joint venture or exporting through an agent would be the safer first step.

AO3 Evaluate licensing as a way to enter a foreign market. [10]

Unit 5 · Operations management
5.1

The role of operations management

Real company case
Greggs (UK): operations behind 2,000 shops

Greggs, the UK's largest bakery chain, runs well over 2,000 shops. Most products are made in its own central bakeries and delivered to shops, where they are baked or finished through the day. Its operations team forecasts demand shop by shop, because too little stock loses sales and too much is wasted. Unsold food goes to charities, to cut-price Greggs Outlet shops or to the Too Good To Go app. When its vegan sausage roll launched in 2019, demand was so strong that production had to be raised quickly.

Apply it: Explain how operations management at Greggs supports its marketing and finance functions.

Read more: Greggs (Wikipedia)

Practice firm for the worked answers · made-up numbers

Sunrise Bakery Ltd bakes 6,000 loaves and pastries a day for three shops and 40 cafés. Waste of unsold bread is 9% of output, the oven runs at 70% of capacity, and café customers complain about late deliveries.

Syllabus map

Syllabus pointHighest AOYou must be able to
Role of operations managementAO2Explain how operations add value and support objectives in goods and services

Key terms AO1

Operations management
Planning, organising and controlling the processes that turn inputs into goods and services efficiently and to the required quality.
Transformation process
Converting inputs (materials, labour, capital, information) into outputs.
Efficiency
Producing output with the fewest resources (low cost per unit, little waste).
Effectiveness
Achieving the intended outcome (right quality, on time, meeting customer needs).
Productivity
Output per unit of input (per worker, per machine hour).
Sustainability
Meeting present needs without compromising future generations: economic, social and environmental.
Production
The process of turning inputs into goods or services that satisfy customers' needs and wants.

  • Sunrise uses ordering software.

Operations in goods

Tangible output can be stored, inspected before sale and produced away from customers. Focus: efficiency, stock control, quality control.

Operations in services

Output is intangible, perishable and produced with the customer present. Focus: capacity at peak times, staff and process consistency (link to 4.5 service Ps).

Operations objectives
  • Cost: a low cost per unit.
  • Quality: meeting expectations every time.
  • Speed: delivering quickly.
  • Flexibility: adapting to changes in demand.
  • Dependability: delivering on time, as promised.
The case in brief: Greggs
  • Scale: 2,000+ shops supplied by central bakeries.
  • Balance waste and lost sales: it forecasts shop by shop and sells surplus via Too Good To Go.
  • Capacity: strong demand can become the constraint.

Exam corner: 5.1

Exam tips

  • Explain how an operations decision affects cost, quality, speed and flexibility.
  • Link operations to the other business functions to earn analysis marks.

Common pitfalls

  • Don't treat operations as only manufacturing. Services, such as banks and hospitals, have operations too.
  • Don't confuse efficiency with effectiveness. Efficiency is about producing at low cost, while effectiveness is about achieving the intended outcome.

5.2

Operations methods

Real company case
Nike and Rolls-Royce: mass, customised and one-off

Nike makes most of its shoes by mass production in contract factories, using flow and batch methods to keep the cost per pair low. Since 1999 it has also offered mass customisation, now called Nike By You: customers choose colours and materials online for certain models, and the shoes are made to order at a higher price. At the other extreme, Rolls-Royce uses job production: each car is built largely by hand to the buyer's own specification.

Apply it: Explain why Nike can charge more for Nike By You shoes, and one operational problem this creates.

Read more: Mass customization (Wikipedia)

Practice firm for the worked answers · made-up numbers

Cedar Furniture makes hand-crafted dining tables to order (8 weeks each, average price $3,200). Demand for a standard oak table from hotels has grown to 1,500 a year. The owner is considering batch production of the standard table, a flow line, or an online configurator letting customers choose size, finish and legs (mass customisation).

Syllabus map

Syllabus pointHighest AOYou must be able to
Job, batch, mass/flow production, mass customisationAO3Evaluate which method suits a product, market and business, and the effects of changing method

Key terms AO1

Job production
Making a single, unique product to a customer's specification.
Batch production
Making a group of identical products together. Each batch moves through every stage before the next batch starts.
Mass / flow production
Continuous production of large volumes of standardised products along a production line.
Mass customisation
Combining the low unit costs of mass production with individual customisation, usually through flexible technology and modular components.
Labour-intensive vs capital-intensive
Relying mainly on workers vs mainly on machinery and technology.
Cell production
A way of organising production in which the line is split into self-contained teams, or cells, each responsible for a complete unit of work and its quality.

Common mistakes
  • Don't write that flow production is always best because its unit costs are lowest. It only pays when demand is large and stable and the firm has the capital to invest in a production line.
  • Don't confuse mass customisation with job production. Mass customisation assembles standard modules in many combinations at scale, whereas job production makes one-off products to order.
The case in brief: Nike and Rolls-Royce
  • Mass production: Nike uses contract factories for low cost per pair.
  • Mass customisation: design-your-own shoes at a higher price.
  • Job production: Rolls-Royce cars are built by hand to order.

Exam corner: 5.2

Exam tips

  • Use the demand figures and the price to judge what volume the firm needs to produce.
  • Consider how a change of method affects staff, through resistance (2.1) and motivation (2.4), and how it affects costs, through break-even.

Common pitfalls

  • Don't forget the effect of the production method on the brand and on quality.
  • Don't ignore the cost and time of switching from one method to another.

Model answer

AO3 Recommend a production method for Cedar Furniture's standard hotel table. [10]

E Batch production suits 1,500 tables a year: jigs and machines can cut components for 50 tables at once, lowering unit cost and lead time compared with 8-week job production, while craftspeople still finish each table. Investment is moderate. E Flow production would give the lowest unit cost, but 1,500 units a year is too small to justify a continuous line, and it would undermine the "hand-crafted" brand. E Mass customisation through an online configurator could open a new consumer market, but requires CNC investment and complex logistics. Ev Cedar should use batch production for the hotel table while keeping job production for bespoke orders. Mass customisation could follow later if consumer demand is proven. Staff should be involved in redesigning work to avoid resistance and loss of craft motivation.
