5.3

Lean production and quality management

HL
Real company case
Toyota and Boeing: lean done well, quality gone wrong

Toyota developed the Toyota Production System, the model for lean production. Parts arrive just in time, so little stock is held; any worker can pull the andon cord to stop the line when they see a problem; and teams keep making small improvements (kaizen). Lean has risks: after the 2011 earthquake in Japan cut off parts supplies, Toyota's output fell sharply.

Quality failures are costly. In January 2024 a door panel blew out of a new Boeing 737 MAX 9 during an Alaska Airlines flight. Regulators capped Boeing's production while it fixed its quality checks, and customers waited longer for planes.

Apply it: Explain how the andon cord is an example of quality assurance, not quality control.

Read more: Toyota Production System (Wikipedia)

Practice firm for the worked answers · made-up numbers

Cedar Furniture (from 5.2) has 6% of tables returned for defects, holds $180,000 of timber stock, and workers wait an average of 40 minutes a day for parts. A large hotel group will only buy from suppliers with ISO 9001 certification.

Syllabus map

Syllabus pointHighest AOYou must be able to
Features of lean productionAO1Describe its aims and features
  • Kaizen, JIT
  • Cradle to cradle
  • QC vs QA
  • Quality circles, benchmarking, TQM
  • Quality standards
AO2Explain each method and its benefits and problems
Impact of lean production and TQMAO3Evaluate the effects on a named organisation

Key terms AO1

Lean production
An approach that aims to minimise all forms of waste while maximising value to the customer.
Kaizen
Continuous, small, incremental improvements suggested and made by all employees.
Just-in-time (JIT)
Inputs arrive exactly when needed and output is produced to order, minimising stock.
Cradle to cradle
Design and manufacturing in which materials are reused or safely returned to nature at the end of a product's life, so there is no waste.
Quality control (QC)
Inspecting finished products (or samples) to detect defects.
Quality assurance (QA)
Building quality into every stage of the process to prevent defects.
Quality circle
A small group of workers meeting regularly to identify and solve quality problems.
Benchmarking
Comparing performance and processes with the best in the industry to find improvements.
Total quality management (TQM)
An organisation-wide culture in which everyone is responsible for quality and customer satisfaction.
Kanban
A lean production system that uses cards or signals to show when more parts or materials are needed, so production is pulled by demand.
Andon
A system that allows any worker to signal a problem and stop the production line, so faults are fixed immediately.
Cradle to grave
A linear production model in which products are made, used and then thrown away at the end of their life.
Defect
A product that does not meet the required quality standard.
Zero defects
The aim of producing goods with no faults at all, by building quality into every stage.
Inspection
Checking products at the end of production, or at stages during it, to find and remove faults.

Lean production AO1AO2

Transport and motionTimber moved across the workshop several times
Excess stock$180,000 of timber stored

Defects6% of tables returned
Type of waste (useful extra)Cedar example
Over-productionCedar makes tables before customers order them.

Excess stockCedar stores $180,000 of timber.

Kaizen

  • In kaizen, many small, low-cost improvements add up to a large gain over time.
  • Kaizen uses workers' knowledge, and empowering them in this way motivates them.
  • However, kaizen needs a supportive culture, the gains slow down over time, and it may not deliver the radical change a firm sometimes needs.

JIT

  • Just-in-time frees cash that would be tied up in stock, and it cuts storage costs and waste.
  • Holding little stock exposes inefficiencies that a large buffer would hide.
  • However, JIT leaves the firm vulnerable to disruption in supply. It needs reliable suppliers and accurate forecasts, and the firm loses bulk-buying discounts.

Cradle to cradle design AO2

Instead of "cradle to grave" (make, use, throw away), products are designed so materials go back into new products (technical cycle) or safely biodegrade (biological cycle). Cedar could use untreated, certified timber and water-based finishes so old tables can be refurbished or composted. Benefits: sustainability image, less raw-material cost long term, regulatory readiness. Problems: redesign cost, sourcing, take-back logistics. Links to circular business models (toolkit).

National and international quality standards AO2

Standards such as ISO 9001 (quality management systems), ISO 14001 (environmental management) or national marks (e.g. the EU CE marking for product safety) certify that a firm follows recognised processes.

Importance

  • Quality standards give customers and buyers confidence, and many business customers, such as the hotel group in the case, require them.
  • They give the firm access to international markets.
  • Meeting the standard improves the firm's internal processes.
  • Certification can be used in marketing as a mark of quality.

Drawbacks

  • Certification and audits cost money.
  • They create paperwork and bureaucracy.
  • A standard certifies the process, not that every product is perfect.

The case in brief: Toyota and Boeing

Exam corner: 5.3

Exam tips

  • Name the type of waste in the case, then the lean method that removes it.
  • Evaluate whether the culture and the suppliers' reliability are good enough for the method to succeed.
  • Link lean production to resistance to change (2.1) and empowerment (2.4).

Common pitfalls

  • Don't confuse quality control with quality assurance. Quality control inspects products after they are made, while quality assurance builds quality into every stage of the process.
  • Don't say that JIT means holding no stock at all. Firms using JIT keep very low stock, delivered just before it is needed.
  • Don't assume that an ISO certificate guarantees perfect products.

Model answer

AO3 Discuss the impact of introducing TQM at Cedar Furniture. [10]

E TQM would make every worker responsible for quality, building checks into each stage rather than relying on final inspection. This should reduce the 6% return rate, cutting rework costs and protecting the brand, and would support the ISO 9001 certification the hotel group demands. E Craft workers already take pride in their work, so quality circles could harness their knowledge and raise motivation. However, TQM requires training, new procedures and management commitment over years, and some staff may see it as extra paperwork. Ev The impact is likely to be strongly positive because quality problems are costing Cedar sales and a major contract depends on certification. Success depends on leadership involving staff from the start and on measuring results such as the return rate.

5.4

Location

Real company case
Zara (Spain): paying more to be close

Inditex, owner of Zara, makes a large share of its clothes in countries close to its Spanish headquarters, such as Spain, Portugal, Morocco and Turkey, even though wages in Asia are lower. Being close lets it deliver new styles to shops within weeks and restock twice a week, so it makes small batches and reacts to what sells. Many rivals source mainly from Asia: cheaper per item, but slower. Other firms are relocating too: Apple has moved a growing share of iPhone assembly from China to India.

Apply it: Explain one benefit and one cost for Zara of producing close to its main markets.

Read more: Zara (Wikipedia)

Practice firm for the worked answers · made-up numbers

Northline Apparel makes clothing in a small factory in southern Europe. Labour costs are rising. It is considering offshoring production to Bangladesh, outsourcing to a contract manufacturer in Portugal, or bringing its outsourced design work back in-house. Customers increasingly want fast delivery and transparent supply chains.

Syllabus map

Key terms AO1

Outsourcing / subcontracting
Paying an external firm to carry out an activity previously done in-house (can be in the same country).
Offshoring
Moving an activity to another country, either to the firm's own operations or to an external supplier.
Insourcing
Bringing a previously outsourced activity back inside the business.
Reshoring
Bringing production that was offshored back to the home country.
Near-shoring (extra)
Moving production to a nearby country (e.g. Portugal or Morocco for a Spanish firm).
Industrial inertia
When a business stays in a location even though the original reasons for choosing it no longer apply, because moving would be costly.
Clustering
When businesses in the same industry locate close to each other to share skilled labour, suppliers, ideas and customers.

Trends to use in evaluationRecent supply-chain disruptions, rising wages in some offshoring destinations, automation and demand for sustainability have led many firms to reshore or near-shore. Cost is only one factor; resilience, speed and reputation matter more than they did.
The case in brief: Zara and Apple
  • Speed over cost: Zara produces near Spain despite cheaper wages in Asia, so it can restock twice a week.
  • Rivals' trade-off: cheaper per item, but slower.
  • Reducing risk: Apple is shifting production from China to India.

Exam corner: 5.4

Exam tips

  • Distinguish clearly between outsourcing and offshoring. Outsourcing is about who does the work, while offshoring is about where it is done.
  • Weigh the cost savings against speed, quality, ethics and risk.
  • Link location decisions to stakeholders (1.4), CSR (1.3) and multinationals (1.6).

Common pitfalls

  • Don't use outsourcing and offshoring as if they meant the same thing.
  • Don't recommend offshoring only because wages are lower.
  • Don't ignore the ethical promises the brand has made.

Model answer

AO3 Recommend whether Northline Apparel should offshore production to Bangladesh or outsource it to Portugal. [10]

E Offshoring to Bangladesh would cut labour costs sharply, helping margins that fell 18%. However, longer lead times conflict with customers' demand for fast delivery, and weaker supply-chain transparency could contradict Northline's mission of fashion "made fairly", risking greenwashing accusations. E Outsourcing to a Portuguese contract manufacturer (near-shoring) costs more than Bangladesh but less than producing at home, delivers to EU customers within days, and operates under EU labour and environmental law, making transparency easier to prove. Northline would have less direct control than owning a factory, so it needs strict contracts and audits. Ev Portugal is the better option: the weighted score (7.3 vs 5.8) and the brand's ethical positioning favour it. The cost saving from Bangladesh would be offset by slower delivery and reputational risk. This recommendation depends on securing a reliable partner and agreed quality standards.

Practice questions (tap to reveal the marking points)

AO2 Distinguish between outsourcing and offshoring. [4]
Outsourcing: external firm does the work, can be domestic. Offshoring: activity moved abroad, own or external. Contrast.
AO3 Evaluate reshoring for a European electronics firm. [10]
Resilience, speed, quality, brand vs labour cost, investment, skills. Judgement with conditions.
5.5

Break-even analysis

Real company case
Ryanair (Ireland): break-even at 30,000 feet

Airlines live by break-even analysis. Most costs of a flight, such as the aircraft, crew and airport charges, are fixed once the flight is scheduled, so each extra passenger adds almost pure contribution. Airlines track their break-even load factor: the share of seats they must fill to cover costs. Ryanair keeps its cost per seat very low and fills over 90% of its seats, which is why it can sell some tickets very cheaply and still make a profit.

Apply it: Explain why an airline may sell its last empty seats at a very low price.

Read more: Ryanair (Wikipedia)

Practice firm for the worked answers · made-up numbers

Lumo Lamps makes designer desk lamps. Fixed costs are $4,000 a month; variable cost is $6 per lamp; the price is $10. It currently sells 1,400 lamps a month and has capacity for 1,600.

Syllabus map

Syllabus pointHighest AOYou must be able to
Total contribution vs contribution per unitAO2Distinguish and calculate
Break-even chart: BEP, profit/loss, margin of safety, target profit output, target profit, target priceAO2AO4
  • Draw, label and read a chart
  • Calculate all elements
Effects of changes in price or costAO2AO4Show the effect graphically and numerically
Benefits and limitationsAO3Evaluate usefulness for a named decision

Key terms AO1

Contribution per unit
Selling price − variable cost per unit: what each unit contributes to fixed costs and then profit.
Total contribution
Contribution per unit × quantity sold (or total revenue − total variable cost).
Break-even point (BEP)
The output at which total revenue equals total cost: no profit, no loss.
Margin of safety
The amount by which actual (or planned) output exceeds break-even output.
Target profit output
The output needed to earn a chosen level of profit.
Target price
The price needed to reach a target profit at a given output.
Break-even revenue
The sales revenue at which total revenue equals total costs; break-even quantity multiplied by price.

Formulas and worked example AO4

Contribution per unit = price − variable cost per unitLEARN IT
Total contribution = contribution per unit × quantityLEARN IT
Break-even quantity = fixed costs ÷ contribution per unitLEARN IT
Profit = total contribution − fixed costsLEARN IT
Margin of safety = actual output − break-even outputLEARN IT
Target profit output = (fixed costs + target profit) ÷ contribution per unitLEARN IT
Target price = (fixed costs + target profit) ÷ quantity + variable cost per unitLEARN IT
Lumo LampsWorkingAnswer
Contribution per unit10 − 6$4
Break-even quantity4,000 ÷ 41,000 lamps
Break-even revenue1,000 × 10$10,000
Total contribution at 1,4004 × 1,400$5,600
Profit at 1,4005,600 − 4,000$1,600
Margin of safety1,400 − 1,000400 lamps (28.6% of sales)
Output for $2,000 profit(4,000 + 2,000) ÷ 41,500 lamps
Price for $2,000 profit at 1,400 lamps(4,000 + 2,000) ÷ 1,400 + 6$10.29
The case in brief: Ryanair
  • Mostly fixed costs: costs are fixed once a flight is scheduled.
  • Contribution: each extra passenger is almost pure contribution.
  • Margin of safety: it fills over 90% of seats, well above the break-even load factor, so it can sell some tickets very cheaply.

The break-even chart AO4

Drawing checklist

1
Axes: x = output (units); y = costs and revenue ($). Title the chart.
2
FC: horizontal line at $4,000.
3
TC: starts at the FC intercept (0, 4,000); plot one more point, e.g. (1,600, 13,600).
4
TR: starts at the origin; plot (1,600, 16,000).
5
Label: BEP with both coordinates; profit and loss areas; margin of safety bracket; profit at current output.

Effects of changes in price or cost AO2AO4

ChangeEffect on chartContributionBEPMargin of safety at 1,400
Price ↑ to $12TR steeper$6667 units ↓733 ↑ (if sales hold)
Price ↓ to $9TR flatter$31,334 units ↑66 ↓
Variable cost ↑ to $7TC steeper$31,334 units ↑66 ↓
Fixed costs ↑ to $5,000FC and TC shift up$41,250 units ↑150 ↓

Remember: a price rise may reduce sales if demand is elastic (4.5 PED), so the actual margin of safety depends on how customers react.

Benefits and limitations AO3

Benefits

  • Break-even analysis is simple and visual, and it allows quick "what if" analysis.
  • The margin of safety shows how much risk the firm faces.
  • It supports decisions about price, costs and output.
  • It is useful in a business plan to persuade lenders.

Limitations

  • It assumes that all output is sold.
  • It assumes the lines are straight, so it ignores bulk discounts and assumes the price stays the same at every level of sales.
  • Fixed costs may rise in steps at higher output, for example when a second machine is needed.
  • It is hard to apply to firms that sell many products, because fixed costs must be shared between them.
  • It is based on estimates and shows a single point in time.

Exam corner: 5.5

Exam tips

  • In every calculation, write the formula, substitute the figures and give the answer with units.
  • Round the break-even quantity up to the next whole unit, because a firm cannot sell 0.3 of a lamp.
  • When asked about a change, show both the new line on the chart and the new figures.

Common pitfalls

  • Don't start the total cost line at the origin. It starts at the level of fixed costs.
  • Don't confuse contribution with profit. Contribution must first cover fixed costs before any profit is made.
  • Don't give the margin of safety in dollars when the question asks for units, or the other way round.
  • Don't forget that a change in price affects demand.

Model answer

AO3 Evaluate the usefulness of break-even analysis for Lumo Lamps' decision to raise its price to $12. [10]

App At $12, contribution rises from $4 to $6, and break-even falls from 1,000 to 667 lamps. E Break-even analysis quickly shows the decision lowers risk: Lumo needs far fewer sales to cover its $4,000 fixed costs. If it still sold 1,400 lamps, profit would rise from $1,600 to $4,400. E However, the analysis assumes all 1,400 lamps are still sold. A 20% price rise for designer lamps with close substitutes could cut sales sharply; if sales fell below 934 lamps, profit would be lower than the current $1,600 (6 × 933 − 4,000 = $1,598). It also ignores rivals' reactions and possible changes in costs. Ev Break-even is useful as a first step to show the financial effect, but Lumo must combine it with market research or PED estimates before deciding. If demand is price inelastic thanks to the brand, the rise is worthwhile.

AO4 Using the same data, calculate the output needed for $6,000 profit. [2]

5.6

Production planning

HL
Real company case
Toyota and Peloton: how much stock is enough?

After the 2011 earthquake in Japan, Toyota, the pioneer of just-in-time, mapped its suppliers' suppliers and asked them to hold months of extra stock of critical parts such as computer chips. When a global chip shortage hit in 2021, Toyota kept producing for longer than most rivals.

By contrast, exercise-bike maker Peloton built far more stock than it could sell when demand fell after the pandemic boom, and paused production of some products in 2022.

Apply it: Explain why buffer stock helped Toyota in 2021 but hurt Peloton in 2022.

Read more: Peloton (Wikipedia)

Practice firm for the worked answers · made-up numbers

Lumo Lamps (from 5.5) uses 100 lamp bases a day. Its supplier takes 3 days to deliver. It keeps a buffer of 200 bases and a maximum of 800. Last month it made 1,400 lamps with 8 workers and $70,000 of capital; capacity is 2,000 lamps; 42 were defective. A supplier offers finished shades at $2.10 each; making them in-house costs $1.60 variable cost plus $600 a month of extra fixed costs that would be avoided.

Syllabus map

Syllabus pointHighest AOYou must be able to
Local and global supply chainAO2Explain stages and risks
JIT vs JICAO3Evaluate which suits a firm
Stock control chartsAO2AO4
  • Draw, label, interpret
  • Calculate reorder level
Capacity utilisation, defect rate, productivity, operating leverageAO2AO4Calculate and interpret
Cost to buy vs cost to makeAO3AO4Calculate and evaluate including qualitative factors

Key terms AO1

Supply chain
All the stages and organisations involved in getting a product from raw materials to the final customer.
Just-in-case (JIC)
Holding buffer stock to cope with unexpected demand or supply delays.
Lead time
Time between placing an order and receiving it.
Buffer stock
The minimum stock held for emergencies.
Reorder level
The stock level at which a new order is placed.
Reorder quantity
The amount ordered each time.
Capacity utilisation
Actual output as a percentage of maximum possible output.
Productivity
Output per unit of input (labour or capital).
Operating leverage
The sensitivity of profit to changes in sales, depending on the share of fixed costs in total costs.
Production planning
Planning what to produce, how much, when and with which resources, so that output matches demand at the lowest cost.
Local supply chain
A supply chain in which suppliers are located close to the business.
Global supply chain
A supply chain in which suppliers are located in different countries around the world.
Stock-out
A situation in which a business runs out of stock and cannot meet demand.

Local and global supply chains AO2

Raw materials→Component suppliers→Manufacturer→Distributors→Retailers→Customers

Global supply chains

  • Global supply chains offer lower costs, specialist suppliers and economies of scale.
  • However, they have long lead times and are exposed to disruption from ports, conflicts and pandemics. Exchange rates add risk, ethical problems are harder to see, and transport adds emissions.

Local supply chains

  • Local supply chains are faster and more flexible, quality is easier to control, emissions are lower, and they help the firm's local reputation.
  • However, local supply often costs more, and there are fewer suppliers to choose from.

JIT vs JIC AO3

Just-in-timeJust-in-case
Stock heldMinimalBuffer stock
BenefitsLess cash tied up, lower storage, less waste and obsolescence
  • Can meet sudden demand
  • Protects against supply shocks
  • Bulk discounts
Drawbacks
  • Vulnerable to delays
  • Needs reliable suppliers and accurate forecasts
  • Frequent orders
  • Storage costs
  • Cash tied up
  • Waste and obsolescence
SuitsStable demand, reliable local suppliers, perishable goodsUnpredictable demand or supply, critical items, long lead times
Just-in-timeJust-in-case
Stock heldThe firm holds very little stock.The firm holds buffer stock.
Benefits
  • Less cash is tied up.
  • Storage costs are lower.
  • Less stock is wasted or becomes obsolete.
  • The firm can meet sudden demand.
  • It is protected against supply shocks.
  • It can win bulk discounts.
Drawbacks
  • Any delay can stop production.
  • It needs reliable suppliers and accurate forecasts.
  • Orders must be frequent.
  • Storage costs money.
  • Cash is tied up.
  • Stock may be wasted or go out of date.
SuitsIt suits stable demand, reliable local suppliers and perishable goods.It suits unpredictable demand or supply, critical items and long lead times.
The case in brief: Toyota and Peloton
  • Buffer stock pays off: Toyota held extra critical parts, so in the chip shortage it kept producing longer.
  • Too much stock: Peloton had far more than it could sell and paused production.
  • Best answer: JIT for cheap parts, and buffer stock for critical ones.

Stock control chart AO4

Reorder level = (usage per day × lead time in days) + buffer stockLEARN IT
Reorder quantity = maximum stock − buffer stock (when delivery arrives exactly at buffer level)LEARN IT

Lumo: reorder level = 100 × 3 + 200 = 500; reorder quantity = 800 − 200 = 600. If lead time rose to 5 days, the reorder level would rise to 700.

Capacity, quality and productivity measures AO4

MeasureFormulaLumoInterpretation
Capacity utilisation rate ON THE SHEETactual output ÷ productive capacity × 1001,400 ÷ 2,000 × 100 = 70%
  • Spare capacity: fixed costs spread over fewer units
  • Room to grow
Defect rate LEARN ITdefective units ÷ total output × 10042 ÷ 1,400 × 100 = 3%
  • Compare with targets and rivals
  • Costs of rework and reputation
Labour productivity LEARN ITtotal output ÷ number of workers (or hours)1,400 ÷ 8 = 175 lamps per workerRaise with training, motivation, better equipment
Capital productivity LEARN ITtotal output ÷ capital input1,400 ÷ 70,000 = 0.02 lamps per $How efficiently machinery is used
Productivity rate ON THE SHEETtotal output ÷ total input × 100e.g. output worth $90,000 from inputs of $75,000 = 120%Rising rate = more efficient

High capacity utilisation

Low unit costs, but no room for extra orders, staff stress, maintenance problems. Around 85–90% is often considered efficient.

Low capacity utilisation

High unit costs; options: rent out space, take contribution-priced orders, rationalise capacity, increase marketing.

Operating leverage AO2AO4

Operating leverage = total contribution ÷ (total contribution − fixed costs) = Q(P − VC) ÷ [Q(P − VC) − FC]LEARN IT
Worked example: Lumo Lamps at 1,400 lamps

Total contribution = 1,400 × ($10 − $6) = $5,600. Operating profit = 5,600 − 4,000 = $1,600. Operating leverage = 5,600 ÷ 1,600 = 3.5.

Meaning: each 1% change in sales changes operating profit by about 3.5%. Check: a 10% rise to 1,540 lamps gives contribution $6,160 and profit $2,160, which is 35% higher. A 10% fall would cut profit by 35% too.

Firms with a high proportion of fixed costs (airlines, software, hotels) have high operating leverage: once fixed costs are covered, extra sales add a lot of profit, but a fall in sales causes a large fall in profit. Firms with mainly variable costs (outsourced manufacturing) have low operating leverage and more stable profits. Link to break-even: high fixed costs mean a higher BEP.

Cost to make vs cost to buy AO3AO4

Cost to make (CTM) = (variable cost per unit × quantity) + fixed costs of makingLEARN IT
Cost to buy (CTB) = supplier price per unit × quantityLEARN IT
Worked example: 1,400 shades a month

CTM = 1.60 × 1,400 + 600 = 2,240 + 600 = $2,840. CTB = 2.10 × 1,400 = $2,940. Making saves $100 a month. Break-even quantity between options: 600 ÷ (2.10 − 1.60) = 1,200 shades; above 1,200, making is cheaper.

Reasons to make

  • Making a component in-house gives the firm control over its quality and design, and it protects its intellectual property.
  • It uses spare capacity: the factory in the case works at only 70% of capacity.
  • Supply is more reliable when the firm controls it.

Reasons to buy

  • Buying in uses the supplier's expertise and economies of scale.
  • It is more flexible and lowers the firm's fixed costs.
  • It lets the firm focus on its core activities.

Exam corner: 5.6

Exam tips

  • Label all five elements of a stock-control chart, and keep the usage line at a constant slope.
  • Always interpret a calculated measure against a benchmark.
  • In make-or-buy decisions, include qualitative factors as well as the figures.

Common pitfalls

  • Don't forget to include buffer stock in the reorder level.
  • Don't include fixed costs that would be paid anyway in the cost to make.
  • Don't say that 100% capacity utilisation is always ideal. It leaves no room for extra orders or maintenance, and it puts staff under strain.

5.7

Crisis management and contingency planning

HL
Real company case
CrowdStrike and Delta (2024): one update, 8.5 million crashes

On 19 July 2024 the cyber-security firm CrowdStrike sent out a faulty software update. About 8.5 million Windows computers crashed, grounding flights and disrupting banks, broadcasters and hospitals worldwide. CrowdStrike's chief executive apologised publicly and a fix was issued within hours, but many machines had to be repaired one by one.

Some organisations recovered within a day. Delta Air Lines took far longer: it cancelled about 7,000 flights over several days as its crew-scheduling system struggled to recover, and said the outage cost it about $500 million. Much of the difference came down to contingency planning: backup systems, practised recovery steps and clear roles.

Apply it: Distinguish between CrowdStrike's crisis management and the contingency planning its customers needed.

Read more: 2024 CrowdStrike-related IT outages (Wikipedia)

Practice firm for the worked answers · made-up numbers

Sunrise Bakery Ltd discovers that a batch of sandwiches sold to 40 cafés may contain undeclared sesame, a serious allergen. Social media posts are already spreading. Sunrise has no written recall plan; its owners are on holiday.

Syllabus map

Syllabus pointHighest AOYou must be able to

Key terms AO1

Crisis
An unexpected event that threatens the business's operations, reputation, people or finances.
Crisis management
The reactive process of responding to a crisis once it happens to limit damage.
Contingency planning
The proactive process of identifying possible crises and preparing responses in advance.
Business continuity
Keeping essential operations running during and after a disruption.
Risk assessment
Identifying possible hazards, judging how likely and serious they are, and deciding how to reduce them.

Crisis management vs contingency planning AO2

Contingency planningCrisis management
TimingBefore the crisisDuring and after the crisis
NatureProactive, planningReactive, response
ActivitiesRisk assessment, scenarios, plans, roles, training, drillsContainment, communication, decisions, recovery, review
ExampleA written product-recall procedure with contactsRecalling the sandwiches today
Contingency planningCrisis management
TimingIt happens before a crisis.It happens during and after a crisis.
NatureIt is proactive planning.It is a reactive response.
ActivitiesIt includes risk assessment, scenarios, written plans, roles, training and drills.It includes containing the damage, communicating, deciding, recovering and reviewing.
ExampleA written product-recall procedure lists who to contact.The firm recalls the sandwiches today.

Typical crises: product recalls, cyber-attacks and data breaches, fires and natural disasters, supply failures, key-person loss, fraud or ethical scandals, pandemics.

Appoint a crisis lead immediately, even with owners away

Sunrise publicly admits the labelling error and explains what it is doing.
CommunicationClear, consistent messages must reach every stakeholder through the right channels.
  • Sunrise calls all 40 cafés.

  • It informs the food authority.

Impact of contingency planning AO3

Impact areaBenefitsCosts / drawbacks
CostReduces the cost of crises: faster recovery, fewer lost sales, lower fines
  • Planning, training, backups, insurance cost money
  • May never be used

Impact areaBenefitsCosts / drawbacks
CostCrises cost less, because recovery is faster, fewer sales are lost and fines are lower.
  • Planning, training, backups and insurance cost money.
  • The plan may never be used.

The case in brief: CrowdStrike outage
  • Crisis: a faulty update crashed 8.5 million computers.
  • Crisis management: it apologised and fixed it within hours.
  • Contingency planning: Delta cancelled 7,000 flights at a cost of about $500 million, while firms with backups and practised plans recovered faster.

Exam corner: 5.7

Exam tips

  • Use the four factors of crisis management (transparency, communication, speed and control) to structure answers about a crisis.
  • Name the stakeholders and the channels the firm should use to communicate with them.
  • Weigh the cost of contingency planning against the probability and the impact of the crisis.

Common pitfalls

  • Don't mix up contingency planning, which is proactive and done in advance, with crisis management, which is reactive and done once the crisis happens.
  • Don't recommend staying silent to protect the firm's reputation. Silence usually makes a crisis worse.

Model answer

AO3 Discuss whether Sunrise Bakery should invest in contingency planning after this crisis. [10]

E Without a recall plan, Sunrise lost time finding café contacts and deciding who was in charge while its owners were away, increasing the risk to allergic customers and to its reputation. A contingency plan with named roles, contact lists and pre-written messages would make the next response faster and more controlled. E The costs are management time, staff training and possibly insurance, which matter for a small firm. Plans cannot foresee every crisis, so they need regular review. Ev Sunrise should invest, because food-safety crises are likely in its industry and potentially catastrophic (illness, legal action, loss of all café contracts). A simple, regularly tested plan for recalls, allergens and supply failure offers high benefit for modest cost.

5.8

Research and development

HL
Real company case
Kodak (USA): inventing the future, then ignoring it

In 1975 Steve Sasson, an engineer at Kodak, built the first digital camera. Kodak patented much of the technology but was slow to build a business on it, because its profits came from selling film, which digital cameras would replace. Rivals such as Canon and Sony, and later smartphones, took the market. Kodak filed for bankruptcy protection in 2012 and sold many of its patents.

R&D alone is not enough: a firm must be willing to let new products replace its old ones. Apple did this when the iPhone took over much of the iPod's market.

Apply it: Explain why owning patents did not protect Kodak.

Read more: Kodak (Wikipedia)

Practice firm for the worked answers · made-up numbers

Lumo Lamps spends 2% of revenue on R&D. A competitor has launched app-controlled lamps that adjust light to the user's sleep cycle. Lumo's engineers have developed a new low-energy LED module that could be patented, but the project would need $400,000 more over two years.

Syllabus map

Syllabus pointHighest AOYou must be able to
Importance of R&DAO3Evaluate whether a firm should invest in R&D
Unmet customer needsAO2Explain how firms identify and meet them
Intellectual property: copyright, patents, trademarksAO2Explain each and why protection matters
Incremental and disruptive innovationAO2Distinguish with examples

Key terms AO1

Research and development (R&D)
Investigating new ideas and turning them into new or improved products and processes.
Invention
Creating a new idea or device for the first time.
Innovation
Successfully bringing a new idea to market as a product, service or process.
Unmet need
A customer need that existing products do not yet satisfy. Customers may or may not be aware of it, and when they are not, it is called a latent need.
Patent
Legal right to stop others making, using or selling an invention for a set period (usually 20 years) in exchange for public disclosure.
Copyright
Automatic protection of original creative works (software, text, music, designs) from copying.
Trademark
A registered sign (name, logo, slogan) identifying a firm's goods or services.
Incremental innovation
Small improvements to existing products or processes.
Disruptive innovation
An innovation that creates a new market or business model and displaces established firms.

Importance of R&D AO3

Benefits

  • R&D creates new products to replace those that are in decline in their life cycle.
  • It gives the firm a competitive advantage and USPs, which can justify premium prices.
  • Process innovation lowers costs.
  • Patents create barriers to entry and can earn licensing income.
  • R&D helps the firm respond to pressure from sustainability concerns and new laws.

Costs and risks

  • R&D is expensive, it takes a long time to pay back, and many projects fail.
  • Demand for the new product is uncertain, and competitors may launch first.
  • It diverts cash from other uses.
  • Shareholders may prefer dividends now.
Judging R&D spendingIt depends on the industry's speed of change (tech vs basic goods), the firm's finance, competitors' activity, the firm's strategy (leader or follower) and the chance of protecting the result with IP.

Meeting unmet needs AO2

Customers often can't describe a need until they see the solution (few people asked for smartphones before 2007). Firms uncover unmet needs through observation, data analytics (5.9), customer feedback, ethnographic research and experimentation. Meeting them can create entirely new markets and first-mover advantage, but carries the risk of no real demand.

The case in brief: Kodak
  • Invention is not enough: it built the first digital camera.
  • Fear of cannibalisation: profits came from film, so it was slow to act.
  • Result: bankruptcy in 2012.
  • Contrast: when the iPhone threatened the iPod, Apple went ahead anyway.

Exam corner: 5.8

Exam tips

  • Distinguish invention, which is creating something new, from innovation, which is turning it into a product or process that is used.
  • Link R&D to the product life cycle, the BCG matrix and investment appraisal.
  • Choose the right type of intellectual property protection for the asset described.

Common pitfalls

  • Don't say that copyright protects inventions. Inventions are protected by patents, while copyright protects creative works such as text, music and software code.
  • Don't call every new product disruptive. Most innovation is incremental.

Model answer

AO3 Discuss whether Lumo should invest $400,000 to complete its LED project. [10]

E Completing the project could give Lumo a patented, low-energy module that rivals cannot copy for years, creating a USP, lowering energy costs for customers and possibly earning licensing income. It responds to sustainability trends and protects Lumo against the competitor's innovation. E However, $400,000 over two years is large relative to 2% R&D spending, and the competitor's app-controlled lamps suggest customers may value smart features more than efficiency. The project is incremental innovation; it may not answer a disruptive shift towards connected, health-focused lighting. Ev Lumo should invest if investment appraisal (payback, NPV) shows acceptable returns and the patent is secure, but should combine the module with smart features, perhaps through a partnership, so that it competes on what customers increasingly want.

Practice questions (tap to reveal the marking points)

AO2 Distinguish between incremental and disruptive innovation. [4]
Small improvements vs market-changing; risk; examples; contrast.
AO2 Explain why a business would register a trademark. [4]
Protects brand identity; prevents copying and confusion; adds asset value; supports licensing/franchising.
5.9

Management information systems (MIS)

HL
Real company case
Tesco Clubcard, M&S and Amazon: the power and risk of data

Tesco launched its Clubcard loyalty scheme in 1995 and uses the data, through its analytics business dunnhumby, to learn what customers buy, personalise offers and plan stock. Since 2020, lower "Clubcard Prices" push most shoppers to scan their card on every visit.

Data brings risks. A cyber-attack on Marks & Spencer in 2025 stopped its online orders for about seven weeks, exposed some customers' personal data and cost about £300 million. Monitoring staff is sensitive too: in 2024 France's data regulator fined Amazon €32 million for over-intrusive tracking of warehouse workers (2.4).

Apply it: Explain one benefit to Tesco and one concern for customers of the Clubcard scheme.

Read more: Tesco Clubcard (Wikipedia)

Practice firm for the worked answers · made-up numbers

FreshMart, a regional supermarket chain with 30 stores, plans to launch a loyalty app that tracks every purchase, uses AI to personalise offers and predict demand, and installs IoT sensors in fridges. It also wants software to monitor warehouse pickers' speed minute by minute. Last year a competitor suffered a data breach exposing 200,000 customers' details.

Syllabus pointHighest AOYou must be able to

Key terms AO1

Management information system (MIS)
A system that collects, stores and processes data to give managers information for decisions.
Data analytics
Examining data to find patterns, trends and insights.
Database
An organised collection of structured data that can be searched and updated.
Cybersecurity
Protecting systems, networks and data from attacks and unauthorised access.
Cybercrime
Crime using computers or the internet: hacking, phishing, ransomware, data theft, fraud.
Big data
Very large, fast-changing and varied data sets that need advanced tools to analyse.
Data mining
Using software to discover hidden patterns and relationships in large data sets.
Digital Taylorism
Using technology to monitor, measure and control employees' work in fine detail.
Machine learning
A form of artificial intelligence in which computer systems improve their performance by learning from data, without being explicitly programmed.
Critical infrastructure
Physical and digital systems that are essential for a business or society to function, such as power, communications and payment networks.
Algorithm
A set of step-by-step rules followed by a computer to solve a problem or make a decision.
Employee surveillance
The monitoring of employees' activities using technology, such as tracking computer use, location or productivity.

Benefits, risks and ethics of MIS AO3

Benefits for decision-making

  • Data lets managers make faster, evidence-based decisions, which links to scientific decision-making (2.3).
  • It improves forecasting and reduces waste (5.6).
  • It allows personalised marketing, which raises sales.
  • Managers can monitor quality and operations in real time.

Risks

  • Cyber-attacks and data breaches can lead to fines under the GDPR and damage the firm's reputation.
  • The systems, and the skilled staff to run them, are expensive.
  • Firms can rely too much on data, and poor data leads to poor decisions.
  • Algorithms can be biased.
  • Automation can lead to job losses.
StakeholderEthical issue
CustomersPrivacy, consent, profiling, manipulation through personalised pricing
EmployeesSurveillance, stress, job security, fairness of algorithmic decisions
Society and governmentData security, monopoly power, environmental cost of data centres
StakeholderEthical issue
CustomersPrivacy, consent, profiling and manipulation through personalised pricing raise concerns.
EmployeesSurveillance, stress, job security and the fairness of decisions made by algorithms raise concerns.
Society and governmentData security, monopoly power and the environmental cost of data centres raise concerns.
The case in brief: Tesco and others
  • Benefits of data: Clubcard data helps personalise offers and plan stock, and Clubcard Prices reward sharing it.
  • Cybersecurity risk: an attack stopped online orders for seven weeks and cost about £300 million.
  • Ethics: Amazon was fined €32 million for monitoring staff.

Exam corner: 5.9

Exam tips

  • Evaluate each technology with a benefit, a risk and the stakeholder it affects.
  • Link digital Taylorism to Taylor's scientific management and to motivation theory.
  • Mention the legal context, such as data-protection law, as a constraint.

Common pitfalls

  • Don't describe a technology without explaining how the business would use it.
  • Don't ignore ethical issues in "evaluate" questions.

Model answer

AO3 Evaluate FreshMart's plan to monitor warehouse pickers minute by minute. [10]

K Digital Taylorism uses technology to measure and control work in detail, extending Taylor's scientific management. E Monitoring could reveal bottlenecks, improve picking speed and support fair performance pay, lowering costs in a competitive industry. E However, constant surveillance removes autonomy and trust, which Herzberg and Deci and Ryan link to demotivation; stress and turnover may rise, and recruitment costs could cancel the efficiency gains. Monitoring must also comply with data-protection rules on employee data. Ev FreshMart should use aggregated data to improve processes and layouts rather than tracking individuals minute by minute, and involve staff in setting targets. This captures most of the efficiency benefit while protecting morale and its reputation as an employer.

Business management toolkit
Toolkit

Business management toolkit: SL and HL tools

All toolkit tools are assessed at AO2 and AO4 alongside the content: you may be asked to construct, complete, apply or interpret them, and to use them to support AO3 judgements. SL and HL: SWOT, Ansoff matrix, STEEPLE, BCG matrix, business plan, decision trees, descriptive statistics, circular business models.

How tools earn marksExaminers reward tools that are applied to the case and used to reach a conclusion. A SWOT copied from the stimulus without analysis earns little; one whose points are weighed and linked to a recommendation earns AO2, AO3 and AO4 marks.

SWOT analysis

HelpfulHarmful
Internal (the firm controls)Strengths: brand, skills, patents, finance, locationWeaknesses: high costs, poor cash flow, skills gaps
External (the environment)Opportunities: growing markets, new technology, trade dealsThreats: competitors, recession, regulation, changing tastes
HelpfulHarmful
Internal (the firm controls)Strengths are internal and helpful, such as a strong brand, skills, patents, finance or a good location.Weaknesses are internal and harmful, such as high costs, poor cash flow or skills gaps.
External (the environment)Opportunities are external and helpful, such as growing markets, new technology or trade deals.Threats are external and harmful, such as competitors, recession, regulation or changing tastes.
Using it well
  • Match strengths to opportunities (SO strategies).
  • Use strengths to counter threats.
  • Fix the weaknesses that block opportunities.
Limitations
  • It is subjective: different people list different factors.
  • It is a snapshot of one moment.
  • It lists factors without priorities.
  • Some items could fit more than one box.

Using it well
  • Place the option on the matrix.
  • State its level of risk.
  • Explain where the risk comes from, using evidence from the case.

Limitations
  • Risk depends on the firm's own capabilities, not only on the quadrant.

Using it well
  • Select the two or three factors that matter most for the decision.

Limitations
  • The analysis can turn into a long list.
  • Factors change quickly.

BCG matrix

The BCG matrix plots a firm's products by market growth and relative market share (see 4.5 product).

What to do with each
  • Stars: invest to keep the lead.
  • Cash cows: harvest the cash, which funds the stars and question marks.
  • Question marks: invest selectively, or sell them.
  • Dogs: drop them unless they are strategic.
Limitations
  • It uses only two variables.
  • The result depends on how the market is defined.
  • It ignores profitability and the links between products.

Uses

Limitations
  • It is based on forecasts.

  • Founders tend to be over-optimistic.

Decision trees

Expected value = Σ (probability × financial outcome); net gain = expected value − costLEARN IT
Workings

Multiply each outcome by its probability and write the result at the end of the branch.

Working
  • Project X: 0.6 × 150 = 90 and 0.4 × 40 = 16, so the expected value is 106. The net gain is 106 − 50 = $56k.
  • Project Y: 0.7 × 90 = 63 and 0.3 × 20 = 6, so the expected value is 69. The net gain is 69 − 30 = $39k.

Choose Project X, and cross out the rejected branch with two short lines. Squares are decision nodes and circles are chance nodes. The probabilities at each chance node must add up to 1.

Strengths

  • A decision tree sets out the options, risks and outcomes clearly.
  • It puts a number on risk and encourages logical thinking.

Limitations

  • The probabilities and payoffs are only estimates.
  • Expected value is an average, so it ignores how much risk the firm is willing to take: option A has a 40% chance of a $10,000 loss, for example.
  • It ignores qualitative factors.

The same seven weeks as a box plot. The box covers the middle half of the weeks, from Q1 to Q3, and the line inside it is the median. The mean (20) sits to the right of the median (18) because the outlier of 38 pulls it up, which is why the median is the better measure of a typical week here.

Charts and infographics: bar charts (comparisons), pie charts (shares of a whole), line graphs (trends), infographics (communicating to non-specialists). Watch for misleading axes and averages that hide variation.

ModelMeaningExample
Circular supplyRenewable, recycled or biodegradable inputs replace new materials.H&M Group uses recycled fibres (1.3).
Resource recoveryFirms recover useful resources from waste or by-products.Breweries sell spent grain as animal feed.
Product life extensionFirms repair, upgrade, refurbish and resell products.
  • Firms sell refurbished phones.
  • Firms offer repair services.
Sharing platformsFirms increase the use of assets that would otherwise sit idle.Car-sharing and tool libraries work this way.
Product as a serviceCustomers pay for use, while the firm keeps ownership and responsibility.A firm leases lighting "per lux" instead of selling lamps.
Benefits
  • It lowers material costs and waste.
  • It creates new revenue streams.
  • It builds customer loyalty.
  • It prepares the firm for new regulations.
Challenges
  • Redesigning products and logistics costs money.
  • Customers must accept the model.
  • Recovered materials may be of lower quality.
The five circular models in the guide
  • Circular supply: renewable, recycled or biodegradable inputs.
  • Resource recovery: collecting used products to recover their materials.
  • Product life extension: products built to last, with repair and refurbishment.
  • Sharing model: many people use one product, as with car-sharing.
  • Product service system: selling the use of a product as a service.

Common pitfalls

  • Don't put external factors among the strengths and weaknesses in a SWOT analysis. Strengths and weaknesses are internal.
  • In a decision tree, check that the probabilities at each chance node add up to 1.
  • Don't use the mean when an outlier makes the median a better average.

Toolkit

Business management toolkit: HL-only tools

HL

HL only, assessed at AO2 and AO4: force field analysis, Gantt chart, Hofstede's cultural dimensions, Porter's generic strategies, contribution (make or buy, contribution costing, absorption costing), critical path analysis, simple linear regression

Gantt chart

A Gantt chart shows tasks as horizontal bars against time, with their start and finish dates, durations, overlaps and progress (the "today" line).

Uses
  • Managers can plan and monitor projects.
  • It helps them allocate resources.
  • It communicates deadlines clearly.
Limitations
  • The links between tasks are less clear than in critical path analysis.
  • It becomes cluttered for large projects.
  • It does not show float precisely.
  • It needs regular updating.

Porter's generic strategies

Lower cost advantage
Differentiation advantage
Broad target
COST LEADERSHIPLowest cost in the industry; price at or below rivals; economies of scale, lean, efficiency (e.g. Ryanair, Lidl)
DIFFERENTIATIONUnique features valued industry-wide; premium price; brand, quality, innovation (e.g. Apple)
Narrow target
COST FOCUSLowest cost within a niche (e.g. a budget student hostel)
DIFFERENTIATION FOCUSUnique offer for a niche (e.g. a craft kombucha brand)
Using it well
  • Identify the firm's current strategy from the case.
  • Judge whether its operations, marketing mix and HR support that strategy.
  • Watch for firms that are "stuck in the middle": neither the cheapest nor clearly different (Porter's warning).
Limitations
  • Some firms succeed with hybrid strategies.
  • Rivals can copy a competitive advantage.
  • The model simplifies complex markets.

Contribution: make or buy, contribution costing, absorption costing

ToolHow it worksUse
Make or buyCompare cost to make (variable costs + avoidable fixed costs) with cost to buyOutsourcing decisions (see 5.6)
Contribution costing
  • Judge products or orders by their contribution (price − variable cost)
  • Fixed costs are not allocated
  • Accept special orders if price > variable cost and capacity is spare
  • Keep products with positive contribution
Absorption (full) costingAllocate all overheads to products on a chosen basis (e.g. floor space, labour hours, % of sales)
  • Full-cost pricing
  • Judging long-run profitability of each product
ToolHow it worksUse
Make or buyCompare the cost of making an item (variable costs plus avoidable fixed costs) with the cost of buying it.It supports outsourcing decisions (see 5.6).
Contribution costing
  • Judge products or orders by their contribution, which is price minus variable cost.
  • Fixed costs are not allocated.
  • Accept a special order if its price is above variable cost and there is spare capacity.
  • Keep products that make a positive contribution.
Absorption (full) costingAllocate all overheads to products on a chosen basis, such as floor space, labour hours or share of sales.
  • It supports full-cost pricing.
  • It shows each product's long-run profitability.
Worked example: three product lines, overheads $30,000
LampsShadesBulbsTotal
Revenue60,00025,00015,000100,000
Variable costs30,00015,00011,00056,000
Contribution30,00010,0004,00044,000
Overheads absorbed by % of revenue18,0007,5004,50030,000
Profit / loss12,0002,500(500)14,000

Under absorption costing, bulbs show a $500 loss. But they make a positive contribution of $4,000; if dropped, the $4,500 of overheads would remain and total profit would fall to $10,000. Contribution costing shows bulbs should be kept (unless the capacity could earn more elsewhere).

Contribution costing

  • Contribution costing avoids sharing out overheads in an arbitrary way.
  • It is good for short-term decisions and special orders.
  • However, fixed costs must still be covered overall, and there is a risk of setting prices too low.

Absorption costing

  • Absorption costing makes sure that every product's price covers its share of all costs.
  • However, the basis for sharing out overheads is arbitrary, and it can lead to wrong decisions to drop products.

Critical path analysis (CPA)

ConceptRule
Earliest start time (EST)
  • Forward pass: EST of next node = EST of previous node + duration
  • Where activities merge, take the highest
Latest finish time (LFT)
  • Backward pass: LFT of previous node = LFT of next node − duration
  • Where activities split, take the lowest
Total floatLFT (end node) − duration − EST (start node)
Free floatEST (end node) − duration − EST (start node): how long an activity can be delayed without delaying the next activity
Critical path
  • Activities with zero total float
  • Their total duration is the minimum project time
Dummy activityDotted line with zero duration that shows a dependency without using resources
ConceptRule
Earliest start time (EST)
  • In the forward pass, the EST of the next node is the EST of the previous node plus the duration.
  • Where activities merge, take the highest value.
Latest finish time (LFT)
  • In the backward pass, the LFT of the previous node is the LFT of the next node minus the duration.
  • Where activities split, take the lowest value.
Total floatTotal float is the LFT of the end node minus the duration minus the EST of the start node.
Free floatFree float is the EST of the end node minus the duration minus the EST of the start node: how long an activity can be delayed without delaying the next one.
Critical path
  • The critical path is made of activities with zero total float.
  • Their total duration is the shortest possible project time.
Dummy activityA dummy activity is a dotted line with zero duration that shows a dependency without using resources.
ActivityDurationDepends onEST (start node)EST (end node)LFT (end node)Total floatFree float
A3—0333 − 3 − 0 = 03 − 3 − 0 = 0
B4A3777 − 4 − 3 = 07 − 4 − 3 = 0
C2A3777 − 2 − 3 = 27 − 2 − 3 = 2
D5B, C7121212 − 5 − 7 = 012 − 5 − 7 = 0

Total vs free float: total float uses the LFT of the end node (delay without delaying the whole project); free float uses the EST of the end node (delay without delaying the next activity). Here C has 2 days of both, because it feeds straight into D. They differ when one non-critical activity is followed by another: using up the first one's free float is safe, but using its total float eats into the next activity's slack.

Note: the guide expects you to complete and analyse a network, calculate the total and free float, and identify the critical path. You are not expected to draw a network from scratch.

Benefits
  • It shows the minimum time for the project.
  • It shows which activities are critical.
  • It shows where resources can be moved.
  • It supports just-in-time ordering.
Limitations
  • It depends on accurate estimates of durations.
  • It becomes complex for large projects.
  • It does not guarantee that the project finishes on time.

Force field analysis HL

Force field analysis lists the driving forces pushing for a change and the restraining forces against it, and gives each a weight, usually from 1 to 5. If the drivers' total is higher, the change is likely to succeed. If not, managers should strengthen the drivers or weaken the biggest restrainers.

Limitations
  • The weights are subjective.
  • Some forces can be missed.
How to draw one
  • Write the change in the middle.
  • List the driving forces on one side and the restraining forces on the other.
  • Score each force from 1 (weak) to 5 (strong), and back each score with a fact from the case.
  • Total each side, then decide: go ahead, don't, or weaken the biggest restraining forces first.
Worked example: hybrid working in an office

The driving forces total 11 and the restraining forces total 8, so the net score is +3. The firm should go ahead, but it should deal with the restraining forces at the same time: train managers to lead remote teams, fix in-office days for teamwork, and invest in secure IT systems.

What to write under any force field(1) State both totals. (2) Say which side is stronger. (3) Name the single strongest force. (4) Recommend weakening the restraining forces first, because pushing harder on the drivers often increases resistance. (5) Say that the scores are subjective, so the decision depends on who scored them.

Hofstede's cultural dimensions HL

Hofstede's model compares national cultures on six dimensions.

The six dimensions
  • Power distance: how far people accept that power is shared unequally.
  • Individualism vs collectivism: whether people look after themselves or belong to close groups.
  • Masculinity vs femininity: whether a culture values competition and achievement, or care and quality of life.
  • Uncertainty avoidance: how uncomfortable people are with risk and ambiguity.
  • Long-term vs short-term orientation: whether people focus on future rewards or on the past and present.
  • Indulgence vs restraint: how freely people satisfy their wish to enjoy life.

Firms use it when they enter a new country, merge with a foreign firm or manage international teams.

Limitations
  • National averages hide differences between individuals and regions.
  • The original data is old: it came from IBM staff in the 1960s and 1970s.

Hofstede's published scores for two countries, from 0 to 100. Compare the size of the gaps rather than the exact numbers.

Worked example: a UK clothing retailer opening stores in Japan
  • Uncertainty avoidance (92 against 35): staff and partners are likely to expect clear rules, detailed plans and careful contracts, so the launch should be planned thoroughly rather than tested and changed as it goes.
  • Long-term orientation (88 against 51): suppliers and landlords may value long relationships, so the retailer should not expect quick returns.
  • Individualism (46 against 89): team bonuses and group recognition may motivate staff better than individual commission.
  • Power distance (54 against 35): staff may expect more direction from managers and a clearer hierarchy.
  • Indulgence (42 against 69): advertising that stresses quality and value may work better than advertising about fun and treats.

In an exam answer, pick the two or three dimensions with the biggest gaps and link each one to a decision about leadership, rewards, marketing or how a change is introduced. Then add the limitation: a national average does not describe every person or every region.

Simple linear regression HL

Simple linear regression is a way to forecast from past data.

Steps
  • Plot the data on a scatter diagram.
  • Draw the line of best fit through the points.
  • Extend the line to predict future values, which is called extrapolation.

Correlation describes how closely two variables move together. It can be positive, negative or absent.

Limitations
  • Correlation does not prove that one thing causes the other.
  • Extrapolation assumes that the past pattern continues.
Worked example: advertising and sales

Advertising spend is the independent variable, so it goes on the x-axis: the firm chooses it. Sales are the dependent variable, so they go on the y-axis: they respond to the advertising. The points lie close to a rising line, so there is a strong positive correlation (r = 0.99). Extending the line to $60k of advertising gives a forecast of about $119k of sales.

That forecast is extrapolation beyond the highest value in the data ($45k), so it is less reliable. The correlation also does not prove that advertising causes the extra sales: a growing market or a new product could explain both.

Exam corner: HL toolkit

Exam tips

  • In critical path analysis, work forwards to find the earliest start times and backwards to find the latest finish times, then calculate the total float and free float for each activity.
  • In contribution questions, base the decision on contribution, then mention fixed costs and capacity.
  • For Porter's generic strategies, name the strategy and test whether the marketing mix supports it.

Common pitfalls

  • In critical path analysis, don't take the lowest earliest start time where activities merge, or the highest latest finish time where they split. Take the highest and the lowest respectively.
  • Don't drop a product that makes a loss under absorption costing if it still makes a positive contribution.
  • Don't treat Gantt charts and critical path analysis as the same thing. A Gantt chart shows when activities happen, while CPA shows which activities are critical and how much float the others have.

Practice questions (tap to reveal the marking points)

AO4 Calculate the total float of an activity with duration 4, start-node EST 6 and end-node LFT 13. [1]
13 − 4 − 6 = 3 days.
AO4 A hotel can sell 50 spare rooms to a tour operator at $40 a night; variable cost $25 a room. Should it accept? [3]
Contribution $15 × 50 = $750 a night (2); accept if rooms are genuinely spare and it won't undercut regular guests (1).
AO2 Using Porter, explain the risk of being "stuck in the middle". [4]
Neither lowest cost nor clearly differentiated; loses price-sensitive and quality-seeking customers; lower margins; example.

How the study modes work

Learn moves each card through four levels: New, Learning, Familiar and Mastered. Multiple choice takes a card up to Familiar; typing the answer correctly makes it Mastered; a wrong answer drops it back to Learning.

Match races the clock, Memory hides the tiles, Gravity makes you type the answer before the card lands, and Blitz is 60 seconds of true or false. Calc drill generates new Paper 2 calculations at three difficulty levels.
